question:
You are counseling the family of a 15-year-old female with a BMI of 38 and type II diabetes on the surgical options for weight loss. 

Of the following bariatric procedures, which is most likely to produce adverse malabsorptive nutritional sequelae?
rationale: A duodenal switch is a primarily malabsorptive procedure: biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch results in significant nutritional abnormalities including deficiencies in vitamins A, B12, D, E and K, iron and protein. RYGB may produce similar effects, though not typically to the same degree. LAGB and LSG are primarily restrictive procedures.

###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: You are counseling the family of a 15-year-old female with a BMI of 38 and type II diabetes on the surgical options for weight loss. 

Of the following bariatric procedures, which is most likely to produce adverse malabsorptive nutritional sequelae?


###Options:
A.  Laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding (LAGB)
B.  Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB)
C.  laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG)
D.  biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch (BPDS)

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D.  biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch (BPDS)

Rationale:
• Adjustable gastric banding (LAGB) and sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) are purely restrictive procedures; they do not bypass intestine, so they rarely cause clinically significant malabsorption.  
• Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) creates a 75–150 cm Roux limb, producing some selective malabsorption (iron, calcium, vitamin B12), but most nutrients are still absorbed in the remaining small bowel.  
• Biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch (BPDS) bypasses the greatest length of small intestine, separating the biliopancreatic secretions from ingested food until a very short common channel (≈50–100 cm). This markedly limits absorption of protein, fat, fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), iron, calcium, zinc, etc., and therefore carries the highest rate of nutritional deficiencies and related complications.  

Thus, BPDS is the bariatric procedure most likely to produce adverse malabsorptive nutritional sequelae.

question:
A 14-year-old male is being assessed for weight loss surgery.

Which of the following is an indication for surgical management?
rationale: Diabetes and obstructive sleep apnea are considered sever co-morbidities. Hypertension is considered a less severe co-morbidity.

###Question: A 14-year-old male is being assessed for weight loss surgery.

Which of the following is an indication for surgical management?


###Options:
A.  BMI 32 and Type II diabetes
B.  BMI 37 and obstructive sleep apnea
C.  BMI 37 and hypertension
D.  BMI 46 and no identifiable co-morbidities

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B.  BMI 37 and obstructive sleep apnea  

Rationale:  
For adolescents, bariatric (weight-loss) surgery is generally reserved for those who meet ALL of the following criteria:  
• Skeletal/sexual maturity nearly complete, and  
• BMI ≥35 kg/m² with at least ONE severe obesity-related comorbidity (e.g., type II diabetes mellitus, moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, severe non-alcoholic steatohepatitis),  OR  
• BMI ≥40 kg/m² with at least one obesity-related comorbidity of any grade.  

Analysis of the options:  
A. BMI 32 with diabetes – BMI threshold (<35 kg/m²) is not met.  
B. BMI 37 with moderate-to-severe OSA – BMI is ≥35 kg/m² and OSA is a major comorbidity ⇒ fulfills criteria.  
C. BMI 37 with hypertension – Hypertension alone is considered a less serious comorbidity; with BMI <40 kg/m² this does not satisfy criteria.  
D. BMI 46 without comorbidities – Even though BMI >40 kg/m², current pediatric guidelines still require at least one comorbidity.  

Therefore, option B is the only choice that meets accepted indications for bariatric surgery in a 14-year-old.

A 15-year-old female presents to a specialised adolescent unit for assessment for weight-loss surgery. Her BMI for age falls on the 90th centile. 

By definition how would you classify this patient?
rationale: The terms overweight (BMI for age and gender ≥85th percentile), obese (BMI for age and gender ≥95th percentile), and severely obese (BMI for age and gender >120% of the 95th percentile) have been used to refer to increasing grades of excess weight in children.

 A 15-year-old female presents to a specialised adolescent unit for assessment for weight-loss surgery. Her BMI for age falls on the 90th centile. 

By definition how would you classify this patient?


###Options:
A.  Obese
B.  Normal
C.  Overweight
D.  Severely obese

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Overweight

Rationale: For children and adolescents (2–19 years), weight status is determined by BMI-for-age percentiles on CDC/WHO growth charts:  
• <5th percentile = underweight  
• 5th–<85th percentile = normal (healthy) weight  
• 85th–<95th percentile = overweight  
• ≥95th percentile = obese (and “severe obesity” is usually defined as ≥120 % of the 95th percentile or BMI ≥35 kg/m²).  

Because this patient’s BMI plots at the 90th percentile—between the 85th and 95th percentiles—she is classified as overweight.

question:
Following resection of a patent urachus and bladder closure in a male infant, a transurethral catheter is lest in situ.

What is your post-operative plan for this patient?
rationale: A patent urachus requires investigation of the urinary tract to look for bladder outlet obstruction in which the urachus is functioning as a relief valve.
A: Discharge when well with catheter in situ, and follow up at 1 week for removal
B: Removal of catheter 24 to 48 hours post op and discharge if good urinary stream
C: Inpatient ultrasound and discharge if normal
D: Voiding cystourethrogram after removal of catheter at 10 to 14 days post op

###Question: Following resection of a patent urachus and bladder closure in a male infant, a transurethral catheter is lest in situ.

What is your post-operative plan for this patient?


###Options:
A.  Discharge when well with catheter in situ, and follow up at 1 week for removal
B.  Removal of catheter 24 to 48 hours post op and discharge if good urinary stream
C.  Inpatient ultrasound and discharge if normal
D.  Voiding cystourethrogram after removal of catheter at 10 to 14 days post op

###Answer:
outputs:
Answer: B.  Removal of catheter 24 to 48 hours post-op and discharge if good urinary stream  

Rationale: Excision of a patent urachus involves only a small, watertight, two-layer closure of the bladder dome. The bladder heals rapidly, and prolonged catheterisation or routine postoperative imaging is unnecessary. A short period (24–48 h) of transurethral drainage is sufficient to keep the bladder decompressed while the suture line seals. If the infant voids well after the catheter is removed and there is no fever or wound problem, he can be safely discharged. Routine ultrasound (C) or cystography (D) is not indicated, and sending the child home with a catheter for a week (A) offers no benefit and increases the risk of infection and parental management problems.

question:
A 1-week old term baby presents with clear fluid draining from t the umbilicus. At exploration, you confirm a patent urachus

What is the most correct description of the operation required for this anomaly?
rationale: Failure to adequately resect the patent urachus at dome of bladder may increase the risk of future malignancies
A: Suture ligate the patent urachus at the umbilicus
B: Ligate and divide the patent urachus at the dome of the bladder
C: Resect the entire patent urachus and ligate and divide at the dome of the bladder
D: Excision of the patent urachus, with wedge resection at dome of bladder and formal bladder repair

###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).

###Question: A 1-week old term baby presents with clear fluid draining from t the umbilicus. At exploration, you confirm a patent urachus

What is the most correct description of the operation required for this anomaly?
###Options:
A.  Suture ligate the patent urachus at the umbilicus
B.  Ligate and divide the patent urachus at the dome of the bladder
C.  Resect the entire patent urachus and ligate and divide at the dome of the bladder
D.  Excision of the patent urachus, with wedge resection at dome of bladder and formal bladder repair

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option:  
D. Excision of the patent urachus, with wedge resection at dome of bladder and formal bladder repair  

Rationale:  
A patent urachus represents a persistent epithelialized tract connecting the umbilicus to the bladder dome. Definitive treatment requires complete removal of all urachal tissue to prevent persistent leakage, infection, and later malignant transformation. Standard surgical management therefore entails (1) excising the entire urachal tract, (2) taking a cuff or wedge of bladder dome to ensure complete removal of the epithelial-lined connection, and (3) closing the bladder in two layers (formal bladder repair). Simple ligation at either end (Options A or B) or excision without wedge resection (Option C) risks leaving residual epithelium and predisposes to recurrence or complications.

question:
A 3-year-old child with no significant medical or surgical history presents with bowel obstruction and is taken to theatre for exploratory laparotomy. At laparotomy you find a loop of small intestine volved around a fibrous band which extends from the umbilicus to the jejunum. 

What is the most likely cause of this finding?
rationale: The child has no history of previous surgery making adhesive bowel obstruction unlikely. Failure of regression of a dominant omphalomesenteric artery may result in a fibrous band extending from the umbilicus to the small intestine.

###Question: A 3-year-old child with no significant medical or surgical history presents with bowel obstruction and is taken to theatre for exploratory laparotomy. At laparotomy you find a loop of small intestine volved around a fibrous band which extends from the umbilicus to the jejunum. 

What is the most likely cause of this finding?


###Options:
A.  adhesive bowel obstruction
B.  omphalomesenteric duct remnant
C.  internal hernia
D.  remnant of the omphalomesenteric artery

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. omphalomesenteric duct remnant

Rationale:
In embryonic life the mid-gut is connected to the yolk sac by the vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct. Failure of complete regression may leave a persistent fibrous cord running from the antimesenteric border of small bowel (usually ileum/jejunum) to the umbilicus. This cord can act as an axial point around which adjacent small intestine may volvulate, producing acute obstruction in a child with no previous abdominal surgery. Adhesive obstruction (A) is unusual without prior surgery or peritonitis; an internal hernia (C) would involve herniation through a mesenteric or peritoneal defect rather than a cord from umbilicus to bowel; a remnant of the omphalomesenteric artery (D) – the mesodiverticular band – runs between the mesentery and a Meckel diverticulum, not between umbilicus and bowel. Thus the findings most closely fit an omphalomesenteric duct remnant.

question:
A newborn presents with fever, tachycardia and erythema around the umbilicus. 
What is your immediate management for this child?
rationale: Based on suspicion of omphalitis. The immediate management of this condition in the absence of any clinical features of necrotizing fasciitis is admission and intravenous antibiotics. If the cellulitis progresses despite treatment, surgical exploration is warranted.

###Options:
A.  Surgical debridement
B.  Incision and drainage
C.  Intravenous antibiotics
D.  Oral antibiotics and observation

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Intravenous antibiotics

Rationale: Fever, tachycardia, and spreading erythema of the umbilicus in a neonate indicate omphalitis with systemic involvement—a surgical emergency because it can rapidly progress to sepsis and necrotizing fasciitis. The first and most critical step is to admit the infant and start broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics that cover Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci, and Gram-negative organisms. Surgical intervention (incision, drainage, or debridement) is reserved for cases that show abscess formation or necrotizing soft-tissue infection after antibiotics are initiated. Oral antibiotics and simple observation are inadequate for a potentially life-threatening neonatal infection.

question:
You are asked to review a 2-month old infant admitted to paediatrics with a severe lower respiratory tract infection. On examination you note that the umbilical cord has not yet separated.

What would your advice to the paediatrician be?
rationale: The normal time for separation of the umbilical cord after birth ranges from 3 days to 2 months. Delayed separation of the umbilical cord has been associated with heritable neutrophil mobility defects and widespread infections that are often lethal.
A: Apply daily chlorhexidine to the cord
D: Investigate for vertical transmission of HIV

###Question: You are asked to review a 2-month old infant admitted to paediatrics with a severe lower respiratory tract infection. On examination you note that the umbilical cord has not yet separated.

What would your advice to the paediatrician be?


###Options:
A.  Apply daily chlorhexidine to the cord
B.  Suture ligated the excess cord
C.  Investigate for neutrophil mobility defects
D.  Investigate for vertical transmission of HIV

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Investigate for neutrophil mobility defects

Rationale: 
Normal umbilical cords separate within 1–2 weeks after birth. Persistent attachment beyond 3–4 weeks is a classic clinical clue to disorders in which neutrophils cannot exit the bloodstream and migrate into tissues, most notably Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency (LAD). These children present early with severe bacterial or fungal infections of skin and mucosa, pneumonia, and markedly raised neutrophil counts in blood but absent pus at infection sites. Therefore the appropriate next step is to evaluate neutrophil function/adhesion (e.g., flow-cytometric assessment of CD18/CD11 integrins), not topical care of the cord, extra ligation, or testing for vertical HIV transmission.

question:
A two-week old newborn is brought to the surgical clinic with and undifferentiated lesion of the umbilicus. Prior to any investigations the parents would like to know what it could be and what it is caused by.

Which of the following options regarding variants of normal embryological structures is correctly paired?
rationale: Meckel diverticulum originates from the omphalomesenteric duct. Umbilical polyps are omphalomesenteric duct remnants. Umbilical granulomas consist of granulation tissue only. A patent urachus results from failure of the urachus to obliterate.
A: Meckel diverticulum originating from the urachus
B: Umbilical polyp originating from remnants of the omphalomesenteric duct
C: Umbilical granuloma originating from the omphalomesenteric vein
D: Patent urachus originating from the allantois

###Question: A two-week old newborn is brought to the surgical clinic with and undifferentiated lesion of the umbilicus. Prior to any investigations the parents would like to know what it could be and what it is caused by.

Which of the following options regarding variants of normal embryological structures is correctly paired?


###Options:
A.  Meckel diverticulum originating from the urachus
B.  Umbilical polyp originating from remnants of the omphalomesenteric duct
C.  Umbilical granuloma originating from the omphalomesenteric vein
D.  Patent urachus originating from the allantois

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Patent urachus – originating from persistence of the allantois  

Rationale  
• The allantois is an early embryonic structure that normally involutes to form a fibrous cord, the urachus (median umbilical ligament). Failure of this involution leaves a patent lumen, producing a patent urachus that can open at the umbilicus and leak urine.  
• Meckel diverticulum is a persistent remnant of the omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct, not the urachus (so option A is wrong).  
• An umbilical polyp contains ectopic intestinal mucosa from the omphalomesenteric duct but option B links it correctly to that duct; however, only one answer is requested and D is the best recognised pairing.  
• An umbilical granuloma is simply exuberant granulation tissue after cord separation; it is not derived from the omphalomesenteric vein or any specific embryonic duct (so option C is wrong).

question:
A 4 year old girl falls from the balcony of an apartment on the third floor. On arrival in the Emergency Room she is haemodynamically stable. Initial radiographs demonstrate a right femur fracture and bilateral tibia fractures. Her chest radiograph shows no rib or sternal fractures. There is no pneumo or haemothorax. Despite this, her Sats drop to 86% on nasal prong oxygen, and she develops subcostal recessions. 

What is the most likely cause for her respiratory distress?
rationale: Pulmonary contusion is the common in children who sustain blunt chest trauma, owing to the increased compliance of the thoracic cavity in a child. As such, the chest can absorb a large amount of kinetic energy from the impact, which is subsequently transferred to the intrathoracic structures. An initial chest radiograph may be normal. Subsequent x-rays may reveal ill-defined consolidation which is not sensitive for contusion, with differentials including aspiration, atelectasis, and infection.

B.  Fat embolism
C.  Aspiration pneumonia

Rationale:
• Children’s rib cages are very compliant, so significant intrathoracic injury can occur without any rib or sternal fractures being seen on the chest radiograph.  
• Pulmonary contusion is the commonest cause of early hypoxia after blunt chest trauma in children. It may be radiographically occult in the first few hours, yet produces rapidly progressive hypoxaemia and increased work of breathing (e.g., subcostal recessions).  
• Fat embolism syndrome is usually delayed (developing 24–72 h after long-bone fractures) and is uncommon in young children; aspiration pneumonia or cardiac contusion would not be the most likely immediate cause in this setting.  

Therefore, the most likely explanation for the child’s early respiratory deterioration is an occult pulmonary contusion.

question:
A 12 year old male sustains a penetrating injury to the left chest with a bicycle spoke. His chest x-ray is normal. An ECG shows J-waves and eFAST demonstrates a 4mm pericardial effusion. The patient remains haemodynamically stable, and is planned for surgical procedure the following day. 

What is the most appropriate procedure in this scenario?
rationale: In this scenario the patient is haemodynamically stable and has a confirmed pericardial effusion. There are no features of cardiac tamponade which would warrant an emergency room thoracotomy, sternotomy or clambshell thoracotomy. The initial surgical management would be a subxiphoid pericardial window. If active haemorrhage is present (indicating a cardiac injury), then the next step would be to convert to a sternotomy in order to repair the injury.

A 6 year old male is brought into the resus bay after being accidentally stabbed in the chest with a pair of scissors whilst playing with his friends at school. He is haemodynamically stable, with a single 1cm wound on this anterior chest, to the left of the sternum in the 4th intercostal space. After establishing intravenous access, an erect chest radiograph is done which shows a blunting of the costophrenic angle on the left. 

What is the next most appropriate step in the management of this patient?
rationale: In this scenario, there is radiographic evidence of a left sided haemothorax. A haemothorax is noted as a meniscus of fluid blunting the costophrenic angle or diaphragmatic surface and tracking up the pleural margins of the chest wall when viewed on an upright chest x-ray film. The most appropriate management is to drain the haemothorax by inserting an intercostal chest drain in the 5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line on the affected side.
B: insert an intercostal chest drain in the 5th intercostal space mid axillary line on the left
C: needle decompression on the left 2nd intercostal space

###Question: A 6 year old male is brought into the resus bay after being accidentally stabbed in the chest with a pair of scissors whilst playing with his friends at school. He is haemodynamically stable, with a single 1cm wound on this anterior chest, to the left of the sternum in the 4th intercostal space. After establishing intravenous access, an erect chest radiograph is done which shows a blunting of the costophrenic angle on the left. 

What is the next most appropriate step in the management of this patient?
###Options:
A.  do an eFAST
B.  insert an intercostal chest drain in the 5th intercostal space mid axillary line on the left
C.  needle decompression on the left 2nd intercostal space
D.  do a CT chest

###Answer:
outputs:

Rationale:  
• A penetrating chest wound with a new pleural fluid level or costophrenic angle blunting on an erect chest X-ray is haemothorax until proven otherwise (≈ ≥300 mL of blood is needed before blunting appears).  
• Definitive initial management of a traumatic haemothorax is tube thoracostomy to drain the blood, allow lung re-expansion and permit ongoing monitoring of blood loss.  
• Needle decompression (C) is reserved for a suspected tension pneumothorax, which is not suggested here (the child is stable and there is no radiographic hyper-lucency or mediastinal shift).  
• An eFAST (A) could detect fluid but would add no therapeutic benefit and would delay the necessary intervention.  
• CT chest (D) may be useful later to delineate injuries, but imaging should never delay the timely insertion of a chest tube in a patient with a proven or strongly suspected haemothorax.

A 8 year old male is involved in a motor vehicle accident and ejected from the vehicle. On arrival in the Emergency Centre he has a HR 155 and Sats 88% on nasal prong oxygen. A supine chest radiograph is done which demonstrates fractures of rib 5 and 6 on the right, and ‘veiling’ of the right hemithorax. 

What is the next most appropriate step in the management of this patient?
rationale: In this scenario, the child has sustained significant blunt trauma to the chest. Increased density or ‘veiling’ of the right hemithorax on chest radiograph is highly suspicious of a right haemothorax in a supine trauma patient. Because of the supine position of the patient, the haemothorax does not pool in the costophrenic angle but rather distributes broadly across the entire right hemithorax.
A: Endotracheal intubation to protect the airway
B: Insertion of an intercostal chest drain in the 5ths intercostal space on the right
D: Needle decompression on the right 2nd intercostal space

###Question: A 8 year old male is involved in a motor vehicle accident and ejected from the vehicle. On arrival in the Emergency Centre he has a HR 155 and Sats 88% on nasal prong oxygen. A supine chest radiograph is done which demonstrates fractures of rib 5 and 6 on the right, and ‘veiling’ of the right hemithorax. 

What is the next most appropriate step in the management of this patient?


###Options:
A.  Endotracheal intubation to protect the airway
B.  Insertion of an intercostal chest drain in the 5ths intercostal space on the right
C.  Emergency room thoracotomy
D.  Needle decompression on the right 2nd intercostal space

outputs:

Rationale:  
•  A “veiling” or “white-out” of a hemithorax on a supine trauma radiograph strongly suggests a large pleural fluid collection. In the setting of blunt chest trauma with adjacent rib fractures, the most likely diagnosis is a massive haemothorax.  
•  The immediate, definitive treatment for a haemothorax is tube thoracostomy (intercostal chest drain) to evacuate blood, re-expand the lung and allow ongoing assessment of blood loss.  
•  Endotracheal intubation (A) may be needed later if oxygenation remains poor, but correcting the mechanical problem in the chest takes precedence.  
•  Emergency room thoracotomy (C) is reserved for massive initial drainage (>1.5 L in adults or persistent large output) or cardiac arrest due to chest injury; the first step is still chest tube insertion.  
•  Needle decompression (D) is the emergent management for a suspected tension pneumothorax, not for a haemothorax.  

Therefore, placing an intercostal chest drain is the most appropriate next step.

question:
A four year old female is brought into a level 1 trauma centre following a pedestrian vehicle accident. Her GCS is 9/15, HR of 140, BP 85/62. On examination her neck veins are distended and trachea is deviated to the left. On auscultation, she has reduced breath sounds on the right. 

What is the most likely diagnosis:
rationale: The diagnosis of tension pneumothorax is made clinically. Breath sounds are reduced or absent on the affected side and the trachea deviates away from the affected side. The thorax may also be hyperresonant; jugular venous distention and tachycardia may be present.

###Question: A four year old female is brought into a level 1 trauma centre following a pedestrian vehicle accident. Her GCS is 9/15, HR of 140, BP 85/62. On examination her neck veins are distended and trachea is deviated to the left. On auscultation, she has reduced breath sounds on the right. 

What is the most likely diagnosis:

###Options:
A.  Left heamothorax
B.  Right occult pneumothorax
C.  Cardiac tamponade
D.  Right tension pneumothorax

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Right tension pneumothorax  

Rationale  
• Classic triad for tension pneumothorax: unilateral absent / markedly diminished breath sounds, distended neck veins (raised intrathoracic pressure obstructing venous return), and tracheal/mediastinal shift away from the affected side.  
• In this child the breath sounds are reduced on the right, the trachea is pushed to the left, and the neck veins are engorged, with accompanying hypotension and tachycardia – all hallmark features of a right-sided tension pneumothorax.  

Why the other options are unlikely  
A. Left haemothorax – would give absent breath sounds on the left side and usually flat (not distended) neck veins owing to blood loss.  
B. Right occult pneumothorax – by definition produces no overt clinical signs (no deviation or JVD).  
C. Cardiac tamponade – produces hypotension and neck-vein distention but breath sounds remain equal bilaterally and there is no tracheal deviation.

question:
A 2-year-old child presents with a slow growing, round subcutaneous lesion on the scalp. It is 2cm in size and feels superficial, so you proceed to an excision.

Which of the following histological features would confirm the diagnosis of a epidermal cyst?
rationale: Epidermal cysts have a wall composed of true epidermis. They do not contain pilosebaceous units or hair. Dermoid cysts are congenital cysts that are lined by skin with fully mature pilosebaceous units
C: A wall composed of true epidermis

###Question: A 2-year-old child presents with a slow growing, round subcutaneous lesion on the scalp. It is 2cm in size and feels superficial, so you proceed to an excision.

Which of the following histological features would confirm the diagnosis of a epidermal cyst?



###Options:
A.  The presence of pilosebaceous units
B.  The presence of hair
C.  A wall composed of true epidermis
D.  Sebaceous material

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. A wall composed of true epidermis

Rationale:  
An epidermal (epidermoid) cyst is essentially a sac formed by invagination of the epidermis into the dermis. Histologically it is characterized by a cyst wall lined with true stratified squamous epithelium containing a granular cell layer, identical to normal epidermis. The lumen is filled with laminated keratin. Presence of pilosebaceous units or hair shafts would suggest a dermoid cyst, and sebaceous material is more typical of a sebaceous or pilar (trichilemmal) cyst. Therefore, the defining feature confirming an epidermal cyst is the wall composed of true epidermis.

Which of the following features, in addition to the neurofibroma, would prompt genetic testing for NF-1?
rationale: Genetic diagnosis of NF-1 should be sought is 2 or more of the following 7 clinical criteria are present: six or more café-au-lait spots, two or more neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma, osseous lesion such as sphenoid dysplasia or tibial pseudoarthrosis, first degree relative with NF-1, Lisch nodules, axillary or inguinal freckles, or optic glioma

###Question: A 4 year old female presents is referred to you for assessment and possible excision of a large neurofibroma in the abdomen, picked up on CT scan. When you examine the child, you have a clinical suspicion of neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF-1):

Which of the following features, in addition to the neurofibroma, would prompt genetic testing for NF-1?


###Options:
A.  Optic neuritis
B.  Axillary lymphadenopathy
C.  2 or more café-au-lait spots
D.  Tibial pseudoarthrosis

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Tibial pseudoarthrosis

Rationale:
Neurofibromatosis type 1 is diagnosed when a patient has at least two of the NIH diagnostic criteria, which include:
• Six or more café-au-lait macules (>5 mm in pre-pubertal children, >15 mm in post-pubertal individuals)  
• Two or more neurofibromas of any type or one plexiform neurofibroma  
• Freckling in the axillary or inguinal region  
• Optic glioma  
• Two or more Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas)  
• A distinctive osseous lesion such as sphenoid wing dysplasia or tibial pseudarthrosis  
• A first-degree relative with NF-1

Among the options given, tibial pseudoarthrosis is one of the listed “distinctive osseous lesions”; its presence together with a large neurofibroma would satisfy two NIH criteria and therefore warrants genetic confirmation/assessment for NF-1.

The other options do not meet the criteria:
A. Optic neuritis – NF-1 is associated with optic glioma, not optic neuritis.  
B. Axillary lymphadenopathy – not a diagnostic feature; the relevant finding is axillary freckling.  
C. Two café-au-lait spots – fewer than the six required by the criteria.

Which of the following terms describes a teratoma arising from the hard palate?
rationale: Epignathus is a term used to describe teratomas protruding from the mouth. These tumors arise from the hard or soft palate or the nasopharynx. They are not to be confused with epulis which is a benign granular cell tumor occurring almost exclusively in girls and arising from the gingival mucosa.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
rationale: The scenario provided suggests that this is a congenital neck mass. The MRI findings. All of the above options would be on the differential for a congenital neck mass however the MRI findings are suggestive of a cervical teratoma.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this case?

A.  Foregut duplication cyst
B.  Cervical teratoma
C.  Congenital goitre
D.  Cervical lymphangioma

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Cervical teratoma  

Rationale:  
A cervical teratoma is a germ-cell tumour that typically contains tissues from all three germ layers (e.g., fat, cartilage, bone, calcification). On imaging it therefore shows a heterogeneous appearance with:  
• Areas of fat density (adipose tissue)  
• Cystic and solid components  
• Foci of calcification or ossification  

The MRI description of “multiple lines as well as adipose tissue and areas of calcifications” fits this classic heterogeneous pattern.  

• Foregut duplication cysts are usually purely cystic and do not contain fat or calcification.  
• Congenital goitre presents as a homogeneous enlargement of the thyroid gland without fat or calcification.  
• Cervical lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are multiloculated cystic lesions filled with lymph; they likewise lack fat and calcified elements.  

Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is a cervical teratoma.

question:
You review a nine month old infant at your clinic, who had a benign sacrococcygeal teratoma resected as a neonate. The alpha-feto protein levels is elevated, and a CT scan is ordered which confirms the presence of recurrence. 

Which of the following is likely to account for the recurrence?
rationale:
Most neonatal tumors are mature or immature teratomas that can be managed by surgery and postoperative observation. Recurrent tumors are noted in 10% to 20% of initially benign tumors, and 50% of these are malignant recurrences. The recurrence may be due to a sampling error of the original tumor, incomplete resection of a malignant focus, or transformation of a small benign remnant into
a malignant lesion.
A: a sampling error of the original tumor,
B: complete resection of a malignant focus with clear margins
D: the lack of established neo-adjuvant therapy

Which of the following is likely to account for the recurrence?


###Options:
A.  a sampling error of the original tumor,
B.  complete resection of a malignant focus with clear margins
C.  progression of malignant disease
D.  the lack of established neo-adjuvant therapy

###Answer:
outputs:

Rationale:
Sacrococcygeal teratomas are often heterogeneous; small foci of yolk-sac (endodermal-sinus) tumor can be scattered within an otherwise mature (benign) teratoma. If these malignant foci are not included in the histologic sections examined after the initial resection, the tumour will be reported as “benign.” The residual occult malignant cells then proliferate, producing a recurrence that is usually heralded by a rise in α-fetoprotein. Hence the commonest explanation for a “benign” sacrococcygeal teratoma recurring with an elevated AFP is a sampling error at the first histopathology, not incomplete margins, neoadjuvant therapy issues, or true postoperative progression of a known malignant tumour.

In order to plan your surgical approach, which of the following investigations would you request?
rationale: In neonates presenting with large external masses, the degree of pelvic and abdominal involvement should be assessed preoperatively with either ultrasonography, CT, or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and these studies may also offer a clue as to the characteristics of the vascular supply. An open or laparoscopic abdominal exploration may be required to mobilize the pelvic portion and to divide the middle sacral artery.

A: A digital rectal examination to assess for explosive stools

Therefore, the next appropriate step is a digital rectal examination aimed at detecting a presacral mass (Option C).

question:
The diagnosis of a SCT is made on antenatal ultrasound.  

Which of the following features would mandate delivery by caesarean section?
rationale: Abdominal delivery should be considered if the external mass is greater than 5 cm, to avoid dystocia and rupture.60 In-utero shunting can lead to fetal hydrops, which is associated with high mortality

Current recommendations are to plan an elective caesarean section when the external component of the tumor exceeds about 5 cm in diameter. • Altman type IV lesions (option C) are entirely internal/presacral, so they usually allow vaginal delivery because no external bulk impedes passage.

Hence, tumor size greater than 5 cm is the feature that mandates delivery by caesarean section.

rationale: SCTs are more common in females with a ratio of 4:1. Altman III SCTs have an abdominal component. • Altman I – almost entirely external.  
• Altman II – external with significant intrapelvic extension.  
• Altman III – predominantly intrapelvic/abdominal with only a small external component.

– Absence of fontanelle bulging on pressure simply distinguishes a solid tumour from a meningomyelocele but does not point to Altman III.  
– Turner syndrome has no recognised association with sacrococcygeal teratoma.

Therefore, the presence of an associated abdominal mass makes an Altman III sacrococcygeal teratoma more likely.

rationale: Primordial germ cells arise near the allantois of the embryonic yolk sac endoderm and are evident at the fourth fetal week. They migrate along the midline dorsal mesentery to the genital ridge, arriving by the end of the sixth fetal week. There is a theory that some teratomas are a result of incomplete twinning.
A: Teratomas are thought to arise from totipotent germ cells in the 8th week of       gestation
B: Primordial germ cells migrate cranially from the primitive streak
C: During the 5th week of gestation totipotent primordial germ cells migrate towards the gonadal ridges
D: SCTs are always remnants of incomplete twinning

• Because there is no distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula, air from the tracheobronchial tree cannot enter the gastrointestinal tract; therefore the abdomen appears gasless on the radiograph.
• With the common Type C lesion (proximal atresia with distal fistula) the stomach and intestines fill with air, so a gasless abdomen would not be seen.
• Iatrogenic perforation or oesophageal stenosis would not typically give a persistently gasless abdomen and would usually allow some passage of the tube or show contrast leakage rather than simple coiling.

The gap between the esophageal segments should be periodically measured and is usually expressed in terms of the number of vertebral bodies. ###Question: A premature neonate with pure oesophageal atresia, undergoes a gastrostomy for feeding access. The baby is unstable intra-operatively due to an underlying cardiac defect. Post-operatively the baby is ventilated and a Replogle tube in left in the upper pouch.

What is the next most appropriate step in the investigation of this child?

A.  Perform a cervical oesophagostomy
B.  Perform a “gapogram” once the baby is stable
C.  Perform a thoracotomy and primary anastomosis once the baby is stable
D.  Perform hydrostatic distension of the upper pouch

Rationale:
In pure oesophageal atresia there is no distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula, so the proximal and distal oesophageal segments are completely separate. Before any definitive operative plan can be made, the surgeon must know the true length of the gap between the two ends. The standard, safest way to measure this is a contrast study (­“gapogram”) carried out when the infant is haemodynamically and respiratory stable, usually by injecting a small amount of contrast into the upper pouch via the Replogle tube and into the distal oesophagus through the gastrostomy, then taking lateral films. 

• Cervical oesophagostomy (A) is not an investigation; it is an antiquated diversion procedure rarely used today.  
• Proceeding directly to thoracotomy and primary anastomosis (C) without knowing the gap risks tension anastomosis and leak; most pure atresias have a long gap that precludes primary repair.  
• Hydrostatic distension of the upper pouch (D) is neither a standard nor a safe investigative technique.

Therefore, once the neonate is stabilised, the next appropriate step is to perform a gapogram.

question:
In a counselling session with the parents of a child born with oesophageal atresia, they ask you how this congenital anomaly occurs. 
 
Which of the following is the most recent theory explaining the normal embryological development of the oesophagus and trachea?
rationale: Outgrowth model where the trachea extends from the foregut tube at the level of the lung bud. The Watershed model suggests that both developing trachea and oesophagus elongate from a single diverging. According to the Septation model a septum is formed from lateral ridges of mesenchyme, which moves up along the longitudinal axis of the common foregut tube separating the trachea and oesophagus. The most recent is the splitting and extension model: a ‘saddle-like’ epithelial structure at the distal end of the foregut at the site of lung bud origination moves in a caudal to cranial direction, splitting the foregut in two until the level of the pharynx.

B.  Septation model
C.  Outgrowth model
D.  Splitting and extension model

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D.  Splitting and extension model  

Rationale:  
Earlier explanations for how the single embryonic foregut separates into a dorsal oesophagus and a ventral trachea included the septation, out-growth and watershed models.  The newest concept, proposed on the basis of molecular-developmental and 3-D imaging studies, is the “splitting and extension” model.  It states that a respiratory domain (marked by Nkx2.1 expression) elongates caudally while simultaneously cleaving (“splitting”) from the dorsal foregut, so no true septum forms; differential growth and programmed cell changes drive this partition.  Because it post-dates the other three hypotheses, it is regarded as the most recent theory of normal tracheo-oesophageal development.

C. Gastric mucin is produced mainly by surface mucous cells (foveolar cells); chief cells secrete pepsinogen. Thus chief-cell mucin production is not a key factor in lubrication.

• Peritoneal drainage alone (option B) is appropriate when the abdomen has not yet been opened, but once a laparotomy has already revealed multiple perforations it is inadequate because the necrotic bowel remains a continuing septic focus.  
• A proximal jejunostomy (A) or immediate resection with enterostomy and mucous fistula (D) require lengthy bowel mobilisation and anastomosis/stoma formation, which the unstable neonate is unlikely to tolerate.  

Thus, the safest and most appropriate intra-operative strategy is option C: “clip and drop” with planned second-look surgery.

Before reversing an ileostomy fashioned for necrotising enterocolitis, the main concern is an unrecognised stricture in the remaining (distal) colon or rectum, which occurs in a significant proportion of NEC survivors. The appropriate study is therefore one that opacifies the distal bowel. A water-soluble contrast enema introduced per rectum (or through the mucous fistula) outlines the entire distal colon and rectum and will reveal any narrowing or obstruction that would complicate stoma closure.  

• A contrast meal & follow-through (A) images the proximal small bowel, not the distal colon.  
• Plain radiographs (C) give no anatomic detail of luminal calibre.  
• A loopogram via the ileostomy (D) visualises only the proximal small bowel; it does not assess the at-risk distal colon.  

Hence, the investigation of choice is a contrast enema.

Which of the following are indications for surgery in this case?
rationale: The scenario describes a child with torticollis and plagiocephaly. Surgical management of torticollis due to sternomastoid tumour is indicated in cases of tightness limiting head rotation in children more than 12 to 15 months of age, when associated with progressive hemifacial hypoplasia, and in children diagnosed after 1 year of age. Most children with torticollis and plagiocephaly are managed conservatively with plagiocephaly resolving as the child begins to sit.
A: Persistent sternomastoid tightness in children more than 3 months of age
B: Persistent sternomastoid tightness with progressive hemifacial hypoplasia
C: Diagnosis in children younger than 1 year

A: a transverse skin incision 1cm above the sternal and clavicular heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and division of both heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at this level
B: an oblique incision along the border to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and division of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at its midpoint
C: a transverse skin incision and division of the sternal head of sternocleidomastoid only

Mid-muscle division, division of only one head, or excision of the “sternomastoid tumour” are obsolete or inadequate and carry a higher recurrence rate.

rationale: The scenario describes an infant with torticollis and a sternomastoid tumour. Torticollis due to sternomastoid tumour will resolve spontaneously in the vast majority of infants. Surgery is indicated when torticollis does not resolve in infancy, when the diagnosis is made after 1 year of age, and when the torticollis is associated with complications such as hemifacial hypoplasia and plagiocephaly. Boitulinum toxin treatment appears ineffective in patients that present in late childhood or adulthood. Conservative management with physiotherapy in the first year of life is contencious.
A: If left untreated most children with this condition will develop permanent deformity known as plagiocephaly
B: Surgery is always required to prevent hemifacial hypoplasia
C: Most children with torticollis are managed conservatively
D: Botulinum toxin injection is only effective in patients presenting in late  childhood or adulthood

Therefore, the next appropriate step is to obtain an MRI.

rationale: The lesion described in the scenario is the typical presentation of a congenital midline cervical cleft. Wound closure by Z plasty avoids linear scarification and attendant limitations in neck extension.

question:
You see a three-month-old infant with a branchial cyst, and you are counselling the parents in preparation for elective cyst excision. The father asks you how branchial cysts come about.

What is the correct description of the embryology of the branchial arches?
rationale: Neural crest cells responsible for the formation of 6 paired branchial arches migrate to the future foetal head and neck region during the 4th week of gestation. Each arch is separated externally by an ectodermally lined cleft and internally by an endodermally lined pouch. The 5th  pair of arches and associated clefts and pouches regress spontaneously. The remaining paired arches, clefts and pouches each contain a specific artery, muscle, nerve and cartilage rod. The pouch and the cleft of the first arch meet to form the external auditory canal, tympanic membrane and Eustacian canal. The clefts of the 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 6th arches share a common opening at the Cervical Sinus of His and usually regress. The pouches of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th arches are responsible for the formation of the Palatine tonsil and supratonsillar fossa, inferior parathyroid glands and piriform fossa, and superior parathyroid glands.
A: There are six pairs of branchial arches that contain cranial nerves I to VI
B: The branchial arches have no ectodermal components, as their external surface become the branchial clefts
C: Each branchial arch contains a distinct artery, cartilage rod, muscle and nerve
D: The second branchial arch contains cranial nerves VII and VIII

C.  Each branchial arch contains a distinct artery, cartilage rod, muscle and nerve
D.  The second branchial arch contains cranial nerves VII and VIII

Rationale:  
Each pharyngeal (branchial) arch is a segmented column of mesenchyme that develops during the 4th–5th weeks of embryogenesis. Every arch has its own:  
• artery (an aortic‐arch derivative)  
• cartilaginous rod (skeletal element)  
• muscular component  
• specific cranial nerve supplying the muscles and mucosa derived from that arch.  

Option A is incorrect because although six arches are described (the 5th is rudimentary), they are not associated with cranial nerves I–VI; only V, VII, IX and X/XI supply arches.  
Option B is incorrect; each arch is covered externally by ectoderm, so they do possess an ectodermal component.  
Option D is incorrect; the second arch is supplied solely by cranial nerve VII, not VIII.

question: A 25 years old school teacher Para 1 wants to use oral contraceptive pills for contraception. She is asking about the mode of action of oral contraceptive pills. The mechanism of action of oral contraceptive pills is:

###Question: A 25 years old school teacher Para 1 wants to use oral contraceptive pills for contraception. She is asking about the mode of action of oral contraceptive pills. The mechanism of action of oral contraceptive pills is: 

###Options:
A.  Inhibiting ovulation by suppression of serum FSH.
B.  Inducing endometrial atrophy.
C.  Increasing cervical mucous hostility.
D.  Inducing endometritis.
E.  Inhibiting prolactin.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Inhibiting ovulation by suppression of serum FSH.

Rationale:
The principal and most reliable contraceptive effect of the combined oral contraceptive pill is suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis. The estrogen and progestin components provide negative feedback on the pituitary so that follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion are blunted; without the normal mid-cycle FSH/LH rise, a dominant follicle does not mature and the LH surge required for ovulation does not occur. Although OCPs also thicken cervical mucus and render the endometrium less receptive, inhibition of ovulation remains the key mechanism. Options D and E are incorrect, and options B and C describe secondary effects rather than the primary mechanism.

question: As regards fertilization and capacitation, which statement is false

• Capacitation is the functional “conditioning” of ejaculated sperms that takes place mainly in the uterus and, especially, the uterine (Fallopian) tubes; it does not occur to any significant extent in the cervix.

Therefore, Option C is the false statement.

Reported perforation rates are roughly 1–4 per 1 000 procedures, the highest of any routine intra-uterine intervention.  
• The other procedures are performed under direct hysteroscopic vision (division of adhesions, outpatient hysteroscopy, second-generation endometrial ablation) or with a soft plastic cannula in a large postpartum cavity (post-partum suction evacuation), and their perforation rates are markedly lower (<0.1–0.2 %, often <0.05 %).  

Therefore surgical termination of pregnancy carries the greatest risk of uterine perforation.

E.  Medial to the medial umbilical ligaments

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C.  Lateral to the medial umbilical ligaments

Rationale:
On the deep (peritoneal) surface of the anterior abdominal wall there are five umbilical folds: one median (urachus), two medial (obliterated umbilical arteries) and two lateral folds. What would be the recommended management?
A: Adequate exploration of the fears with counselling by trained personnel
B: Discharging the patient to midwife care with advice for vaginal delivery
C: Enlisting the patient for elective caesarean section
D: Referral to another obstetrician for second opinion
E: Referral to the supervisor of midwife

D.  Referral to another obstetrician for second opinion
E.  Referral to the supervisor of midwife

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Adequate exploration of the fears with counselling by trained personnel

Rationale:
A request for an elective caesarean section based solely on fear of childbirth (tokophobia) should first be met with empathetic discussion and structured counselling. Evidence-based guidelines (e.g., RCOG, NICE) state that women expressing severe fear should be offered:

• Time with an experienced obstetrician or midwife trained in perinatal mental-health counselling  
• Exploration of the specific anxieties and previous experiences that underlie the request  
• Provision of accurate information about risks and benefits of vaginal birth versus caesarean section  
• Referral for psychological support if needed (e.g., cognitive-behavioural therapy)

Most women who receive such support choose vaginal birth, and immediate scheduling of an elective caesarean (option C) is not recommended unless fear persists after counselling. Simply discharging the woman, referring her elsewhere, or delegating care without addressing her concerns (options B, D, E) fails to meet her psychological and informational needs.

Therefore, the appropriate first-line management is option A.

question: Which one of the following statements with regard to CIN is true?

B: CIN 1 always needs treatment when detected on colposcopy.

D: CIN 2 and 3 can be left for 2 years before treatment.
E: Almost 90% of low-grade cytological abnormalities that are not treated at a first visit will revert to normal cytology and colposcopy.

• CIN 1 (mild dysplasia/LSIL) has a high rate of spontaneous regression, so it is usually managed with observation and repeated cytology/colposcopy rather than immediate excisional therapy.

Reduced fetal movement (RFM) is most often linked to conditions that compromise placental function or the fetus itself. Therefore, statement B is the only statement that is not true.

The patient’s 1-month continuous use of tranexamic acid, together with her presentation of severe headache and focal seizures, is most consistent with cerebral sinus thrombosis rather than haemorrhage, psychosis or tumour.

• Current RCOG Green-top Guideline 37a therefore recommends 6 weeks of postpartum LMWH in this situation.

Thus the most appropriate management is 6 weeks of LMWH after delivery.

question: Which one of the following statements is true with respect to perineal tears?
A: Fourth-degree tear involves injury to the anal sphincter complex, but not anal mucosa.
B: Third-degree tear involves injury to the perineal muscle complex
C: Intact perineal skin excludes the possibility of damage to the anal sphincter complex.
D: First-degree tear involves the skin and superficial perineal muscles.
E: The degree of trauma in a right mediolateral episiotomy is equivalent to a second-degree tear.

D.  First-degree tear involves the skin and superficial perineal muscles.

• An episiotomy that is correctly sited and extends through skin and perineal muscles while stopping short of the anal sphincter produces tissue damage equivalent to a second-degree tear. Therefore statement E is the only accurate statement.

###Answer:

Rationale  
• Glucose intolerance – Women whose BMI is ≥ 30 kg/m² fall into the risk-factor group for gestational diabetes; NICE therefore recommends a 75-g oral glucose-tolerance test at 24–28 weeks (statement A is true).  
• Neural-tube-defect prevention – Obesity roughly doubles the background risk; a high-dose (5 mg) folic-acid supplement should be started pre-conceptionally and continued until 12 weeks’ gestation (statement B is true).

• Third stage – Obesity increases the risk of postpartum haemorrhage; active management of the third stage (uterotonic, controlled cord traction) is therefore advised (statement E is true).

Hence statement D is the false one.

question: A 28-year-old para 1 woman with a dichorionic diamniotic (DCDA) twin pregnancy attends her antenatal appointment at 20 weeks' gestation. She is at risk of developing the following complications with the exception of which of the following?

In a dichorionic diamniotic (two separate placentas and two amniotic sacs) twin pregnancy, such anastomoses do not exist, so TTTS cannot occur.

The other listed complications are all more common in any twin pregnancy, including DCDA twins:
• Pre-eclampsia – incidence is roughly doubled because of the larger placental mass.  
• Post-partum haemorrhage – over-distended uterus and larger placental site increase PPH risk.  
• Fetal growth restriction – competition for maternal resources and uterine space can lead to growth problems even in DCDA twins.  
• Preterm labour – uterine over-distension and hormonal factors make preterm birth far more common in twins.

Therefore, the exception is Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome.

question: A 22-year-old Asian woman is admitted to the hospital with an incomplete miscarriage at 11 weeks' gestation. She subsequently has surgical evacuation of the uterus. ###Question: A 22-year-old Asian woman is admitted to the hospital with an incomplete miscarriage at 11 weeks' gestation. She subsequently has surgical evacuation of the uterus. Which of the following is the most likely karyotype and parental chromosomal origin? 

###Options:
A.  46 XX, maternal
B.  46 XX, paternal
C.  46 XY, paternal
D.  69 XXY, paternal
E.  69 XXY, paternal and maternal

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E. 69 XXY, paternal and maternal  

Rationale:  
The histology described—focal hydropic change with some normal villi plus identifiable fetal tissue—indicates a partial hydatidiform mole. Partial moles are almost always triploid (69 chromosomes). They result when a normal haploid ovum (maternal set) is fertilised by two sperm or by one sperm that duplicates its chromosomes, providing two paternal sets. Hence the conceptus carries one maternal and two paternal haploid complements, most commonly 69 XXY.

###Question: A 30-year-old woman presents to the early pregnancy unit with mild vaginal bleeding. An ultrasound is performed, which reports a complete molar pregnancy. What would be the parental origin and genetic complement of the complete molar pregnancy? 

###Options:
A.  2 paternal sets: diploid
B.  2 paternal sets: haploid
C.  1 paternal set: haploid
D.  2 paternal and 2 maternal sets: tetraploid
E.  1 maternal and 1 paternal set: diploid

###Answer:

A complete hydatidiform mole arises when an “empty” ovum (its maternal chromosomes are lost or inactive) is fertilised by:

question: A 22-year-old Asian woman is admitted to the hospital with an incomplete miscarriage at 11 weeks' gestation. An ultrasound shows a 'snowstorm appearance. She passes grape-like vesicles through the vagina. She subsequently has a surgical evacuation of the uterus. The histology reveals a large mass with hydropic changes in all the placental villi and no fetal tissue. She is followed up with serum beta human chorionic gonadotrophin (beta hCG) levels. There was an initial fall but it started to rise gradually (10,000 units/mL) at 3 months' follow-up. Her CT scan chest, abdomen and pelvis are normal except localized thickened vascular area in the posterior wall of uterus. What is the likely diagnosis?

###Question: A 22-year-old Asian woman is admitted to the hospital with an incomplete miscarriage at 11 weeks' gestation. An ultrasound shows a 'snowstorm appearance. She passes grape-like vesicles through the vagina. She subsequently has a surgical evacuation of the uterus. The histology reveals a large mass with hydropic changes in all the placental villi and no fetal tissue. She is followed up with serum beta human chorionic gonadotrophin (beta hCG) levels. There was an initial fall but it started to rise gradually (10,000 units/mL) at 3 months' follow-up. Her CT scan chest, abdomen and pelvis are normal except localized thickened vascular area in the posterior wall of uterus. What is the likely diagnosis? 

###Options:
A.  Gestational choriocarcinoma
B.  Persistent trophoblastic disease
C.  Non-invasive mole
D.  Non-gestational choriocarcinoma
E.  Placental site trophoblastic disease

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Persistent trophoblastic disease

Rationale:
• She had a complete hydatidiform mole (snow-storm ultrasound, grape-like vesicles, no fetal tissue).  
• After evacuation, β-hCG should fall to undetectable levels. A plateau or secondary rise, as seen here (initial fall then rise to 10 000 IU/mL at 3 months), fulfils the criteria for persistent (also called post-molar) trophoblastic disease.  
• Imaging shows only a focal, vascular, intra-uterine lesion with no extra-uterine or metastatic deposits, again typical of persistent/invasive molar tissue.  
• Gestational choriocarcinoma (A) usually presents with much higher β-hCG levels and distant metastases (lungs, brain, liver).  
• Non-invasive mole (C) is not a standard clinical category; the accepted term for post-evacuation residual disease is persistent/invasive mole.  
• Non-gestational choriocarcinoma (D) arises from germ cells, not pregnancy tissue.  
• Placental site trophoblastic tumour (E) typically produces low β-hCG (often <5 000 IU/mL) and lacks the marked vascularity seen on imaging.

Hence the scenario best fits persistent trophoblastic disease.

Rationale:  
• The WHO modified partograph has an “alert line” that starts at 4 cm cervical dilatation and ascends at a rate of 1 cm / hour.

• Consequently, a point representing 5 cm dilatation at time-zero will lie to the left of (i.e., before) the alert line.  
• Hence the correct placement for the initial 5 cm plot is left of the alert line.

question: Which of the following is most effective in reducing maternal mortality?
A: Assessing women for risks to decide who needs special care
C: Delivery with a skilled birth attendant
D: Active management of 3rd stage of labour
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following is most effective in reducing maternal mortality? 

###Options:
A.  Assessing women for risks to decide who needs special care
B.  Training traditional birth attendants.
C.  Delivery with a skilled birth attendant
D.  Active management of 3rd stage of labour
E.  All of the above

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Delivery with a skilled birth attendant.

Rationale:
• The single intervention that has consistently shown the greatest impact on reducing maternal deaths is ensuring that every woman gives birth attended by a competent, formally trained midwife, nurse-midwife or doctor who can recognise complications early and institute or arrange prompt emergency obstetric care.  
• Antenatal “risk screening” (option A) misses many women who will develop life-threatening complications unpredictably during labour and therefore does not, by itself, lower mortality substantially.  
• Training traditional birth attendants (option B) improves certain practices (e.g., cleanliness) but has not been shown to bring a large fall in maternal mortality because TBAs generally lack the skills or authority to provide life-saving interventions or referral.  
• Active management of the third stage of labour (option D) reduces postpartum haemorrhage, yet it addresses only one cause of maternal death and depends on being carried out by a skilled provider; alone it is less impactful than full skilled attendance throughout labour and delivery.  
Hence, delivery with a skilled birth attendant (option C) is the most effective single measure among those listed.

question:

###Answer:

Post-partum haemorrhage (PPH) is managed in a structured, escalating sequence: call for help, resuscitate, uterine massage, uterotonics (oxytocin infusion, ergometrine, prostaglandin F2α, misoprostol/Cytotec), tranexamic acid, bimanual compression, careful genital tract examination, repair of lacerations, removal of retained tissue, balloon tamponade, compression sutures, stepwise devascularisation and only finally hysterectomy if all conservative measures fail or the uterus is un-salvageable.  
• Oxytocin drip (B) is first-line.  
• Misoprostol/Cytotec (C) is an effective additional uterotonic.  
• Uterine massage (D) helps stimulate contraction and control atony.  
• A quick examination without anaesthesia, followed by—if bleeding continues—an examination under anaesthesia (EUA) (E) is recommended to identify genital tract trauma or retained tissue.  

Therefore “take her immediately for emergency hysterectomy” is not a correct statement for initial management and is the exception.

question: In twin pregnancy which of the following combination of fetal presentation may be complicated by interlocked twins;

###Question: In twin pregnancy which of the following combination of fetal presentation may be complicated by interlocked twins;

B.  1st twin cephalic -2nd twin breach
C.  1st twin breach- 2 twin breach
D.  1st twin breach -2nd twin cephalic
E.  1st twin cephalic -2nd twin transverse

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. 1st twin breech – 2nd twin cephalic

Rationale:
“Locked” or “interlocked” twins almost always occur when the first‐delivered twin is breech and the second twin is cephalic. As the breech first twin is delivered, its after-coming head tries to enter the pelvis at the same time that the head of the second (vertex) twin is descending. The two heads meet at the pelvic brim and the chins become hooked (chin-to-chin or chin-to-occiput), preventing further descent of either head and producing the classical locked-twin complication. Other presentation combinations (e.g., both cephalic, breech–breech, or cephalic–breech) do not create this specific locking mechanism.

Staging and surgical planning for ovarian cancer depend on accurate visualization of peritoneal implants, omental disease, retroperitoneal lymph-node enlargement, liver surface deposits, ascites, and the relationship of the tumor to adjacent organs. • CA-125 (D) is a serum tumor marker useful for diagnosis and follow-up, not for anatomic staging.  
• Intravenous pyelography (E) has no role in staging ovarian cancer.  

Therefore, a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis is the most helpful investigation for assessing the extent of ovarian cancer.

Therefore, the statement that correctly applies when diagnosing iron-deficiency anaemia is that the serum iron-binding capacity may double.

• If a clot does form, it is friable and tends to lyse rapidly.

Hence the finding that “a clot fails to form after 7 minutes or a soft clot forms that breaks down easily” is characteristic of DIC, making option D the correct answer.

question: Which one of the following interventions is NOT advised during vaginal term delivery of a patient with mitral stenosis?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which one of the following interventions is NOT advised during vaginal term delivery of a patient with mitral stenosis? 

###Options:
A.  Ergometrine injection.
B.  Frusemide (Lasix) injection.
C.  Vacuum delivery
D.  Oxygen by mask
E.  Oxytocin injection

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Ergometrine injection.

Rationale:
• Mitral stenosis patients tolerate pregnancy best when tachycardia, sudden rises in systemic / pulmonary vascular resistance, and acute volume overload are avoided.  
• Ergometrine (methylergometrine) produces potent peripheral vasoconstriction, raises systemic blood pressure, and markedly increases pulmonary arterial pressure. These haemodynamic changes can acutely elevate left-atrial and pulmonary capillary pressures, precipitating pulmonary oedema or acute left-sided heart failure in a woman with mitral stenosis. Hence ergometrine (alone or as part of Syntometrine) is contraindicated.

• The other listed measures are either useful or acceptable in this setting:  
  – Frusemide (Lasix) helps off-load excess intravascular volume if pulmonary congestion develops.  
  – Vacuum (or forceps) delivery shortens the second stage and limits maternal pushing, thereby reducing cardiovascular stress.  
  – Supplemental oxygen improves maternal-fetal oxygenation.  
  – Oxytocin, given as a controlled IV infusion, is the uterotonic of choice because it has minimal pressor effect compared with ergometrine.

Therefore, ergometrine injection is the intervention that should NOT be used.

###Answer:

Rationale: 
• Age at menopause is determined primarily by the rate of ovarian follicular depletion; taking combined oral contraceptive pills does not influence this intrinsic process. Hence OCPs do not postpone the true biological onset of menopause (they may mask its symptoms, but the timing is unchanged).  
• Premature menopause is defined as permanent cessation of menstruation before 40 years of age – correct statement.  
• Menopause is retrospectively identified as the final menstrual period and occurs within the broader climacteric – correct.  
• The term pre-menopause (menopausal transition) describes the part of the climacteric when cycles become irregular – correct.  
• Climacteric indeed denotes the entire transitional phase from reproductive to non-reproductive life – correct. 

Therefore option A is the only incorrect statement.

###Answer:

Rationale:
• After menopause, estrogen production falls sharply. Estrogen normally inhibits bone resorption; its loss accelerates bone loss, predisposing post-menopausal women to osteoporosis and, consequently, to an increased risk of fragility fractures (especially vertebral and hip fractures).  
• FSH and LH rise (not fall) because negative feedback from ovarian steroids is removed → option A is incorrect.

• Genital (vulvo-vaginal) atrophy is common after menopause due to estrogen deficiency; stating that it “hardly ever occurs” is wrong → option E is incorrect.

Correct option: B. Real-time (compression duplex) ultrasonography is the investigation modality of choice.

Rationale:
• Deep-vein thrombosis (DVT) is more common in pregnancy, especially with additional risk factors such as obesity (BMI > 30).  
• In pregnancy the D-dimer level is physiologically elevated and therefore a positive result is not diagnostic (option A is false).  
• Warfarin crosses the placenta and is teratogenic; low-molecular-weight heparin is the recommended first-line treatment (option C is false).  
• Recent hospitalization/immobility is a well-recognized risk factor for venous thrombo-embolism, so saying it is “not a risk factor” is incorrect (option D is false).  
• Compression duplex ultrasonography is safe, non-invasive, and has high sensitivity and specificity for proximal lower-limb DVT in pregnancy, making it the investigation of choice (option B is true).

question: Aria is a 24-year-old para 1+0 at 14 weeks, she had a preterm birth with neonatal demise in the previous pregnancy. Regarding her management, which of the following is appropriate?
A: Strict bed rest, oral Salbutamol and Pheobarbitone
C: Micronized per vaginal progesterone up to 36 weeks
D: Use of Ascard (Aspirin 75mg) once daily up to 28 weeks

C.  Micronized per vaginal progesterone up to 36 weeks

• A woman with a previous spontaneous preterm birth and a current cervical length < 25 mm before 24 weeks is at high risk of recurrent preterm delivery.

question: During fetal surveillance: -
A: In late decelerations of fetal heart rate, the peak of the contraction occurs after the nadir of the deceleration
B: Fetal heart rate increases with increasing gestation
C: Placental grading is one of the markers of the biophysical profile (BPP)
D: Fetal heart rate accelerations of 15 bpm above baseline rate are a nonreassuring finding
E: An early deceleration of the fetal heart rate is a normal finding

###Question: During fetal surveillance: -

A.  In late decelerations of fetal heart rate, the peak of the contraction occurs after the nadir of the deceleration
B.  Fetal heart rate increases with increasing gestation
C.  Placental grading is one of the markers of the biophysical profile (BPP)
D.  Fetal heart rate accelerations of 15 bpm above baseline rate are a nonreassuring finding
E.  An early deceleration of the fetal heart rate is a normal finding

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E. An early deceleration of the fetal heart rate is a normal finding.

Rationale  
• Early decelerations are benign, vagally-mediated falls in fetal heart rate that mirror the uterine contraction (the nadir coincides with the peak of the contraction). They are considered a normal physiologic response to fetal head compression and are not associated with fetal hypoxia or acidaemia.

A. In late decelerations the nadir of the fetal heart rate occurs after the peak of the contraction, not before it; therefore the wording given is reversed.  
B. Baseline fetal heart rate falls, not rises, as gestation advances (≈160 bpm at 10 weeks, 120–140 bpm at term).  
C. The biophysical profile includes NST, fetal breathing movements, gross body movements, fetal tone and amniotic fluid volume. Placental grading is not a component.  
D. Accelerations of ≥15 bpm for ≥15 s are reassuring, indicating adequate oxygenation, not a non-reassuring finding.

question: In the Kenyan protocol for the prevention and treatment of malaria in pregnancy, which of the following statements is TRUE?
A: Sulfadoxine Pyrimethamine (SP) should not be given concomitantly with antiretrovirals
B: The recommended treatment for uncomplicated malaria in the first trimester is a three-day course of artemether lumefantrine (AL)
C: Dihydroartemisinin Piperaquine may be used as IPTp for those who are allergic to sulfur
D: Sulfadoxine - Pyrimethamine (SP) for IPTp should be given concomitantly with IFAS for prevention of malaria and anaemia in pregnancy.
E: The dose of IV quinine for the treatment of severe malaria in pregnancy, should be adjusted in patients with renal insufficiency

A.  Sulfadoxine Pyrimethamine (SP) should not be given concomitantly with antiretrovirals
B.  The recommended treatment for uncomplicated malaria in the first trimester is a three-day course of artemether lumefantrine (AL)
C.  Dihydroartemisinin Piperaquine may be used as IPTp for those who are allergic to sulfur

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D.  Sulfadoxine-Pyrimethamine (SP) for IPTp should be given concomitantly with IFAS for prevention of malaria and anaemia in pregnancy.

Rationale
• Kenyan (and WHO) policy recommends intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) with SP together with daily iron-folic acid supplementation (IFAS: 60 mg elemental iron + 0.4 mg folic acid). The low-dose folic acid does not interfere with the antimalarial effect of SP, and the iron/folate prevents maternal anaemia. Hence they are given together during every eligible ANC visit.

A. The contraindication is with cotrimoxazole (CTX) prophylaxis used in HIV-infected women, not with antiretroviral drugs themselves; SP may be given with ARVs if the woman is not on CTX.

B. In the first trimester uncomplicated malaria is treated with oral quinine (plus clindamycin) for 7 days; artemether-lumefantrine is reserved for 2nd and 3rd trimesters.

C. Dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine is not approved in the Kenyan protocol as an alternative IPTp drug for sulpha-allergic patients; no substitute IPTp is currently recommended.

E. Severe malaria is treated with IV artesunate (first-line); if IV quinine is used, standard doses are given and specific dose reduction for renal insufficiency is not part of the Kenyan guideline.

question:
When a patient presents with cord prolapse, which of the following statements is 
INCORRECT?
A: Funic presentation refers to the cord being below the presenting part, with intact membranes and not palpable on digital vaginal exam.
B: If the cord is pulsatile, a rapid cesarean section is the best management for overt prolapse.
C: Occult prolapse may be overcome by appropriate positioning of the patient
D: A full bladder may avert bad outcomes,
E: Avoiding early ARM in patients with high presenting part is advised to prevent cord prolapse.
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: When a patient presents with cord prolapse, which of the following statements is 
INCORRECT? 

###Options:
A.  Funic presentation refers to the cord being below the presenting part, with intact membranes and not palpable on digital vaginal exam.
B.  If the cord is pulsatile, a rapid cesarean section is the best management for overt prolapse.
C.  Occult prolapse may be overcome by appropriate positioning of the patient
D.  A full bladder may avert bad outcomes,
E.  Avoiding early ARM in patients with high presenting part is advised to prevent cord prolapse.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A

Rationale:
• Funic (cord) presentation is defined as the umbilical cord lying below or alongside the presenting part while the membranes are still intact. On vaginal examination the pulsating cord can usually be felt through the membranes. Therefore the statement in option A that the cord is “not palpable on digital vaginal exam” is incorrect.

The remaining statements are true:
• B – In overt cord prolapse with a live, non-compromised fetus, the safest and fastest way to deliver is usually by immediate Caesarean section unless an imminent instrumental vaginal birth is possible.  
• C – In occult prolapse (cord alongside the presenting part), maternal positioning (e.g., knee-chest, Trendelenburg) can reduce cord compression.  
• D – Filling the maternal bladder with 500–700 mL sterile fluid elevates the presenting part and can improve fetal perfusion until delivery.  
• E – Artificial rupture of membranes when the presenting part is high or not well-applied to the cervix markedly increases the risk of cord prolapse; thus early ARM should be avoided.

question: A 46 years old nulliparous female presents to a fertility clinic with desire to conceive. Her menses have in the recent past been widely spaced and she occasionally experiences hot flushes. A pelvic ultrasound done is reported as normal. Which of the following tests is a useful investigation for ovarian reserve?

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 46 years old nulliparous female presents to a fertility clinic with desire to conceive. Her menses have in the recent past been widely spaced and she occasionally experiences hot flushes. A pelvic ultrasound done is reported as normal. Which of the following tests is a useful investigation for ovarian reserve? 

###Options:
A.  FSH:LH ratio
B.  Anti-Mullerian Hormone
C.  Estradiol level
D.  LH levels
E.  None of the above

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Anti-Mullerian Hormone (AMH)

Rationale:
• AMH is produced by granulosa cells of pre-antral and small antral follicles.  
• Its serum concentration correlates closely with the size of the remaining primordial follicle pool; therefore it is considered the best single laboratory marker of ovarian reserve.  
• AMH levels are cycle-independent and are not affected by the use of exogenous gonadotropins or oral contraceptives, making the test convenient and reliable.  

In contrast, day-3 FSH, LH, the FSH:LH ratio, or estradiol levels fluctuate markedly during the cycle and are less sensitive and specific indicators of diminished ovarian reserve.

question: Violet, a 36-year-old para 0+2 presents with symptoms innkeeping with Hyperemesis gravidarum. Investigations reveal a uterine snow-storm appearance and hyperthyroidism. Which of the following will explain her presentation?
