###Question: Violet, a 36-year-old para 0+2 presents with symptoms innkeeping with Hyperemesis gravidarum. Investigations reveal a uterine snow-storm appearance and hyperthyroidism. Which of the following will explain her presentation? 

###Options:
A.  Complete Molar pregnancy
B.  Partial molar pregnancy
C.  Grave's disease
D.  Hashimoto's disease
E.  None of the above

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Complete molar pregnancy

Rationale:
• A “snow-storm” or “cluster-of-grapes” appearance on uterine ultrasound is classic for a complete hydatidiform mole.  
• Complete moles produce markedly elevated β-hCG levels. Excess β-hCG can stimulate TSH receptors, leading to clinical or biochemical hyperthyroidism.  
• The very high hCG levels also explain severe hyperemesis gravidarum.  
• Partial moles generally have a fetus or fetal parts, lower hCG levels, and a less uniform cystic pattern. Graves’ disease or Hashimoto’s thyroiditis would not create the characteristic uterine ultrasound findings.  

Therefore, a complete molar pregnancy best accounts for the combination of severe vomiting, snow-storm ultrasound appearance, and hyperthyroidism.

D.  She can be repaired perfectly by an intern on duty

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. She suffered a 3rd-degree tear.

Rationale:
Perineal tears are classified as:
• 1st degree – skin only  
• 2nd degree – perineal muscles but not anal sphincter  
• 3rd degree – involves anal sphincter complex (3a <50 % external sphincter, 3b >50 %, 3c both external & internal) with intact anorectal mucosa

The description given (extension from vagina, through perineal muscles, involving both external and internal anal sphincters, but sparing the anorectal mucosa) matches a 3rd-degree tear.  
Options A, B and D are incorrect: blaming the patient is inappropriate; 3rd-degree tears should be repaired as soon as possible in theatre (not after 24 h) by an experienced clinician, not by an unsupervised intern.

question: Which of the following statements is correct concerning operative abdominal delivery?
A: A hemogram, renal function test and grouping/crossmatch are mandatory tests before a caesarian section is done
B: Maternal morbidity and mortality from a caesarian section is not higher than vaginal
C: There is documented evidence that a classical uterine incision is better than a lower uterine segment transverse incision
D: There is no role in prophylactic antibiotics in elective caesarian sections
E: The sub-umbilical midline incision is the most popular abdominal entry technique in JOORTH
model_prompt:

###Question: Which of the following statements is correct concerning operative abdominal delivery? 

###Options:
A.  A hemogram, renal function test and grouping/crossmatch are mandatory tests before a caesarian section is done
B.  Maternal morbidity and mortality from a caesarian section is not higher than vaginal
C.  There is documented evidence that a classical uterine incision is better than a lower uterine segment transverse incision
D.  There is no role in prophylactic antibiotics in elective caesarian sections
E.  The sub-umbilical midline incision is the most popular abdominal entry technique in JOORTH

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E

Rationale  
• Pre-operative requirements: a full blood count and blood grouping / cross-match are obligatory, but a renal-function test is not routinely mandated; therefore statement A is inaccurate.  
• Both short- and long-term maternal morbidity and mortality are clearly higher after caesarean section than after vaginal birth, making statement B wrong.  
• Large comparative studies show the lower-segment transverse uterine incision to have less blood loss, lower infection rate and far better future obstetric performance than the classical vertical incision, so statement C is incorrect.  
• All modern guidelines recommend a single prophylactic dose of a broad-spectrum antibiotic for EVERY caesarean section, elective or emergency; hence statement D is false.  
• At JOORTH the quickest and most commonly employed skin incision for caesarean section is the sub-umbilical midline vertical incision, making statement E the only correct choice.

question: A 32-year-old female, known hypertensive patient on losartan/hydrochlorothiazide, presents for pre-conception care, ALL of the following are advised EXCEPT?
C: Change blood pressure medication to Methyldopa
D: Encourage her to take liver at least three times a week to improve iron stores
E: Advise her to start ANC when she learns that she is pregnant.
model_prompt:

###Question: A 32-year-old female, known hypertensive patient on losartan/hydrochlorothiazide, presents for pre-conception care, ALL of the following are advised EXCEPT?  

###Options:
A.  Folic Acid supplementation
B.  Quit alcohol and cigarette smoking
C.  Change blood pressure medication to Methyldopa
D.  Encourage her to take liver at least three times a week to improve iron stores
E.  Advise her to start ANC when she learns that she is pregnant.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Encourage her to take liver at least three times a week to improve iron stores

Rationale:
• Pre-conception care aims to optimise maternal health and minimise teratogenic exposures.  
• Folic acid supplementation (0.4–5 mg daily depending on risk) is strongly recommended to prevent neural-tube defects (Option A ‑ advised).  
• Cessation of alcohol and cigarette smoking decreases risks of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, miscarriage, growth restriction, placental abruption, etc. (Option B ‑ advised).

• Women should be counselled to book for antenatal care as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, ideally in the first trimester (Option E ‑ advised).  
• Frequent ingestion of liver is discouraged because it contains very high amounts of pre-formed vitamin A; excess vitamin A (>10,000 IU/day) in early pregnancy is teratogenic (craniofacial, cardiac and CNS defects). Therefore recommending liver three times a week is NOT appropriate (Option D ‑ not advised).

question: In the consideration, evaluation and management of persistent breech presentation:
A: When the estimated fetal weight is less than 1500 gms. vaginal delivery is usually without risk
B: External Cephalic Version may be offered at 28 weeks with the aim of a consequent vertex delivery
C: A well-flexed fetal neck is necessary for a vaginal breech delivery
D: The fetal bisacromial diameter is smaller than the intertrochanteric diameter
E: The Lovset maneuver is used to overcome head entrapment.
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: In the consideration, evaluation and management of persistent breech presentation:

###Options:
A.  When the estimated fetal weight is less than 1500 gms. vaginal delivery is usually without risk
B.  External Cephalic Version may be offered at 28 weeks with the aim of a consequent vertex delivery
C.  A well-flexed fetal neck is necessary for a vaginal breech delivery
D.  The fetal bisacromial diameter is smaller than the intertrochanteric diameter
E.  The Lovset maneuver is used to overcome head entrapment.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C

Rationale  
A. False – Very-low-birth-weight breech fetuses (<1500 g) have a high incidence of head entrapment and birth trauma; vaginal delivery is not “usually without risk.”  
B. False – Routine external cephalic version is recommended at 36-37 weeks, not at 28 weeks, because most fetuses will turn spontaneously before that gestation and early version carries a risk of reversion and pre-term complications.  
C. True – For a safe vaginal breech birth the fetal head must be fully flexed; an extended (deflexed) neck greatly increases the danger of head entrapment.  
D. False – The bisacromial (shoulder-to-shoulder) diameter (~12 cm) is actually larger than the bitrochanteric/inter-trochanteric diameter (~10 cm).  
E. False – The Lovset manoeuvre is used to deliver entrapped arms/shoulders, not to relieve head entrapment; head entrapment is managed with manoeuvres such as Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit, Piper forceps or Duhrssen incisions.

Hence, only statement C is correct.

question: Which of the following patients with primary hyperparathyroidism should undergo parathyroidectomy?
B: A 54-year-old woman with fatigue and depression
C: A 42-year-old woman with a history of kidney stones
D: A 60-year-old woman with mildly decreased bone mineral density measured at the hip of less than 2 standard deviations below peak bone density
E: A 70-year-old man with recurrent episodes of pancreatitis

###Question: Which of the following patients with primary hyperparathyroidism should undergo parathyroidectomy?  

###Options:
A.  A 62-year-old asymptomatic woman
B.  A 54-year-old woman with fatigue and depression

###Answer:

Rationale:  
Parathyroidectomy is recommended for primary hyperparathyroidism when any of the following guideline criteria are present:  
• Age < 50 years.  
• Symptomatic disease (classic symptoms include nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis, skeletal complications, or overt neuromuscular manifestations).  
• Serum calcium > 1 mg/dL (0.25 mmol/L) above the upper limit of normal.  
• Creatinine clearance < 60 mL/min, 24-hour urinary calcium > 400 mg, or presence of nephrolithiasis on imaging.  
• Bone mineral density T-score ≤ –2.5 at lumbar spine, total hip, femoral neck, or distal one-third radius, or a fragility fracture.

Option C meets two surgical criteria—age under 50 and a documented complication of nephrolithiasis—so parathyroidectomy is indicated.

The other options do not meet guideline criteria:  
A. Asymptomatic and > 50 years.  
B. Nonspecific symptoms (fatigue/depression) without objective complications.  
D. Bone density only mildly reduced (not ≤ –2.5).  
E. Recurrent pancreatitis is not an established surgical indication in current guidelines.

question: A 1-year-old child presents with crying continuously and drawing his legs up. The mother reports associated episodes of passing bloody mucus per rectum. A long, thin mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. No peritoneal signs are present. Intussusception is suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

E: Administration of IV fluids and observation

B.  Diagnostic laparoscopy with laparoscopic reduction

D.  Decompressive colonoscopy with placement of a rectal tube

• A 1-year-old with intermittent colicky pain, leg-flexing, and “currant-jelly” stools plus a sausage-shaped RUQ mass is the classic presentation of ileocolic intussusception.  
• In a hemodynamically stable child without peritoneal signs or perforation, the recommended first-line management is a contrast or air enema. The procedure is simultaneously diagnostic (confirms the intussusception radiographically) and therapeutic (pneumatic or hydrostatic pressure reduces the telescoped bowel in >90 % of cases).  

Why the other choices are not appropriate first:  
B. Diagnostic laparoscopy is reserved when enema reduction fails or perforation is suspected.  
C. Exploratory laparotomy and resection are indicated only for unsuccessful non-operative reduction, necrotic bowel, or perforation.  
D. Colonoscopy with rectal tube is used for volvulus, not intussusception.

question: Which of the following is a typical cause of neonatal intestinal obstruction?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following is a typical cause of neonatal intestinal obstruction? 

###Options:
A.  Intussusception
B.  Meconium ileus
C.  Pyloric stenosis
D.  Meckel's diverticulum
E.  Hirschsprung's disease

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Meconium ileus  

Rationale:  
• Neonatal intestinal obstruction presents in the first hours-to-days of life with abdominal distension, bilious vomiting and failure to pass meconium.  
• A classic and common neonatal cause is meconium ileus, produced by inspissated, tenacious meconium impacting the distal ileum—most often in infants with cystic fibrosis.  
• Intussusception (A) usually appears after the first few months of life (classically 6–18 months).  
• Pyloric stenosis (C) causes gastric-outlet, not intestinal, obstruction and presents at 2–8 weeks with non-bilious vomiting.  
• Meckel’s diverticulum (D) may cause obstruction or bleeding later in infancy or childhood, not typically in the newborn period.  
• Hirschsprung’s disease (E) can present neonatally, but it is a colonic obstruction and is less common overall than meconium ileus as a distinct neonatal intestinal blockage.  

Therefore, meconium ileus is the prototypical neonatal intestinal obstruction.

Maintenance fluids in pediatrics are calculated with the Holliday-Segar method:  
• First 10 kg: 100 mL/kg/day → 10 kg × 100 = 1000 mL  
• Next 10 kg (11-20 kg): 50 mL/kg/day → 10 kg × 50 = 500 mL  
• Remaining weight (>20 kg): 20 mL/kg/day → 2 kg × 20 = 40 mL  

Total for a 22-kg child: 1000 mL + 500 mL + 40 mL = 1540 mL ≈ 1550 mL.

question: Which of the following statements are TRUE regarding the premature neonate?
A: A 15% to 20% right-to-left shunt occurs across the foramen ovale and patent ductus arteriosus
B: Surfactant levels are normal after 30 weeks' gestation
C: Fluid requirements are lower than in a full-term baby
D: Rectal temperature is the best indicator of core body temperature
E: Premature neonates have a higher risk of hypoglycemia

B.  Surfactant levels are normal after 30 weeks' gestation
C.  Fluid requirements are lower than in a full-term baby
D.  Rectal temperature is the best indicator of core body temperature
E.  Premature neonates have a higher risk of hypoglycemia

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A and E

Rationale  
A. TRUE – In the immediate post-natal period pulmonary vascular resistance remains relatively high, especially in the premature infant, so about 15-20 % of the cardiac output can still bypass the lungs through the foramen ovale and/or a patent ductus arteriosus.  

B. FALSE – Adequate surfactant production usually is not reached until about 34-36 weeks’ gestation; at 30 weeks levels are still insufficient, which is why respiratory distress syndrome is common in very pre-term babies.  

C. FALSE – Premature neonates actually require larger fluid volumes per kilogram than term infants because of their greater insensible water losses (large surface-area-to-weight ratio, thin skin) and limited renal concentrating ability.  

D. FALSE – Rectal temperature may lag behind true core temperature and carries a risk of mucosal injury or perforation in the very small infant. Esophageal or properly placed skin probes are preferred for monitoring.  

E. TRUE – Premature babies have limited glycogen stores, minimal adipose tissue, and a high metabolic rate, all of which predispose them to hypoglycemia.

question: Which of the following statements is TRUE of infants with gastroschisis?

B: There is a high incidence of associated anomalies

D: It is associated with chromosomal syndromes
E: It frequently results in complications from infection

D.  It is associated with chromosomal syndromes
E.  It frequently results in complications from infection

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. There is prolonged adynamic ileus following repair.

Rationale:
• In gastroschisis the exposed bowel is bathed in amniotic fluid for months, producing marked serositis and edema. After reduction and closure, intestinal motility is slow to recover; feeds are often not tolerated for 2–3 weeks and the infant commonly needs prolonged parenteral nutrition—i.e. a prolonged adynamic ileus.

Why the other statements are false  
A. Although far less common than with omphalocele, malrotation can still be present (reported in up to 5–10 %); therefore it cannot be said to be “not associated.”  
B. Extra-intestinal congenital anomalies are uncommon (≈10 %), unlike the high rate seen with omphalocele.  
D. Gastroschisis has no consistent link with chromosomal syndromes; omphalocele, not gastroschisis, is the defect frequently associated with trisomies 13 and 18.  
E. Despite the absence of a protective sac, infection is not a major cause of morbidity when modern peri-operative care is used; problems are dominated by nutritional and motility issues rather than sepsis.

###Question: The following neonatal conditions are associated with maternal polyhydramnios EXCEPT:

B.  Duodenal atresia
C.  Hirschsprung's disease
D.  Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
E.  Anencephaly

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Hirschsprung's disease  

Rationale: Maternal polyhydramnios usually occurs when the fetus is unable to swallow and absorb amniotic fluid (e.g., upper gastrointestinal obstruction or severe neurologic impairment) or when there is excessive fetal urine production.  

• Esophageal atresia and duodenal atresia both block passage of swallowed fluid into the intestine, so the fluid accumulates → polyhydramnios.  
• Anencephaly eliminates the fetal swallowing reflex, also causing polyhydramnios.  
• Congenital diaphragmatic hernia is frequently accompanied by polyhydramnios because herniated abdominal viscera can interfere with normal swallowing and gastrointestinal transit.  

Hirschsprung's disease involves distal colonic aganglionosis; fetal swallowing and proximal gut transit remain essentially normal, so it is not typically linked to polyhydramnios.

• The “boot-shaped” (coeur en sabot) heart shadow is characteristic of tetralogy of Fallot – statement D is true.  

Hence the only false statement in the list is option E.

question: Which of the following is TRUE regarding benign prostate hyperplasia and prostate related issues

– N1 = metastasis to mobile/movable ipsilateral level I–II axillary lymph nodes.  
– N2 = fixed/matted axillary nodes or internal mammary nodes.  
– N3 = infraclavicular, supraclavicular, or combined axillary + internal mammary involvement.  
– The nodes are described as mobile ipsilateral axillary nodes → N1.  

• Metastasis (M):  
– M0 = no distant metastasis; M1 = distant metastasis present.  
– No evidence of distant spread → M0.  

Hence the TNM classification is T2N1M0.

question: Which of the following can cause secondary brain injury?

###Question: Which of the following can cause secondary brain injury?

A.  Hypoxia
B.  Hypotension
C.  Raised ICP
D.  Reduced cerebral perfusion
E.  All of the above

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E. All of the above

Rationale:
Secondary brain injury refers to the cascade of cellular, biochemical and hemodynamic insults that worsen the initial (primary) brain damage. Factors that precipitate or exacerbate secondary injury include:

• Hypoxia – inadequate oxygen delivery leads to cellular energy failure and neuronal death.  
• Hypotension – systemic low blood pressure lowers cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) and oxygen delivery.  
• Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) – elevated ICP decreases CPP (CPP = MAP − ICP) and impairs cerebral blood flow.  
• Reduced cerebral perfusion – whether from hypotension, raised ICP or vascular pathology, it deprives brain tissue of oxygen and substrates.

Because each listed factor independently contributes to secondary brain injury, the correct choice is “All of the above.”

question: Which of the following compensatory mechanisms maintain normal ICP in the face of an increasing intracranial mass lesion in adults?
model_prompt:

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following compensatory mechanisms maintain normal ICP in the face of an increasing intracranial mass lesion in adults?

###Options:
A.  Reduction in venous blood volume
B.  Increase in skull volume
C.  Sunsetting eyes
D.  Increase in CSF production.
E.  None of the above

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Reduction in venous blood volume

Rationale: In the rigid, non-expandable adult skull, the Monro-Kellie doctrine states that the sum of volumes of brain tissue, blood, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) must remain constant. When a new intracranial mass enlarges, the intracranial system initially compensates by displacing CSF into the spinal subarachnoid space and by reducing intracranial venous blood volume (venous sinus compression and venous outflow). These adjustments help keep intracranial pressure (ICP) near-normal in the early phase. The skull cannot expand in adults (so option B is incorrect), “sunsetting eyes” is merely a clinical sign of raised ICP (option C), and increasing CSF production would worsen rather than compensate for the pressure rise (option D). Therefore, reduction in venous blood volume is the correct compensatory mechanism.

question: How is cerebral perfusion pressure defined?
A: Systolic arterial blood pressure minus diastolic blood pressure
B: Systolic arterial blood pressure minus venous pressure
C: Mean arterial blood pressure minus venous pressure
D: Mean arterial blood pressure minus intracranial pressure (ICP)
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: How is cerebral perfusion pressure defined?

###Options:
A.  Systolic arterial blood pressure minus diastolic blood pressure
B.  Systolic arterial blood pressure minus venous pressure
C.  Mean arterial blood pressure minus venous pressure
D.  Mean arterial blood pressure minus intracranial pressure (ICP)
E.  Venous pressure minus ICP

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Mean arterial blood pressure minus intracranial pressure (ICP)

Rationale:
Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) represents the pressure gradient that drives blood flow through the brain. It is calculated as the difference between the mean arterial pressure (MAP) supplying the brain and the opposing pressure inside the skull, which is the intracranial pressure (ICP). Hence:

CPP = MAP − ICP (or − central venous pressure if that is higher).

Maintaining an adequate CPP is critical because if ICP rises or MAP falls, cerebral blood flow can decrease, leading to brain ischemia.

Rationale: In a healthy adult, intrinsic cerebral autoregulation keeps cerebral blood flow relatively constant over a plateau of mean arterial pressures roughly between 50–60 mmHg at the lower limit and 150–160 mmHg at the upper limit. Compartment syndrome represents a true surgical emergency. Temporising manoeuvres—such as splitting or bivalving the plaster cast, keeping the limb at the level of the heart, or removing tight dressings—should be done immediately when the condition is suspected, but they do not guarantee adequate reduction of intracompartmental pressure. Once clinical (or measured) evidence of compartment syndrome is present, urgent operative decompression is mandatory; delay markedly worsens functional outcome.

When the tumor’s size, location, neurovascular involvement, or extent of soft-tissue contamination makes limb-sparing resection impossible or unsafe, amputation is the standard and most appropriate procedure to achieve local tumor control and prevent metastasis.  
• Mangled or degloved limbs, while sometimes ending in amputation, are first assessed for vascular status and reconstructive possibilities; amputation is only a secondary, situational choice.  
• Cellulitis is treated medically with antibiotics and rarely necessitates amputation.  
• Chronic pain that is otherwise untreatable is an exceptional, controversial indication and is usually managed with non-amputative strategies.  

Thus osteosarcoma represents the clearest primary indication among the options.

C.  30-40%
D.  40-50%
E.  >50%

###Answer:

Correct option: C. 30-40 %

Rationale:
ATLS classifies hemorrhagic shock into four classes based on estimated blood-volume loss and physiologic responses.

• Class I (<15 % loss): HR <100 bpm, normal BP, normal or slightly ↑ RR, normal urine output.  
• Class II (15–30 % loss): HR 100-120, pulse pressure ↓, BP usually normal, RR 20-30, urine output 20-30 mL/h.  
• Class III (30–40 % loss): HR 120-140, systolic BP ↓, marked pulse-pressure narrowing, RR 30-40, urine output 5-15 mL/h, mental status anxious/confused.  
• Class IV (>40 % loss): HR >140, profound hypotension, RR >35, urine output negligible, mental status obtunded.

This patient has:
• HR 135 bpm (within 120-140)  
• Systolic BP 85 mm Hg (hypotensive)  
• Urine output ≈13 mL/h (low but not absent)

These findings align best with Class III hemorrhagic shock, corresponding to an estimated 30-40 % loss of circulating blood volume.

question: Surgery is the preferred option of treatment in which of the following cases of thyrotoxicosis?

###Question: Surgery is the preferred option of treatment in which of the following cases of thyrotoxicosis?

B.  Severe manifestations of Graves’ ophthalmopathy
C.  Relapse of Graves
D.  Presence of local compressive symptoms.
E.  All of the above

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E. All of the above  

Rationale  
Surgery (thyroidectomy or lobectomy, depending on the lesion) is preferred in several special situations of thyrotoxicosis:  

• Solitary/toxic (functioning) nodule – removal of the hyper-functioning lobe cures the thyrotoxicosis, avoids lifelong medication and eliminates any risk of malignancy within the nodule.  

• Severe Graves’ ophthalmopathy – radio-iodine can aggravate eye disease, so thyroidectomy, after achieving euthyroidism with antithyroid drugs, is the treatment of choice.  

• Relapse (or failure) of Graves’ disease after a full course of antithyroid drugs – definitive therapy is required; surgery provides a rapid, reliable cure, especially in young patients, pregnant women (2nd trimester) or when radio-iodine is contraindicated.  

• Large goitres producing local compressive symptoms (dysphagia, dyspnoea, retrosternal extension) – debulking by surgery immediately relieves the pressure and corrects the thyrotoxic state.  

Since each of the situations listed in options A, B, C and D represents a standard indication for operative management, the best answer is option E.

question: Which of the following are true regarding medical therapy for thyrotoxicosis?
A: Propranolol and nadolol reduce free T3 (fT3) and free T4 (fT4) levels.
B: Antithyroid drugs most often cure thyrotoxicosis due to a toxic nodule.
C: Carbimazole can be safely given in pregnancy and lactation.
D: Agranulocytosis is an uncommon problem with antithyroid drugs.
E: Patients with ophthalmopathy respond best to medical management
model_prompt:

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following are true regarding medical therapy for thyrotoxicosis?

###Options:
A.  Propranolol and nadolol reduce free T3 (fT3) and free T4 (fT4) levels.
B.  Antithyroid drugs most often cure thyrotoxicosis due to a toxic nodule.
C.  Carbimazole can be safely given in pregnancy and lactation.
D.  Agranulocytosis is an uncommon problem with antithyroid drugs.
E.  Patients with ophthalmopathy respond best to medical management

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D  

Rationale  
A. Propranolol (in high doses) can lower serum T3 slightly by inhibiting peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion, but it does not appreciably change free T4, and nadolol lacks this effect. Hence the statement that both drugs lower both fT3 and fT4 is incorrect.  

B. Toxic (autonomous) nodules are rarely “cured” by antithyroid drugs; the drugs only control hormone excess while they are taken. Definitive therapy is usually radio-iodine ablation or surgery.  

C. Carbimazole/methimazole is teratogenic in the first trimester, so propylthiouracil is preferred early in pregnancy; carbimazole can be used only after the first trimester and is safe during lactation. Therefore the blanket statement that it can be “safely given in pregnancy” is not true.  

D. Agranulocytosis is a well-recognized but rare adverse effect of thionamides, occurring in roughly 0.1–0.5 % of treated patients—hence it is uncommon.  

E. Thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy responds poorly to antithyroid drug therapy alone; moderate-to-severe cases require glucocorticoids, orbital radiation or surgery. Thus medical management of thyrotoxicosis is not the “best” treatment for ophthalmopathy.

• Repeat upper endoscopy with biopsy confirms histology but does not provide depth-of-invasion detail.  
• PET scan is useful for detecting metabolically active distant metastases, not for assessing tumor depth.  

Therefore, endoscopic ultrasound is the best study for assessing T status in esophageal adenocarcinoma.

A classic Z-plasty is created by making three incisions that form the letter “Z”; the two lateral limbs are usually set at about 60° to the central limb. question: A 65-year-old man sustains a 50% TBSA burn while burning trash in the backyard. The patient is resuscitated with lactated Ringer (LR) solution using the Parkland formula and a weight of 80 kg. What is the rate of LR given in the first 8 hours?

###Question: A 65-year-old man sustains a 50% TBSA burn while burning trash in the backyard. The patient is resuscitated with lactated Ringer (LR) solution using the Parkland formula and a weight of 80 kg. What is the rate of LR given in the first 8 hours?  
###Options:
A.  100 mL/h
B.  500 mL/h
C.  1000 mL/h
D.  5000 mL/h
E.  2000 mL/h

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. 1000 mL/h  

Rationale:  
The Parkland (4 mL) formula for burn resuscitation is:  
Total LR in first 24 h = 4 mL × weight (kg) × %TBSA burned  
= 4 mL × 80 kg × 50  
= 16 000 mL over 24 h.  

Half of this volume (8 000 mL) is infused in the first 8 h after the burn, giving:  
8 000 mL ÷ 8 h = 1 000 mL/h.

question: The nurse in the ward informs you that a patient developed difficulties in breathing and neck swelling 4 hours after thyroidectomy. You are the medical intern on call.  What is the next step in the management of this patient?

###Answer:

Rationale:

Oxygen, steroids, tracheostomy or intubation can be considered afterward, but they cannot be relied on to reverse the mechanical compression as rapidly as prompt wound decompression.

question: Which of the following statements is false regarding direct inguinal hernias?
A: The most likely cause is the destruction of connective tissue as a result of physical stress.
B: Direct hernias should be repaired promptly because of the risk of incarceration.
C: A direct hernia may be a sliding hernia involving a portion of the bladder wall.
D: A direct hernia may pass through the external inguinal ring
E: They are less common than indirect hernias
model_prompt:

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following statements is false regarding direct inguinal hernias?

A.  The most likely cause is the destruction of connective tissue as a result of physical stress.
B.  Direct hernias should be repaired promptly because of the risk of incarceration.
C.  A direct hernia may be a sliding hernia involving a portion of the bladder wall.
D.  A direct hernia may pass through the external inguinal ring
E.  They are less common than indirect hernias

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B  

Rationale:  
• Direct inguinal hernias arise through a weakened transversalis fascia in Hesselbach’s triangle; this weakening is usually related to age-associated loss of connective-tissue strength and repetitive increases in intra-abdominal pressure, making option A true.  
• Because the hernial neck is wide and the hernia simply bulges forward rather than following a narrow sac into the canal, direct hernias rarely incarcerate or strangulate. Therefore the assertion that they must be repaired promptly “because of the risk of incarceration” is incorrect, making option B the false statement.  
• A portion of the urinary bladder can form part of the wall of a direct (sliding) hernia, so option C is true.  
• A large direct hernia can protrude through the external (superficial) inguinal ring, so option D is true.  
• Indirect hernias are more common than direct hernias, so option E is true.

###Answer:

Rationale:  
Open mesh (Lichtenstein) inguinal hernia repair has a low recurrence rate and a low incidence of serious complications. The complication seen most frequently is chronic postoperative groin pain (inguinodynia), usually defined as pain persisting ≥3 months after surgery. It occurs in roughly 10 %–30 % of patients, largely related to irritation, entrapment, or neuroma formation of the ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric, or genitofemoral nerves.

• Urinary retention (B) occurs in only about 1 %–5 % of cases and is transient.  
• Reduced fertility (C) and ischemic orchitis (E) are rare.  

Therefore, chronic pain is the most common complication.

question: 32-year-old man comes to the emergency department with an acutely incarcerated inguinal hernia. With sedation, the hernia is reduced and he feels better. Eighteen hours later, he complains of increasing abdominal pain and has diffuse tenderness on examination. He most likely had which of the following?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: 32-year-old man comes to the emergency department with an acutely incarcerated inguinal hernia. With sedation, the hernia is reduced and he feels better. Eighteen hours later, he complains of increasing abdominal pain and has diffuse tenderness on examination. He most likely had which of the following?

###Options:
A.  Diastasis recti
B.  Petit’s (lumbar) hernia
C.  Epigastric hernia
D.  Amyand’s hernia
E.  Richter’s hernia

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E. Richter’s hernia  

Rationale:  
• A Richter’s hernia contains only the antimesenteric wall of the intestine, so the lumen is usually still patent; therefore classic signs of bowel obstruction are often absent.  
• When such a hernia becomes incarcerated/strangulated and is then “reduced,” the devitalized rim of bowel can be pushed back into the peritoneal cavity unrecognized.  
• Hours later the ischemic segment perforates, producing diffuse abdominal pain and peritonitis, exactly as occurred in this patient 18 hours after reduction.  

The other choices do not explain delayed peritoneal symptoms after successful reduction of an inguinal hernia:  
A Diastasis recti – no hernial sac, not incarcerated.  
B Petit’s (lumbar) hernia – occurs in lumbar triangle, not inguinal.  
C Epigastric hernia – through linea alba above umbilicus, unlikely here.  
D Amyand’s hernia – contains appendix; reduction would not typically cause diffuse peritonitis unless appendicitis was already present.  

Thus, the presentation is most characteristic of a Richter’s hernia.

question: A competent lower oesophageal junction prevents the reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus. This function is compromised when
A: The length of the sphincter is 3 cm or more
B: The sphincter complex is drawn into the distal oesophagus due to oesophageal fibrosis
C: The resting pressure of the sphincter is at 20mmHg
D: A previously obese person loses excess weight
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A competent lower oesophageal junction prevents the reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus. This function is compromised when 

 
  

 


###Options:
A.  The length of the sphincter is 3 cm or more
B.  The sphincter complex is drawn into the distal oesophagus due to oesophageal fibrosis
C.  The resting pressure of the sphincter is at 20mmHg
D.  A previously obese person loses excess weight
E.  The lower esophageal sphincter relaxes

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E. The lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes.

Rationale  
Reflux is most commonly precipitated by inappropriate or prolonged relaxations of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LES). A normal LES is 2–4 cm long and maintains a basal pressure of about 15–30 mm Hg, preventing retrograde flow of gastric contents.  
• A length ≥3 cm (option A) and a resting pressure of 20 mm Hg (option C) are both within the normal range and therefore do not, by themselves, impair competence.  
• Drawing the sphincter “into the distal oesophagus” (option B) is not the mechanism that compromises competence; in fact, what usually produces incompetence is displacement of the sphincter into the thorax as in a sliding hiatus hernia.  
• Weight loss in a previously obese person (option D) generally lessens, rather than worsens, reflux.  
• Transient or sustained relaxation of the LES (option E) removes the high-pressure barrier and allows gastric contents to regurgitate into the oesophagus, so this is the situation in which competence is truly lost.

A.  Femoral nerve
B.  Hypogastric nerve
C.  Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
D.  Ilioinguinal nerve
E.  Vagus nerve

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Ilioinguinal nerve

Rationale:
• The ilioinguinal nerve (L1) traverses the inguinal canal, runs just inferior to the spermatic cord, and provides sensory innervation to the ipsilateral upper scrotum/labia majora, root of the penis/ mons pubis, and the medial portion of the upper thigh.  
• During an open inguinal hernia repair this nerve is commonly encountered and, if stretched, entrapped in scar, or transected, can produce postoperative chronic groin pain.  
• Typical findings of ilioinguinal nerve injury include:  
  – Hyperesthesia or allodynia over the hernia incision/scar.  
  – Numbness or dysesthesia of the ipsilateral scrotum and medial upper thigh.  
  – Pain that radiates into the testicle and is exacerbated by hip flexion or prolonged sitting (which stretches the nerve).  

The other choices do not match the sensory pattern described:  
A. Femoral nerve – supplies anterior thigh and medial leg below the knee; no scrotal innervation.  
B. Hypogastric nerve – autonomic; not responsible for cutaneous sensation.  
C. Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve – supplies lateral thigh (meralgia paresthetica).  
E. Vagus nerve – cranial parasympathetic; no role in groin sensation.

Therefore, injury to the ilioinguinal nerve best explains this patient’s persistent post-herniorrhaphy pain pattern.

• Epididymo-orchitis – although less common than the other complications, an undescended testis can become acutely infected.  
• Infertility – prolonged exposure to body-cavity temperature damages the germinal epithelium, reducing sperm production.  
• Malignancy (especially seminoma) – the risk of testicular cancer is 3–10× higher in a retained testis.

Since each of the options A-D represents a documented complication, “All the above” is the correct choice.

• Option E – Symptoms usually worsen, not improve, with advancing age.

Therefore option B is the only true statement.

Two doses of FFP (10 ml/kg) were also administered. What is the next appropriate step with regard to the patient’s developing dilutional coagulopathy? 

###Options:
A.  Order PT, aPTT, platelet count, and fibrinogen level STAT and order more FFP (10 ml/kg), platelets (10 ml/kg), and 3 pooled units of cryoprecipitate.
B.  Order platelets (10 ml/kg) and more FFP (10 ml/kg) x 3 doses.
C.  Order platelets only and then PT, aPTT, fibrinogen.
D.  Order more pRBCs (emergency release) and give platelets (10 ml/kg), then  order more FFP (10 ml/kg).
E.  Administer vitamin K and continue to monitor coagulation parameters.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A

Rationale  
• Massive transfusion (15 U of packed red cells ≈ 4.5 L) has replaced >2 × the patient’s total blood volume, making dilution of platelets, fibrinogen and other clotting factors inevitable.  
• When >1 blood-volume has been transfused, current recommendations are to draw coagulation studies STAT (PT, aPTT, platelet count, fibrinogen) and, without waiting for results, give balanced replacement of:  
  – Fresh-frozen plasma 10 mL/kg (≈4 units in a 40-kg patient) to replete the vitamin-K-dependent and other soluble factors;  
  – Platelets 10 mL/kg (one apheresis or 5–6 pooled-random donor units) to restore the platelet count;  
  – Cryoprecipitate (usually 10 units, 2–3 pooled bags) to raise fibrinogen (the first factor to fall to a critical level).  
• Option A is the only choice that simultaneously obtains the necessary laboratory data and empirically replaces all three depleted components (FFP, platelets, cryoprecipitate).  
• Options B–E fail to supply cryoprecipitate, omit laboratory assessment, or provide unnecessary additional red cells/vitamin K, and therefore do not adequately address dilutional coagulopathy.

Hence, option A is most appropriate.

The patient has septic shock secondary to an acute intra-abdominal process (fever, tachycardia, hypotension, peritonitis, absent bowel sounds). First-hour (“golden hour”) management of severe sepsis/shock requires:

• Rapid crystalloid bolus (initial target ≈30 mL/kg; a 1-L bolus is an acceptable immediate start while more fluid is being prepared).  
• Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics that cover gram-negative enteric organisms and anaerobes (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole).

Rationale:  
Fournier’s gangrene is a rapidly progressive necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and genital region. The infection spreads along fascial planes, producing systemic sepsis and high mortality if not promptly treated. The cornerstone of therapy is:

• Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms, started as soon as possible and continued after surgery.

Flap coverage (option C) is considered only after infection is controlled and healthy granulation tissue is present, not at the initial presentation. Palliative care (D) or oral analgesics (E) do not address the life-threatening sepsis. Therefore, option B is the mainstay of management.

The ALVARADO score in this patient is

###Options:
A.  8
B.  7
C.  6
D.  3

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. 8

Rationale:

Alvarado (“MANTRELS”) scoring for suspected acute appendicitis  
• M – Migration of pain to RIF … 1  
• A – Anorexia (loss of appetite) … 1  
• N – Nausea / vomiting … 1  
• T – Tenderness in right iliac fossa … 2  
• R – Rebound tenderness … 1  
• E – Elevated temperature (> 37.3 °C) … 1  
• L – Leukocytosis (WBC > 10 ×10⁹/L) … 2  
• S – Shift to left (neutrophilia > 75 %) … 1  
Maximum score = 10

Patient’s findings  
• Migration – not reported … 0  
• Anorexia present … +1  
• Nausea/vomiting present … +1  
• RIF tenderness present … +2  
• Rebound tenderness absent … 0  
• Temperature 37.8 °C … +1  
• WBC 22 ×10⁹/L … +2  
• Neutrophils 95 % … +1  

Total = 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 8

Therefore, the Alvarado score is 8.

###Answer:

Continued hemorrhage or any situation that markedly reduces tissue perfusion lowers oxygen delivery to cells. In response, cells switch to anaerobic metabolism, producing lactic acid. Rationale:
A leftward shift of the oxyhaemoglobin-dissociation curve indicates an increased affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen (i.e., oxygen is bound more tightly and released less readily to tissues). Factors that produce a left shift include:

• ↓ temperature

In primary hypothyroidism the thyroid gland fails to produce adequate thyroxine (T4). Hence, a high TSH is the parameter most indicative of hypothyroidism.

Biochemical androgen estimation (e.g., serum total or free testosterone) can support the diagnosis but is not mandatory if clinical hyperandrogenism is evident, and serum FSH/LH levels are no longer required for diagnosis. Therefore this statement is false.  

C) Infertility in PCOS is predominantly due to chronic anovulation — true.  

D) Because PCOS ovaries contain many small antral follicles and are highly gonadotrophin-sensitive, women with PCOS have an increased risk of OHSS during both simple ovulation induction (e.g., with clomiphene or letrozole) and controlled ovarian hyperstimulation for IVF — true.  

E) Lifestyle modification and even modest weight loss (5-10 % of body weight) can restore ovulation and improve metabolic parameters; hence weight loss is recommended as first-line therapy — true.

• Amantadine (C) can give modest benefit and may even help dyskinesias, but its antiparkinsonian efficacy is limited and it is not the preferred long-term single agent in a 52-year-old newly diagnosed patient.  
• Ropinirole (A) is a non-ergot dopamine D2/D3 agonist. It is effective as initial monotherapy in younger patients, postpones the need for levodopa (thereby delaying levodopa-induced dyskinesias), and, unlike ergot derivatives, is not associated with pulmonary or cardiac fibrotic complications. A: A Loss of the vaginal backboard support to the urethra leads to urethral hypermobility
B: B Loss of the vaginal backboard support to the urethra leads to intrinsic sphincter deficiency
C: C Damage to the striated urogenital sphincter and/or the vascular submucosal tissues causes intrinsic sphincter deficiency
D: D The anterior vaginal wall gains stability through its lateral attachment to the levator ani muscles and the arcus tendinous fasciae pelvis (ATFP)

model_prompt:

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following statements is not true regarding pathophysiology of stress incontinence
###Options:
A.  A Loss of the vaginal backboard support to the urethra leads to urethral hypermobility
B.  B Loss of the vaginal backboard support to the urethra leads to intrinsic sphincter deficiency
C.  C Damage to the striated urogenital sphincter and/or the vascular submucosal tissues causes intrinsic sphincter deficiency
D.  D The anterior vaginal wall gains stability through its lateral attachment to the levator ani muscles and the arcus tendinous fasciae pelvis (ATFP)
E.  E Urinary continence requires a well vascularized urethral submucosal tissue, a functioning straited urogenital sphincter and an intact vaginal wall support.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B

Rationale:
Stress urinary incontinence results from either (1) loss of anatomic support of the urethra and bladder neck (urethral hyper-mobility) or (2) intrinsic sphincter deficiency (ISD).

• When the “vaginal backboard” (the sub-urethral portion of the anterior vaginal wall that is anchored to the pelvic side-wall) is attenuated or detached, the urethra loses its firm hammock and becomes mobile; this produces urethral hypermobility—not ISD (Option A is true).

• ISD, on the other hand, is produced by direct injury or degeneration of the urethral sphincter mechanism itself—damage to the striated sphincter, its innervation, or its richly vascular submucosa (Option C is true).

• The anterior vaginal wall is stabilized laterally by the arcus tendineus fasciae pelvis and the levator ani muscles (Option D is true).

• Continence depends on an intact urethral submucosa, a competent sphincter, and adequate vaginal/ligamentous support (Option E is true).

Therefore, the statement that loss of the vaginal backboard support “leads to intrinsic sphincter deficiency” (Option B) is incorrect.

Rationale:  
During storage of whole blood at 4 °C a number of biochemical and cellular “storage lesions” occur:  

• 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) levels fall markedly, so Hb binds oxygen more tightly and releases less to tissues (statement A is true).  
• Viability and function of leucocytes fall rapidly; granulocytes are essentially non-functional after 24 h (statement B is true).  
• Platelets lose viability within about 24 h in refrigerated whole blood; they are therefore considered non-functional (statement C is true).  
• Red cells develop membrane changes; ATP falls, they become more rigid and fragile, and are more easily damaged (statement D is true).  

Because 2,3-DPG falls and membrane changes occur, the blood’s ability to deliver oxygen to the tissues actually declines; it does not “improve.” Therefore statement E is incorrect and is the exception.

###Answer:

Rationale:  
When a patient is kept strictly NPO and receives only routine crystalloid or 5 % dextrose/normal saline for several days, no significant source of phosphate is provided. ###Question: 42. In the management of hyperkalaemia, which of the measures is instituted to avert cardiac arrest
###Options:

B.  b.Nebulization with salbutamol
C.  Administration of sodium bicarbonate
D.  d.Administration of dextrose and insulin
E.  Administration of normal saline

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Administration of calcium chloride

Rationale:
In severe hyperkalaemia, the immediate life-threatening concern is ventricular arrhythmia leading to cardiac arrest. Intravenous calcium (calcium chloride or calcium gluconate) does not lower the serum potassium, but it rapidly stabilises the cardiac myocyte membrane, raising the threshold potential and counteracting the depolarising effect of high extracellular potassium. This protective effect begins within 1-3 minutes and can last 30-60 minutes, buying time for other therapies (e.g., insulin-dextrose, nebulised β2-agonists, sodium bicarbonate) that actually shift potassium into the cells or remove it from the body. Therefore, calcium chloride is the measure specifically instituted to avert imminent cardiac arrest in hyperkalaemia.

###Options:

###Answer:

Correct option: E.  All of the above  

Rationale:  
An incisional hernia develops through a weakness in the musculofascial layers at the site of a previous laparotomy wound. Any factor that compromises wound healing or markedly increases intra-abdominal pressure during the postoperative period predisposes to this complication.

• Post-operative wound infection (A) impairs collagen deposition and causes fascial necrosis, weakening the scar.  
• Wound dehiscence (B) is a direct failure of fascial closure; survivors almost invariably develop an incisional hernia later.  
• Persistent coughing (C) greatly raises intra-abdominal pressure, exerting stress on the fresh suture line.  
• Chronic straining during micturition from benign prostatic hyperplasia (D) similarly increases intra-abdominal pressure and stresses the wound.

Since each of these factors independently promotes incisional hernia formation, the best answer is “All of the above.”

###Answer:

Correct option: C. white, blue, red

Rationale:
Raynaud’s phenomenon produces a classic triphasic color change of the affected digits as blood flow is altered:
1. White (pallor) – intense digital arteriolar vasoconstriction sharply reduces blood flow.

3. Red (hyperemia) – reperfusion and reactive vasodilatation cause flushing and erythema.

Therefore the typical sequence is white → blue → red, corresponding to option C.

C.  c.Ringer’s lactate
D.  d.Dextrose-Normal Saline
E.  Gelofusine

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Ringer’s lactate

Rationale: “Physiological” implies a crystalloid whose electrolyte composition, osmolality and acid–base effect resemble that of normal plasma. Ringer’s lactate (Hartmann’s solution) contains sodium, chloride, potassium, calcium and lactate in concentrations close to those in extracellular fluid; the lactate is metabolised to bicarbonate, helping maintain physiologic pH. Hence Ringer’s lactate is the most physiological of the listed fluids.

###Answer:

Rationale  
A patient with small–bowel obstruction and repeated bilious (upper intestinal) losses is usually volume depleted and acidotic. The best initial resuscitation fluid is an isotonic, “balanced” crystalloid that:  
• rapidly expands the intravascular volume,  
• supplies sodium, chloride and a small amount of potassium and calcium, and  
• contains lactate, which is metabolised to bicarbonate and helps correct the metabolic acidosis produced by the loss of alkaline intestinal secretions.  

Ringer’s lactate (Hartmann’s solution) fulfils these requirements and is therefore preferred over plain normal saline (high chloride, can worsen acidosis) or glucose-containing solutions (not suitable for rapid volume replacement).

question: The following are accepted indications for induction of labour

D.  D) History of precipitate labour

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C) Intra-uterine fetal death  

Rationale:  
Induction of labour is undertaken when ending the pregnancy clearly offers more benefit than continuing it. Accepted medical indications include conditions such as post-term pregnancy, pre-labour rupture of membranes, maternal hypertension or diabetes, fetal growth restriction, chorio­amnionitis, and intra-uterine fetal demise.  

• Suspected macrosomia alone is not a recommended reason for induction; the evidence does not show improved outcomes and caesarean may be preferred for very large fetuses.  
• A previous caesarean section is not an indication; in fact, it is a relative contraindication to pharmacological induction because of the risk of uterine rupture.  
• Intra-uterine fetal death requires delivery, and induction is the standard management once the diagnosis is confirmed.  
• A history of precipitate (very rapid) labour and maternal request, in the absence of other obstetric or medical indications, are not accepted medical reasons for induction.

E. An early, high-pitched “blowing” diastolic murmur along the left sternal border is classic for aortic regurgitation (incompetence).

###Answer:

Pulsus paradoxus is defined as an exaggerated fall (> 10 mm Hg) in systolic arterial pressure during inspiration. D: d.1L of RL, 1L of NS and 2L

###Question: 30. A 48-year-old man living in Liberia had an elective left hemicolectomy on account of adenocarcinoma of the caecum. Today is POD 2 following the surgery. The patient is stable and well hydrated. Bowel function has not resumed. Patient is being kept nil per os. What is the fluid requirement of this patient?
###Options:
A.  a.1L of RL and 2L of 5% Dextrose.
B.  b.2L of RL and 1L of 5% Dextrose
C.  2L of NS and 1L of RL
D.  d.1L of RL, 1L of NS and 2L

Rationale  
• A 70-kg adult needs ≈ 25–30 mL kg⁻¹ day⁻¹ of water (≈ 2–2.5 L), 1 mmol kg⁻¹ day⁻¹ of Na⁺ (≈ 70–100 mmol) and a similar amount of Cl⁻, plus K⁺ supplementation.  
• During the first 48 h after major abdominal surgery the gut is atonic, so maintenance fluids must be given IV with isotonic solutions to replace extracellular losses and some free water.

• Regimens with only 1 L RL (option A) under-replace electrolytes; those with large amounts of NS (option C, D) risk hyperchloremic acidosis; oral intake (option E) is not yet appropriate.  

Hence, 2 L RL + 1 L 5 % dextrose best meets the patient’s POD-2 maintenance fluid needs.

question: The jugulovenous pressure
A: Is raised if it is 2 cm from the sternal angle with the patient seated at 45°
B: Tall 'a' waves may be seen in pulmonary hypertension
C: Irregular cannon waves indicate complete heart block
D: Regular cannon waves may indicate a nodal rhythm
E: Giant 'v' waves and a pulsatile liver indicate tricuspid regurgitation
model_prompt:

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: The jugulovenous pressure	

###Options:
A.  Is raised if it is 2 cm from the sternal angle with the patient seated at 45°
B.  Tall 'a' waves may be seen in pulmonary hypertension
C.  Irregular cannon waves indicate complete heart block
D.  Regular cannon waves may indicate a nodal rhythm
E.  Giant 'v' waves and a pulsatile liver indicate tricuspid regurgitation

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: B, C, D, and E

Rationale  
A. False – A JVP 2 cm above the sternal angle at 45° is within the normal range (normal ≤3–4 cm); it is therefore not “raised.”  
B. True – Tall (giant) ‘a’ waves occur when right-atrial contraction meets a high downstream resistance, as in pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary stenosis or tricuspid stenosis.  
C. True – In complete heart block there is AV dissociation; occasional atrial contractions coincide with a closed tricuspid valve, producing intermittent (irregular) cannon ‘a’ waves.  
D. True – When every beat originates from a junctional (nodal) rhythm with retrograde atrial activation, cannon ‘a’ waves occur with each cycle and are therefore regular.  
E. True – Severe tricuspid regurgitation causes regurgitant flow into the right atrium during systole, giving rise to giant ‘v’ (or fused ‘cv’) waves in the JVP and a pulsatile, systolic-expanding liver.

question: The physical signs of an uncomplicated large pneumothorax is associated with one of these except?
A: The trachea deviated to the opposite side
B: A clicking sound asynchronous with the heart beat
D: Increased breath sounds over the pneumothorax
E: Increased percussion note over the pneumothorax

B.  A clicking sound asynchronous with the heart beat
C.  Symmetrical expansion of the chest
D.  Increased breath sounds over the pneumothorax
E.  Increased percussion note over the pneumothorax

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D.  Increased breath sounds over the pneumothorax  

Rationale  
In an uncomplicated (simple) large pneumothorax the affected hemithorax is full of free air, so the lung is collapsed and virtually silent. Typical physical findings are:  
• Hyper-resonant or “increased” percussion note.  
• Markedly diminished or absent breath sounds.  
• Reduced (often absent) chest movement on the affected side; if the pneumothorax is very large the opposite lung may push the mediastinum across, producing tracheal deviation.  
• Occasionally a mediastinal “click” (Hamman’s sign) may be heard, especially with a large left-sided lesion.  

What is never found is louder (increased) breath sounds over the pneumothorax, because the collapsed lung cannot conduct air entry to the chest wall. Therefore option D is the single statement that is not a physical sign of an uncomplicated large pneumothorax.

question: Which is true about electrocardiogram

D: Left bundle branch block is suggested by broadening of the QRS complex to 0.10 seconds (two and a half little squares), and positive RSR' waves in V4-V6.

###Question: Which is true about electrocardiogram

A.  The PR interval is measured from the peak of the P wave to the start of the QRS complex
B.  Right axis deviation is indicated by a QRS axis of -35°

###Answer:

Rationale:
A The PR interval is measured from the onset (not the peak) of the P wave to the onset of the QRS complex, so A is incorrect.

question: About heart failure which is false?

B: Congestion of the pulmonary veins alone does not result in orthopnoea
C: Chronic congestive heart failure leads to secondary hyperaldosteronism
D: Causes of heart failure include ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, and thiamine deficiency
E: Clinical features of right heart failure include a raised JVP, ankle oedema, and hepatomegaly

Rationale:
• Left-sided heart failure commonly presents with tachycardia, basal lung crepitations, and may show pulsus alternans → statement A is true.

question: 29. The main aim of the Ebb phase of the metabolic response to trauma is
A: a.Conservation of blood volume and energy store
B: b.Breakdown of tissues to produce raw materials for wound healing
C: c.Building up of lost body tissues
D: d.Mobilization of amino acids and glucose
E: e.Increase the production of acute phase reactants
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: 29. The main aim of the Ebb phase of the metabolic response to trauma is 
###Options:
A.  a.Conservation of blood volume and energy store
B.  b.Breakdown of tissues to produce raw materials for wound healing
C.  c.Building up of lost body tissues
D.  d.Mobilization of amino acids and glucose
E.  e.Increase the production of acute phase reactants

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Conservation of blood volume and energy store  

Rationale:  
After significant injury the body passes through two classic metabolic phases: the early “Ebb” phase (first 12-24 h) and the subsequent “Flow” phase.  
• Ebb phase: character­ised by reduced metabolic rate, decreased oxygen consumption, lower cardiac output, and hormonal changes that aim to maintain vital organ perfusion and limit further losses. The overriding purpose during this acute period is to conserve circulating blood volume and energy reserves while the patient is stabilised.  
• Flow phase: follows once resuscitation is achieved; it is hyper­metabolic and catabolic, involving mobilisation of amino acids and glucose, breakdown of tissues, and increased synthesis of acute-phase proteins to support wound healing.  

Therefore the main aim of the Ebb phase is conservation of blood volume and energy stores, making option A the correct choice.

question: Concerning hypertension which is true
A: An average diastolic blood pressure of >90 mmHg over prolonged observation is an indication for drug treatment in uncomplicated hypertension
B: Thiazide diuretics are the least effective antihypertensive drugs
C: Thiazide diuretics work on the loop of Henle in the kidney
D: Resistant hypertension is defined as a failure to control the blood pressure adequately with a good three-drug regimen
E: Thiazide diuretics are not contraindicated in gout and diabetes
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).

###Question: Concerning hypertension which is true

###Options:
A.  An average diastolic blood pressure of >90 mmHg over prolonged observation is an indication for drug treatment in uncomplicated hypertension
B.  Thiazide diuretics are the least effective antihypertensive drugs
C.  Thiazide diuretics work on the loop of Henle in the kidney
D.  Resistant hypertension is defined as a failure to control the blood pressure adequately with a good three-drug regimen
E.  Thiazide diuretics are not contraindicated in gout and diabetes

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D  

Rationale  
A. Persistently elevated diastolic pressure usually has to be ≥95 mm Hg (or systolic ≥140 mm Hg) before routine drug therapy is started in otherwise uncomplicated hypertension; therefore a value just above 90 mm Hg alone is not, in most guidelines, an automatic indication for drugs.  
B. Thiazides are among the most effective, evidence-based agents for lowering blood pressure and reducing cardiovascular events.  
C. Thiazides inhibit the Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, not in the loop of Henle (loop diuretics act there).  
D. Resistant hypertension is defined as blood pressure that remains above target despite adherence to an appropriate three-drug regimen (of different classes, one ideally being a diuretic) at optimal doses. Hence this statement is true.  
E. Thiazides can raise serum uric acid and glucose; they may precipitate gout and can worsen glycaemic control, so they are relatively contraindicated in gout and used cautiously in diabetes.

question: The following are not associated with pansystolic murmur except
model_prompt:

###Question: The following are not associated with pansystolic murmur except

D.  Atrial septal defect

###Answer:

Rationale:  
A pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur begins with S₁ and extends uniformly through systole to S₂. It characteristically occurs when there is a constant pressure gradient between two chambers throughout systole. Classic causes are:

• Mitral regurgitation  
• Tricuspid regurgitation  
• Ventricular septal defect  

The other listed conditions produce different murmurs:  
• Mitral stenosis – mid- to late-diastolic rumbling murmur.  
• Aortic regurgitation – early diastolic decrescendo murmur.  
• Atrial septal defect – typically has a fixed split S₂ with an ejection systolic flow murmur.  
• Aortic stenosis – crescendo–decrescendo (ejection) systolic murmur.

Thus, among the options, only tricuspid regurgitation is associated with a pansystolic murmur.

more often if membrane folding or liquor discordance occurs

C.  . II and III
D.  . II only

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. I and III

Rationale  

I) True – For monochorionic twin pregnancies the principal purpose of frequent scans is to detect early signs of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS).  If “early warning” features such as membrane folding or developing liquor discordance are seen, UK- and US-based guidelines advise increasing the surveillance interval (e.g. weekly instead of fortnightly) because the risk of rapid progression to significant TTTS is higher.

II) False – Routine surveillance for fetal growth discordance is not advised every 2 weeks from 20 weeks in all multiple pregnancies.  Current guidance recommends:
• Monochorionic twins: growth assessment every 2 weeks from 16 weeks until 28 weeks, then every 3–4 weeks.  
• Dichorionic twins: every 4 weeks from 24 weeks.  
• Triplets: every 2 weeks from 16 weeks.  
Thus “every 2 weeks from 20 weeks” is not the recommended schedule for all twin and triplet pregnancies.

III) True – Large trials and systematic reviews have not demonstrated a clear benefit from routine umbilical artery Doppler studies in otherwise uncomplicated multiple pregnancies. Therefore routine Doppler screening for fetal growth problems is not currently supported by evidence and is reserved for cases where growth restriction or abnormal fluid volumes are already suspected.

Therefore only statements I and III are correct.

A: Anticipated difficulty with the patient’s anxiety (i., he might falsely claim chest pain during the test)
B: The increased risk associated with these high blood pressure readings
C: Concern about the heart murmur, a relative contraindication to stress testing

The thought of performing a routine Bruce protocol treadmill exercise test (stress test) comes to mind, but is rejected, primarily due to which of the following?

B.  The increased risk associated with these high blood pressure readings

E.  Concern that this represents the onset of unstable angina with unacceptable risk of MI with stress testing

###Answer:

Rationale:
The diagnostic value of a routine treadmill (Bruce-protocol) exercise ECG depends on one’s ability to interpret exercise-induced ST-segment shifts. When the resting ECG already contains abnormal ST-T repolarisation changes—such as those produced by left ventricular hypertrophy with “strain” pattern—additional ST depression or T-wave abnormalities produced by exercise cannot be distinguished from the baseline abnormality. This markedly lowers the specificity (and therefore the clinical usefulness) of a standard exercise ECG and is considered a relative contraindication / poor indication for the test; a stress modality that adds imaging (stress echo or nuclear perfusion) would be preferred.

• Anxiety may make the test uncomfortable but is not a contraindication (A).
• Mild-moderate hypertension (140–150/90–100 mm Hg) is acceptable for exercise testing (B).
• A soft (grade 1/6) systolic murmur without other findings does not preclude testing (C).
• The patient’s chest pain has been evaluated, enzymes are negative, and there is no evidence of ongoing unstable angina (E).

Therefore, the baseline LVH with secondary ST-T changes is the principal reason to avoid a routine treadmill ECG stress test.

C.  Uterine Rupture
D.  Maternal hypotension
E.  Magnesium sulphate administration

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E. Magnesium sulphate administration

Rationale:  
Fetal distress is most commonly the result of acute or chronic impairment of uteroplacental or umbilical cord blood flow, leading to fetal hypoxia and acidosis.

• Cord prolapse (A) → umbilical cord compression → sudden interruption of fetal oxygen supply → rapid fetal distress.  
• Abruptio placentae (B) → premature separation of the placenta → loss of maternal-fetal gas exchange → acute fetal hypoxia and distress.  
• Uterine rupture (C) → catastrophic loss of uterine integrity and placental separation → profound fetal hypoxia/distress.  
• Maternal hypotension (D) → decreased uterine perfusion → reduced fetal oxygen delivery → fetal distress.

Magnesium sulphate (E), used for seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia/eclampsia and for fetal neuroprotection, may transiently reduce baseline FHR variability but does not typically produce true fetal hypoxia or distress. Therefore, it is the exception.

###Question: Select the CORRECT statement regarding abnormal labour:

A.  A primary arrest is when labour does not progress past the latent phase over 8 hours
B.  A primary arrest is when labour does not progress past the latent phase over 8 hours
C.  Primary arrest is commonly due to fetal malposition
D.  Secondary arrest is typically from uterine dysfunction
E.  In secondary arrest, it is impossible for the baby to be born vaginally

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D

Rationale  
In abnormal labour, arrest disorders are usually related to the quality of the uterine contractions (“powers”).  
• Primary arrest (primary dysfunctional labour) is present from the outset of the active phase and is classically due to inadequate uterine activity, not to malposition or CPD.  
• Secondary arrest (secondary uterine inertia) follows a period of normal progress; contractions then fade and labour stops. This pattern is therefore typically the result of uterine dysfunction (hypotonic or in-coordinate action). It often responds to augmentation with oxytocin, and a vaginal birth is still achievable.  

Why the other choices are wrong  
A / B  Primary arrest is defined in the active phase, not the latent phase, and the diagnostic time-limit is loss of progress for ≥2 h, not “over 8 h” in latent labour.  
C Fetal malposition most commonly causes secondary arrest, not primary arrest.  
E Secondary arrest does not make vaginal delivery impossible; correction of the uterine activity or instrumental/rotational delivery can still result in a vaginal birth.

Rationale:
This elderly patient describes the classic symptom triad of aortic stenosis—exertional angina (“substernal chest pressure”), exertional dyspnea/heart-failure signs (bibasilar rales), and syncope. Calcific degeneration of the aortic valve is the most common cause in patients >65 years. The hallmark auscultatory finding of aortic stenosis is a harsh, systolic, crescendo-decrescendo (ejection) murmur that peaks in mid-systole and is best heard at the right second intercostal space (upper right sternal border), typically radiating to the carotids.  

Why the other choices are incorrect  
B. Diastolic decrescendo murmur at the mid-left sternal border → typical of aortic regurgitation.  
C. Holosystolic murmur at the apex → typical of mitral regurgitation.  
D. Midsystolic click → characteristic of mitral valve prolapse.  
E. Pansystolic murmur (holosystolic) without the described location/radiation most often implies mitral regurgitation or a VSD.

Thus, option A matches the clinical picture.

• Fertilization (often loosely called “conception”) takes place in the ampullary portion of the fallopian tube, so the fallopian tube is the anatomical site of conception → statement C is true.

###Answer:
outputs:

Rationale:
Ropinirole is a non-ergot, selective dopamine D2/D3 receptor agonist. It directly stimulates central dopamine receptors, thereby substituting for the diminished endogenous dopamine characteristic of Parkinson’s disease. question: Mrs. A. E. G6P5 delivers a 4.2kg male baby at 38weeks gestation by spontaneous vaginal delivery. The blood loss at her delivery is estimated to be 1200mls. She is still bleeding. Which of the following is preferred for her resuscitation?

###Question: Mrs. A. E. G6P5 delivers a 4.2kg male baby at 38weeks gestation by spontaneous vaginal delivery. The blood loss at her delivery is estimated to be 1200mls. She is still bleeding. Which of the following is preferred for her resuscitation?
###Options:
A.  Colloid solutions and ephedrine
B.  Crystalloid and ephedrine
C.  Colloid solutions and blood
D.  crystalloids and blood
E.  None of the above

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Crystalloids and blood  

Rationale:  
Post-partum haemorrhage with ≥1 000 mL blood loss and continuing bleeding is a medical emergency that needs rapid restoration of circulating volume and oxygen-carrying capacity. Initial volume expansion is best begun with warmed isotonic crystalloids (e.g., Ringer’s lactate or normal saline) because they are readily available, inexpensive, and effective for intravascular volume replacement. At the same time, or as soon as cross-matched units are available, packed red blood cells should be transfused to replace ongoing losses and maintain haemoglobin/oxygen delivery. Vasopressors such as ephedrine should not be given until adequate volume has been restored, and colloid solutions are not superior to crystalloids for initial resuscitation and add cost and potential adverse effects. Therefore the recommended combination is crystalloids plus blood.

During obstetric haemorrhage the key aim is to maintain adequate circulating volume and tissue perfusion. Urine output, however, directly reflects renal and hence systemic perfusion; a rate ≥30 mL/hour indicates that resuscitation is adequate, whereas falling output is an early, sensitive sign of continuing hypovolaemia. For this reason, continuous monitoring of urine output with an indwelling catheter is regarded as one of the most important observations in the ongoing management of obstetric haemorrhage.

###Options:

B.  Alteplase
C.  Dexamethasone
D.  Aspirin
E.  NONE OF THE ABOVE

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Aspirin  

Rationale:  
• The presentation (acute focal deficit, normal CT) is consistent with an ischaemic stroke.  
• Intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase is only licensed up to 4.5 hours from symptom onset; this patient is already 5 hours from onset, so thrombolysis is contraindicated.  
• Once intracranial haemorrhage has been excluded by CT, the recommended initial therapy for an ischaemic stroke that is not eligible for thrombolysis is oral/rectal aspirin 300 mg as soon as possible (and within 24 h).  
• Low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin) is not recommended for acute stroke treatment (used only for DVT prophylaxis).  
• Dexamethasone has no role in routine management of acute ischaemic stroke.  

Therefore, aspirin is the most appropriate initial management.

###Answer:

Rationale:
Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is a paraneoplastic disorder (often with small-cell lung cancer) caused by antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type Ca²⁺ channels.

• Unlike myasthenia gravis, muscle strength in LEMS improves—rather than worsens—after repeated contraction (post-tetanic facilitation). Therefore statement D is false.

Because the question asks for the feature that is NOT characteristic, option D is the correct choice.

###Answer:

Rationale:
Massive obstetric haemorrhage rapidly produces profound hypovolaemia, loss of oxygen-carrying capacity and dilutional/consumptive coagulopathy. Audits of maternal deaths (e.g., UK CEMD/CEMACH and similar reviews in low-resource countries) show that the most frequent avoidable factor leading to death is failure to replace the lost blood promptly and in sufficient volume. Crystalloids or colloids alone cannot correct the deficit, and delay or inadequacy in providing packed red cells and blood components is therefore the commonest cause of maternal mortality in massive blood loss situations—more so than renal failure, fluid resuscitation with clear fluids, or monitoring deficiencies.

###Question: Which of the following conditions can result in significant consumptive coagulation?

C.  Pre Eclampsia with severe features
D.  Gram-negative bacterial sepsis

###Answer:

Rationale: Consumptive coagulopathy, or disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), occurs when extensive activation of the coagulation cascade consumes platelets and clotting factors faster than they can be replaced. Hence each of the individual choices (A, B, C, and D) can lead to significant consumptive coagulation, making “All of the above” the correct answer.

question: In a patient that developed hemianopia with predominately the lower quadrants being affected. What is the most likely lesion

###Question: In a patient that developed hemianopia with predominately the lower quadrants being affected. What is the most likely lesion
###Options:
A.  Brainstem lesion
B.  Craniopharyngioma
C.  Frontal lobe lesion
D.  Pituitary macroadenoma
E.  NONE OF THE ABOVE

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Craniopharyngioma  

Rationale:  
• The lower (inferior) visual-field quadrants are carried by fibres that arise from the superior retinal quadrants and occupy the upper part of the optic chiasm.  
• A suprasellar mass that compresses the chiasm from above therefore damages these upper chiasmal fibres first, producing a bitemporal hemianopia that is most marked in the lower quadrants.  
• Craniopharyngiomas typically arise above the sella turcica and press downward on the optic chiasm, fitting this pattern.  
• In contrast, pituitary macroadenomas grow upward from below the chiasm and initially affect the inferior chiasmal fibres, causing loss that begins in the upper temporal quadrants.  
• Brain-stem or frontal-lobe lesions do not characteristically give this visual-field pattern.

Hence, a craniopharyngioma is the most likely lesion.

###Question: A 55-year-old man is referred to the neurology clinic due to a resting tremor and an abnormal gait characterised by short, shuffling steps. Which one of the following features would point towards a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease rather than parkinsonism of another cause?

B.  Bradykinesia
C.  Impairment of vertical gaze
D.  Poor response to levodopa therapy
E.  NONE OF THE ABOVE

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Asymmetrical tremor  

Rationale:  
• Idiopathic Parkinson’s disease classically begins on one side of the body and remains asymmetrical for years. A resting tremor that is clearly worse in one limb than the other therefore favours Parkinson’s disease.  
• Bradykinesia (option B) is a core diagnostic feature but is present in all parkinsonian syndromes, so it does not distinguish idiopathic Parkinson’s disease from other causes.  
• Impairment of vertical gaze (option C) is typical of progressive supranuclear palsy, an atypical parkinsonism, and argues against idiopathic Parkinson’s disease.  
• A poor response to levodopa (option D) likewise suggests an atypical parkinsonian disorder (e.g., PSP, MSA, CBD) rather than idiopathic Parkinson’s disease, which usually shows a good, sustained response.

Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae) commonly colonises the genitourinary tract of pregnant women.
