###Question: The best treatment of subdural haematoma in a deteriorating patient
###Options:
A.  Use of steroid
B.  Oxygenation
C.  Surgical evacuation
D.  Infusion of oral Mannitol
E.  Mechanical Ventilation

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Surgical evacuation

Rationale:
In a patient with an acute subdural haematoma who is neurologically deteriorating, the priority is to urgently decompress the brain and remove the clot that is causing mass effect and raised intracranial pressure. Surgical evacuation (usually via craniotomy or, in select cases, burr-hole drainage) achieves this definitive decompression. Steroids have no proven benefit in acute subdural bleeding, osmotic agents such as mannitol provide only transient ICP reduction, and supportive measures (oxygenation or mechanical ventilation) are adjuncts rather than definitive therapy. Therefore, prompt surgical evacuation is the treatment of choice.

Troponins done were normal. What diagnosis best fits with the clinical scenario?

###Options:
A.  Non ST elevation myocardial infarction
B.  Unstable angina
C.  Non cardiac chest pain
D.  Stable angina
E.  ST elevation myocardial infarction

###Answer:

Rationale:  
• Typical anginal pain: substernal discomfort precipitated by exertion (tennis, walking, treadmill) and relieved by rest; each episode lasts <20 min.  
• Pattern has remained essentially unchanged for ≥2 months, so it is “stable,” not “unstable.”  
• No resting pain, no acceleration in frequency/severity, and no pain at minimal exertion—all argue against unstable angina.  
• Normal troponins exclude myocardial infarction (rules out STEMI and NSTEMI).  
• ECG shows LVH with strain (T-wave inversion in V5–V6); this is a chronic finding and not diagnostic of an acute coronary syndrome.  
Hence, the presentation is most consistent with stable effort angina.

question: A 40-year-old man presents to the Emergency Unit with retrosternal chest pain which occurred while jogging. He reports a similar previous episode while playing football 2 weeks prior. His father died suddenly at 42 years and his brother died at the age of 21. Examination reveals a fourth heart sound and a systolic murmur loudest at the left sternal border. What diagnosis fits best with the clinical findings?

###Question: A 40-year-old man presents to the Emergency Unit with retrosternal chest pain which occurred while jogging. He reports a similar previous episode while playing football 2 weeks prior. His father died suddenly at 42 years and his brother died at the age of 21. Examination reveals a fourth heart sound and a systolic murmur loudest at the left sternal border. What diagnosis fits best with the clinical findings?

###Options:
A.  Primary dilated cardiomyopathy
B.  Aortic stenosis
C.  Coronary artery disease
D.  Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
E.  Restrictive cardiomyopathy

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Rationale:
• Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is typically inherited (autosomal-dominant) and is a common cause of sudden death in young or middle-aged individuals, especially during exertion; the patient’s father and brother died suddenly at young ages, supporting a familial HCM.  
• Exertional chest pain or syncope is characteristic because the dynamic left-ventricular outflow tract obstruction worsens with exercise.  
• Physical findings: a mid- to late-systolic crescendo–decrescendo murmur best heard along the left sternal border and an S4 due to a stiff, hypertrophied ventricle.  
• Primary dilated cardiomyopathy and restrictive cardiomyopathy do not usually present with a harsh systolic murmur or such strong familial sudden-death history.  
• Aortic stenosis produces a systolic murmur best at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids, and is less likely to cause sudden death at such young ages without typical valve disease history.  
• Coronary artery disease is possible but does not explain the murmur and prominent family sudden-death pattern.

Therefore the presentation fits hypertrophic cardiomyopathy best.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

###Question: A 22-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with history of sudden onset palpitations. Blood pressure on arrival is 85/50 mmHg. ECG done shows atrial fibrillation with heart rate of 140 bpm and he is electrically cardioverted. Repeat ECG shows sinus rhythm but a short PR interval and delta waves. What is the most likely diagnosis?

###Options:
A.  Brugada syndrome
B.  Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
C.  Long QT syndrome
D.  Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
E.  Hyperthyroidism

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome

Rationale:
A short PR interval (<120 ms) together with a slurred upstroke of the QRS complex (delta wave) is the classic ECG signature of pre-excitation via an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent), which defines Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome. Patients with WPW are prone to paroxysmal tachyarrhythmias, including atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia and atrial fibrillation, which can present with haemodynamic compromise as in this case. The other listed disorders do not produce the combination of a short PR interval and delta waves.

question: Which of the following causes a diastolic murmur?

###Question: Which of the following causes a diastolic murmur?

C.  Mitral stenosis
D.  Aortic stenosis
E.  Mitral valve prolapse

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Mitral stenosis  

Rationale:  
• Diastolic murmurs occur when abnormal flow happens during ventricular relaxation (diastole).  
• Mitral stenosis narrows the mitral valve orifice, so blood flowing from the left atrium to the left ventricle during diastole generates a low-pitched, rumbling diastolic murmur often preceded by an opening snap.  
• The other listed conditions all characteristically produce systolic murmurs:  
  – Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur from LV outflow tract obstruction.  
  – Ventricular septal defect: holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur.  
  – Aortic stenosis: crescendo–decrescendo systolic ejection murmur.  
  – Mitral valve prolapse: late systolic murmur with midsystolic click.

question: A 24 year old man who has suffered from recurrent shoulder dislocation is found to have an early diastolic murmur best heard at left third intercostal space. He is tall and thin with a long arm span. What is the likely cause of the murmur?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 24 year old man who has suffered from recurrent shoulder dislocation is found to have an early diastolic murmur best heard at left third intercostal space. He is tall and thin with a long arm span. What is the likely cause of the murmur?

###Options:
A.  Aortic regurgitation
B.  Aortic stenosis
C.  Pulmonary stenosis
D.  Tricuspid regurgitation
E.  Mitral stenosis

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Aortic regurgitation

Rationale:  
The patient’s physical habitus (tall, thin, increased arm-span) and joint laxity causing recurrent shoulder dislocation point toward a connective-tissue disorder such as Marfan syndrome. Marfan patients frequently develop dilation of the aortic root, leading to incompetence of the aortic valve. Aortic regurgitation produces a high-pitched, early decrescendo diastolic murmur that is classically best heard along the left sternal border at the 2nd–4th intercostal spaces (often described at the left 3rd ICS). ###Answer:

Answer: B. Romano-Ward syndrome  

Rationale: The key abnormality on this patient’s ECG is a prolonged corrected QT (QTc) interval. Congenital long-QT syndromes present in otherwise healthy young people with palpitations, syncope or sudden collapse precipitated by emotional stress or exercise. Romano-Ward syndrome is the common autosomal-dominant form of congenital long-QT syndrome and classically shows a prolonged QTc on a resting ECG.  
• Brugada syndrome produces characteristic coved ST-segment elevation in V1–V3, not QT prolongation.  
• Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes syncope with exertion but does not prolong the QT interval.  
• Wolff-Parkinson-White shows a short PR interval and delta wave.  
• Atrial myxoma presents with positional symptoms or embolic phenomena, not isolated QT prolongation.  

Thus the most likely cause of his symptoms and ECG finding is Romano-Ward syndrome.

Primary pulmonary hypertension produces a sustained elevation of pulmonary-artery pressures. The right ventricle must pump against this high afterload; over time it hypertrophies and then dilates. Left-sided findings such as LV hypertrophy, mitral regurgitation, or left-atrial enlargement are not typical consequences of isolated pulmonary hypertension, and pulmonary stenosis is a separate valvular lesion unrelated to the condition.

question: Which of the following causes a loud first heart sound?

###Question: Which of the following causes a loud first heart sound?

B.  Mitral stenosis
C.  Aortic regurgitation
D.  Tricuspid regurgitation
E.  Pulmonary hypertension

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Mitral stenosis

Rationale:
The first heart sound (S₁) is generated by closure of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves. It becomes louder when these valves are widely separated at the onset of ventricular systole yet remain mobile enough to close briskly. This situation is classically seen in rheumatic mitral stenosis: elevated left-atrial pressure holds the mitral valve leaflets open during diastole, and because the leaflets are still relatively pliable, they snap shut forcefully, producing a loud S₁.  
• Aortic stenosis (A) and aortic regurgitation (C) primarily affect the aortic valve and usually make S₁ normal or soft.  
• Tricuspid regurgitation (D) may soften or vary S₁.  
• Pulmonary hypertension (E) accentuates the pulmonary component of the second heart sound (P₂), not S₁.

D.  Atrial myxoma

###Answer:

Rationale:
In mitral valve prolapse (MVP) the mitral leaflets billow back (“prolapse”) into the left atrium during ventricular systole. When the redundant leaflet and chordae suddenly tense, a sharp, high-frequency sound—the midsystolic (or mid-late systolic) click—is produced. As systole continues, the regurgitant flow through the incompletely closed valve generates a late systolic murmur that follows the click. This click-late systolic murmur combination is the classic auscultatory hallmark of MVP and is not typical of isolated mitral regurgitation, mitral stenosis, atrial myxoma, or aortic regurgitation.

###Question: The following is seen in patients with complete heart block except

C.  Atrioventricular dissociation on ECG
D.  Responsiveness to atrial pacing
E.  Sudden death

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D.  Responsiveness to atrial pacing

Rationale:
• Complete (third-degree) heart block is characterized by absence of conduction through the AV node, producing atrioventricular dissociation.  
• Clinical and electrocardiographic findings commonly include:  
  – Syncopal (Stokes–Adams) attacks due to transient asystole or very slow ventricular escape rhythm.  
  – Cannon ‘a’ waves in the jugular venous pulse when the right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve.  
  – AV dissociation on ECG, with independent atrial (P-wave) and ventricular (QRS) rhythms.  
  – Risk of sudden death from prolonged asystole or malignant ventricular arrhythmias.  
• Because the block is below (or within) the AV node, impulses originating in the atria—whether spontaneous or generated by an atrial pacemaker lead—cannot reach the ventricles; therefore the patient does not respond to atrial pacing. Ventricular (or dual-chamber) pacing is required.

Thus “Responsiveness to atrial pacing” is the feature NOT seen in complete heart block.

question: Concerning Melanoma, which of the following statements is True?
A: Ulceration of the primary lesion is associated with worsening of prognosis
B: A brisk tumor infiltrating lymphocyte response is associated with worse prognosis
C: Clark’s level III implies invasion of the reticular dermis
D: Suspicious lesions should be evaluated by initial incision biopsy
E: Sentinel lymph node mapping should be considered for lesions of intermediate depth

D.  Suspicious lesions should be evaluated by initial incision biopsy
E.  Sentinel lymph node mapping should be considered for lesions of intermediate depth

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option(s): A and E  

Rationale  

A. Ulceration is an adverse prognostic feature in melanoma. In every modern staging system (e.g., AJCC), the presence of ulceration up-stages the T category and is independently associated with lower disease-specific survival.  

B. A brisk tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) response actually correlates with a better, not worse, prognosis.  

C. Clark level III denotes invasion through the papillary dermis and into the papillary–reticular dermal interface; invasion of the reticular dermis is Clark level IV.  

D. The recommended initial diagnostic procedure for a suspicious cutaneous melanoma is an excisional biopsy with 1–2 mm clinical margins. Incisional (or punch) biopsy is reserved only when complete excision would be impractical (e.g., large facial lesions).  

E. Sentinel lymph-node (SLN) mapping is routinely considered for melanomas of intermediate thickness (≈1–4 mm) because this group carries a significant yet not inevitable risk of nodal metastasis, and SLN status provides important prognostic and therapeutic information.

question: Which of the following statements is True in normal wound healing?
B: Fetal wounds heal by regeneration without fibrosis so do not result in scars
C: Haemostasis creates a protective wound scab beneath which cell migration and movement of the wound edges can occur
D: Partial thickness wounds regenerate much more rapidly than full thickness wounds of the same surface area
E: In adults, full thickness wounds are repaired by fibrosis (scar tissue)
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following statements is True in normal wound healing?
###Options:
A.  Partial thickness wounds are painless
B.  Fetal wounds heal by regeneration without fibrosis so do not result in scars
C.  Haemostasis creates a protective wound scab beneath which cell migration and movement of the wound edges can occur
D.  Partial thickness wounds regenerate much more rapidly than full thickness wounds of the same surface area
E.  In adults, full thickness wounds are repaired by fibrosis (scar tissue)

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C  

Rationale  
•  Haemostasis produces a platelet–fibrin clot that quickly dries to form a protective scab. This stabilises the wound surface; epithelial cells, fibroblasts and other reparative cells migrate underneath the scab and the wound edges can move (contract) beneath it.  

Why the other options are incorrect  
A. Partial-thickness wounds are usually painful because many dermal nerve endings remain intact.  
B. Only early-gestation fetal wounds heal without scarring; later-gestation fetal wounds and therefore “fetal wounds” in general cannot be said never to scar.  
D. Rate of healing correlates mainly with wound surface area; a small full-thickness wound may heal faster than a large partial-thickness abrasion, so the statement is not universally true.  
E. Adult full-thickness wounds heal by a combination of epithelial regeneration and fibroplasia; they are not repaired solely by fibrosis.

A 76-year-old man is admitted with a right hemiparesis. He first noticed weakness on his right side around six hours ago. A CT scan shows an ischaemic stroke and aspirin 300mg is commenced. terms of further management in the acute phase, 
which one of the following values should not be corrected?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 76-year-old man is admitted with a right hemiparesis. He first noticed weakness on his right side around six hours ago. A CT scan shows an ischaemic stroke and aspirin 300mg is commenced. terms of further management in the acute phase, 
which one of the following values should not be corrected? 

###Options:
A.  A.	BP 170/110
B.  B.	Blood glucose 11.2 mmol/l
C.  C.	Oxygen saturation 93%
D.  D.	Temp 38.3ºC
E.  NONE OF THE ABOVE

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. BP 170/110 mm Hg

Rationale  
• Blood pressure – In the acute phase of an ischaemic stroke, a moderate elevation of blood pressure is usually left alone because cerebral perfusion may depend on it. Current guidelines advise lowering BP only if:  
  – the patient is a candidate for thrombolysis and BP > 185/110 mm Hg, or  
  – BP > 220/120 mm Hg in patients not receiving thrombolysis, or there is another compelling reason (e.g. aortic dissection, acute heart failure).  
  A reading of 170/110 mm Hg therefore should not be actively reduced.

• Blood glucose – Hyperglycaemia (> 10 mmol/L) is associated with worse neurological outcome; it should be corrected with insulin if necessary (glucose here is 11.2 mmol/L).

• Oxygen saturation – Hypoxia (SpO₂ < 95 %) should be corrected with supplemental oxygen; saturation of 93 % warrants oxygen therapy.

• Temperature – Fever (≥ 37.5–38 °C) should be treated with antipyretics and search for infection, as hyperthermia worsens neuronal injury; temperature is 38.3 °C.

Therefore, among the listed parameters, only the blood pressure of 170/110 mm Hg should not be corrected acutely.

High-quality randomized controlled trials and Cochrane reviews show that a short course of oral corticosteroid (e.g., prednisolone 50-60 mg daily for 5–10 days started within 72 h of onset) significantly increases the likelihood of complete recovery in Bell’s palsy. Surgical decompression is not routinely recommended, and “no treatment” is inferior to corticosteroid therapy. Therefore, prednisolone is the evidence-based first-line management.

Rationale  
“Humoral” immunity refers to immune mechanisms mediated by soluble factors present in the body fluids (“humors”), chiefly antibodies found in plasma, serum, and lymph. It does not refer to the cellular components of blood.

Therefore, the false statement is option A.

Osteophytes are bony outgrowths that form at the joint margins as a reparative response to articular cartilage degeneration. Thus, marginal osteophytes on an X-ray most strongly indicate degenerative (osteo)arthritis.

• Reactive arthritis (D) requires a preceding GI/GU infection and typically shows other features such as conjunctivitis or urethritis.

Therefore, the most likely pathology is psoriatic arthritis spondylitis.

###Answer:

Felty syndrome is defined by the triad of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis, splenomegaly, and neutropenia (leukopenia). The patient has well-established RA, now presents with a palpable spleen and a white blood cell count of 2 500/µL—all classic features of Felty syndrome.

• Rheumatoid nodules are extra-articular manifestations of RA but do not disrupt bone-marrow architecture to cause leukopenia.  
• A normal variation would not explain both splenomegaly and a WBC count this low.

Therefore, Felty syndrome is the most likely diagnosis.

question: Which one of the following selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors has the highest incidence of discontinuation symptoms?

###Question: Which one of the following selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors has the highest incidence of discontinuation symptoms? 
###Options:
A.  Paroxetine
B.  Citalopram
C.  Escitalopram
D.  Fluoxetine
E.  NONE OF THE ABOVE

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Paroxetine  

Rationale: Discontinuation symptoms are most likely when a serotonin-reuptake inhibitor has a short plasma half-life and no long-acting active metabolite, because serum levels fall abruptly if a dose is missed or the drug is stopped. Paroxetine fits this profile (t½ ≈ 21 h, no active metabolite) and consistently shows the highest rate of withdrawal symptoms (e.g., dizziness, flu-like feelings, insomnia, anxiety). Citalopram and escitalopram have intermediate half-lives, and fluoxetine has a very long half-life plus the long-acting metabolite norfluoxetine, so clinically significant discontinuation reactions are uncommon with them. Therefore, paroxetine is the SSRI most associated with discontinuation syndrome.

Rationale:
The tri-phasic color change (white → blue → red) precipitated by cold, vibration or emotional stress is characteristic of Raynaud phenomenon.

• Internal organ involvement is not inevitable; in primary Raynaud there is none, and even in secondary forms it depends on the underlying disease (option D is false).

B: B.	Reserpine inhibits activities of prolactin

###Question: Which of the following is not true about reserpine?

A.  A.	Reserpine binds tightly to adrenergic storage vesicles in central and peripheral adrenergic neurons for prolonged periods of time
B.  B.	Reserpine inhibits activities of prolactin
C.  C.	The overall result is that of   pharmacological sympathectomy.
D.  D.	Reserpine-induced depletion of biogenic amines correlates with evidence of sympathetic dysfunction and antihypertensive effects.
E.  NONE OF THE ABOVE

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B

Rationale:  
• Reserpine irreversibly blocks the vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT), so it binds tightly to storage vesicles in central and peripheral adrenergic neurons for long periods (statement A is true).  
• By depleting vesicular dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, reserpine actually REDUCES the tonic dopaminergic inhibition of prolactin release; this results in increased, not decreased, prolactin levels (galactorrhea, gynecomastia). Therefore, “Reserpine inhibits activities of prolactin” is incorrect (statement B is false).  
• The widespread loss of norepinephrine from sympathetic nerve endings mimics a chemical sympathectomy (statement C is true).  
• The antihypertensive effect of reserpine correlates with depletion of norepinephrine, dopamine, and serotonin, leading to signs of sympathetic dysfunction (statement D is true).

Thus, option B is the statement that is NOT true.

###Answer:
outputs:

Rationale:
Drugs that produce a generalized ganglionic blockade interrupt transmission in both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia.  
• Parasympathetic blockade → loss of tone in visceral smooth muscle, causing atony of the gastrointestinal tract and urinary bladder (so option A is true).

• Interruption of autonomic ganglia also abolishes baroreceptor-mediated circulatory reflexes (so option D is true).  
• Parasympathetic blockade markedly reduces secretions, giving a dry mouth; it does NOT cause salivation (option C is false).

Therefore, salivation is the exception.

question: Which of the following features on neurologic examination is most likely to be associated with a lesion of the cerebellar vermis?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following features on neurologic examination is most likely to be associated with a lesion of the cerebellar vermis?
###Options:
A.  A.	Truncal ataxia
B.  B.	Limb ataxia
C.  C.	Lhermite sign
D.  D.	Rhomberg sign
E.  NONE OF THE ABOVE

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Truncal ataxia  

Rationale:  
The cerebellum is functionally divided into the midline vermis and the lateral hemispheres.  
• The vermis coordinates axial (truncal) and proximal muscle control; damage here produces instability of the trunk and a broad-based, “drunken” gait—referred to as truncal or gait ataxia.  
• The cerebellar hemispheres coordinate distal limb movements; lesions there cause limb (appendicular) ataxia such as dysmetria or intention tremor.  
• Lhermitte sign (an electric-shock sensation down the spine on neck flexion) is typically due to cervical spinal cord lesions, not cerebellar disease.  
• A positive Romberg sign reflects impaired proprioception or vestibular function, not primary cerebellar vermis dysfunction.  

Therefore, truncal ataxia (option A) is the feature most closely linked to a cerebellar vermis lesion.

• Radial neuropathy causes sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand, not the palmar surface.  
• Multiple sclerosis would not present with an isolated, unilateral median-nerve distribution deficit.  

Therefore, carpal tunnel syndrome is the most likely diagnosis.

• Opioid withdrawal (C) causes mydriasis, lacrimation, diaphoresis, rhinorrhea, piloerection, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea, not dry skin or anticholinergic signs.  
• Phencyclidine (PCP) intoxication (D) may cause agitation and nystagmus; pupils are usually normal or may be small, and skin is often moist from diaphoresis.  
• “None of the above” (E) is unnecessary because one option clearly fits.

Therefore, anticholinergic intoxication is the most likely cause.

###Question: Your patient has a loss of general sensation and ageusia on the posterior one third of the tongue, and touching the lateral wall of the throat fails to elicit a gag reflex. The neural structure that is the most likely to have been lesioned is the
###Options:

Rationale:
• Posterior one-third of tongue – General somatic sensation and taste (ageusia) are both carried by cranial nerve IX (glossopharyngeal).  
• Gag reflex – The afferent (sensory) limb runs in the glossopharyngeal nerve from the mucosa of the oropharynx; the efferent limb is via the vagus (CN X). Loss of the reflex when the pharyngeal wall is touched therefore indicates a lesion of the afferent glossopharyngeal component.  
• Vagus (CN X) lesions would more typically present with dysphonia, palatal droop, or loss of the efferent limb of the gag reflex, but taste/sensation on the posterior tongue would be intact.  
• Facial (CN VII) supplies taste to the anterior two-thirds, not the posterior one-third.  
• Trigeminal (CN V) supplies general sensation to the anterior two-thirds only.  

Thus the constellation of findings best localises to damage of the glossopharyngeal nerve.

question: Alcoholic ‘‘blackouts’’ during alcohol intoxication most likely occur because of effects of alcohol on which of the following CNS structures?

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Alcoholic ‘‘blackouts’’ during alcohol intoxication most likely occur because of effects of alcohol on which of the following CNS structures?
###Options:
A.  Cerebellum
B.  Frontal lobes
C.  Hippocampi
D.  Medial vestibular nuclei
E.  NONE OF THE ABOVE

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option:  
C. Hippocampi  

Rationale:  
An alcoholic “blackout” is an episode of anterograde amnesia in which the intoxicated person can carry on conversations and appear awake but later cannot recall events that occurred during that period. Formation of new explicit (episodic) memories requires intact hippocampal function, particularly the ability of hippocampal neurons to undergo long-term potentiation. High blood levels of ethanol selectively depress hippocampal activity and disrupt this memory consolidation process, leading to the characteristic amnesia. In contrast, cerebellar involvement causes ataxia, frontal lobe impairment causes disinhibition and poor judgment, and vestibular nuclei effects lead to vertigo and nystagmus, none of which specifically produce the memory gap of a blackout.

• Bell’s palsy (A) presents with identical facial weakness but lacks the zoster vesicular eruption.  
• Neurosarcoidosis (B) is a more indolent, multisystem disease.  
• Pontine infarction (C) would usually produce additional brainstem signs (e.g., diplopia, limb weakness, ataxia).  
Therefore, Ramsay Hunt syndrome is the most likely diagnosis.

###Question: Your patient has a lesion that has resulted in a loss of touch sensations in the face. The patient still feels pain and temperature sensations, and there is no jaw weakness. The neural structure most likely affected is the
###Options:
A.  Aspinal nucleus of V
B.  Trigeminal ganglion
C.  Principal nucleus of V
D.  Mesencephalic nucleus of V
E.  NONE OF THE ABOVE

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Principal nucleus of V

Rationale:  
• Discriminative (fine) touch and vibration from the face synapse in the principal (chief) sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve in the pons.  
• Pain and temperature fibers descend in the spinal tract of V and synapse in the spinal (caudal) nucleus of V, so they are spared if only the principal nucleus is damaged.  
• The motor (masticatory) nucleus of V is separate; therefore a lesion confined to the principal nucleus does not produce jaw weakness.  
• A trigeminal ganglion lesion would abolish all facial sensations (touch, pain, temperature).  
• A spinal nucleus lesion would remove pain-temperature, not touch.  
• A mesencephalic nucleus lesion would affect proprioception/jaw-jerk reflex, not selectively touch.  

Thus, selective loss of touch with preserved pain–temperature and normal jaw strength localizes the lesion to the principal nucleus of V.

###Question: A 35-year-old man presents for evaluation of muscle weakness. He was well until 3 days ago, when he started developing progressive weakness in his arms and legs. On the morning of presentation, he had significant difficulty walking and presented to the emergency department. He reports an episode of severe diarrhea 4 weeks ago and denies associated pain. Examination reveals normal facial strength; quadriparesis with 3/5 strength in proximal upper and lower extremities and 0/5 strength in bilateral ankle dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, inversion and eversion; intact sensory function; and generalized areflexia. Nerve conduction studies demonstrate reduced distal motor amplitudes, but no evidence of conduction block. Sensory conduction studies are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
###Options:
A.  Aute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP)
B.  Acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN)
C.  Acute motor-sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN)
D.  Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP)
E.  NONE OF THE ABOVE

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option:  
B. Acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN)

Rationale:  
• Time course – rapidly progressive over days, typical of an acute Guillain-Barré spectrum disorder rather than a chronic process such as CIDP.  
• Clinical picture – pure motor weakness with normal sensory examination points to a motor-predominant variant.  
• Reflexes – generalized areflexia fits any GBS variant.  
• Nerve-conduction study – markedly reduced distal motor amplitudes (axonal loss) with no conduction block or demyelinating features, and completely normal sensory studies. This electrophysiologic pattern characterizes the AMAN variant.  
• AIDP would show demyelinating features (slowed conduction velocity, prolonged distal latencies, conduction block) and often mild sensory involvement.  
• AMSAN would show axonal loss in both motor and sensory nerves (sensory potentials would be abnormal).  
• CIDP is excluded by the subacute-to-chronic time course required (>8 weeks).

Therefore, the presentation most strongly fits Acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN).

question: A 45-year-old man with diabetes mellitus is evaluated for abrupt-onset headache and double vision. Examination shows left ptosis and lateral and downward deviation of the left eye. The left pupil is dilated and its constriction to light is impaired. When the left eye is abducted, attempts to look down fail to elicit intorsion of the globe. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 45-year-old man with diabetes mellitus is evaluated for abrupt-onset headache and double vision. Examination shows left ptosis and lateral and downward deviation of the left eye. The left pupil is dilated and its constriction to light is impaired. When the left eye is abducted, attempts to look down fail to elicit intorsion of the globe. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
###Options:
A.  Anterior midbrain infarction
B.  Cavernous sinus aneurysm
C.  Expanding posterior communicating artery aneurysm
D.  Ischemic oculomotor neuropathy
E.  NONE OF THE ABOVE

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Expanding posterior communicating artery aneurysm  

Rationale:  
• The patient has a complete left third-nerve palsy: ptosis (levator palpebrae), “down-and-out” position of the globe (unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique) and a dilated, poorly reactive pupil (parasympathetic fibers that run superficially on CN III are compressed).  
• Abrupt onset of severe headache plus a pupil-involving oculomotor palsy is the classic presentation of a compressive posterior communicating (PCoA) artery aneurysm.  
• When the eye is first abducted, downward gaze depends on the inferior rectus (also supplied by CN III); because that muscle is paralyzed, attempted depression produces neither downward movement nor the intorsion that normally accompanies it—this finding is therefore consistent with a third-nerve lesion, not a trochlear lesion.  
• An ischemic diabetic third-nerve palsy (choice D) typically spares the pupil.  
• Cavernous sinus lesions (choice B) usually involve multiple cranial nerves (III, IV, VI, V1) and often spare the pupil because the parasympathetic fibers have already left CN III by the time it reaches the cavernous sinus.  
• Anterior midbrain infarction (choice A) would be accompanied by contralateral long-tract signs (hemiparesis, ataxia, etc.), which are not present here.  

Therefore, an expanding PCoA aneurysm best explains the constellation of findings.

His neurologic history is notable for vision loss in the right eye 5 years ago, for which he did not seek any medical attention. His examination shows 20/400 vision in the right eye with associated right optic disc pallor and a right afferent pupillary defect; 3/5 power in both arms; paralysis of both legs; and bilateral extensor plantar responses. MRI of the brain shows minimal nonspecific T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) white matter hyperintensities not located in periventricular or juxtacortical locations. ###Options:
A.  Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)
B.  Multiple sclerosis
C.  Neuromyelitis optica (NMO
D.  Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
E.  NONE OF THE ABOVE

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Neuromyelitis optica (NMO)

Rationale:
• Clinical pattern: NMO classically produces severe, often permanently vision-threatening optic neuritis and episodes of transverse myelitis causing paraparesis or quadriparesis. This patient had a remote, severe optic neuritis with residual optic atrophy and now has an acute cervical myelitis producing quadriparesis.

• MRI findings: In NMO the brain MRI is frequently normal or shows only scattered, nonspecific white-matter lesions that do not fulfill the typical multiple-sclerosis (MS) dissemination-in-space criteria (no periventricular or juxtacortical plaques). That is exactly what is described.

• Rule-outs:
  – MS usually shows characteristic periventricular/juxtacortical lesions; optic neuritis tends to recover better than in this case.  
  – ADEM is a monophasic, post-infectious process (mainly in children) and would not explain two attacks 5 years apart.  
  – PML requires immunosuppression and does not present with optic neuritis or acute transverse myelitis.

Therefore neuromyelitis optica is the most likely diagnosis.

###Answer:

Rationale:  
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) is a rare, potentially life-threatening complication that typically arises in the third trimester or early postpartum period. It results from micro-vesicular fatty infiltration of the liver, often linked to defects in fetal long-chain 3-hydroxy-acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD). Hepatic failure leads to impaired gluconeogenesis, so maternal hypoglycaemia is characteristic. Other common findings include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, jaundice, coagulopathy and renal dysfunction. Ultrasound is usually normal or nonspecific and therefore not diagnostic; definitive diagnosis is clinical, supported by laboratory abnormalities (elevated aminotransferases, hyperbilirubinaemia, coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia) and, when necessary, liver biopsy. Hence only statement D is correct, whereas options A, B and C are incorrect.

###Answer:

Rationale:  
• Oral bisphosphonates are well-recognised causes of pill-induced oesophagitis; healing of the ulceration can lead to a benign fibrotic stricture in the distal oesophagus.

• Oesophageal carcinoma typically starts with dysphagia to solids and later involves liquids, and it is not specifically linked to bisphosphonate therapy.  
Therefore a benign oesophageal stricture secondary to bisphosphonate-induced injury is the most likely diagnosis.

question: Which of the following is true about ischaemic hepatitis?

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Cardiac Failure is an important predisposing factor.

Rationale:
Ischaemic hepatitis (“shock liver”) is an acute, diffuse liver injury caused by a sudden reduction in hepatic blood flow and oxygen delivery, most commonly seen in settings of profound hypotension or low-output states. Congestive or cardiogenic heart failure, cardiac arrest, massive pulmonary embolism and other causes of circulatory collapse are well-recognised precipitants. Hence cardiac failure is a major predisposing factor (Option A is true).  
• Option B is false because ischaemic hepatitis typically accompanies systemic hypotension/shock.  
• Option C is false; liver function tests show striking, transient elevations (AST/ALT often >1000 IU/L).  
• Option D is false; prompt fluid resuscitation and correction of the underlying haemodynamic disturbance are essential parts of emergency management.

question: Which of the following is consistent with acute gouty arthritis

###Answer:

Correct option: A.  Negatively birefringent crystals in synovial fluid

Rationale:
The characteristic – indeed virtually diagnostic – finding in an acute attack of gout is the presence of needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals that show strong negative birefringence under polarised light in the synovial fluid of the affected joint.

• Low-grade fever (pyrexia) and a peripheral polymorphonuclear leucocytosis may occur but are variable and non-specific inflammatory responses, not features that are invariably present.  

Thus, of the options listed, the one finding you would consistently expect – and that is diagnostic – is A.

question: A 75-year-old hypertensive woman presents with whirling vertigo, nausea, and weakness on the right side of her body. On exam she has nystagmus, left facial sensory loss, and right arm and leg weakness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 75-year-old hypertensive woman presents with whirling vertigo, nausea, and weakness on the right side of her body. On exam she has nystagmus, left facial sensory loss, and right arm and leg weakness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
###Options:
A.  Internal carotid artery
B.  Middle cerebral artery
C.  Midbasilar artery
D.  Anterior cerebral artery
E.  Penetrating branch, middle cerebral artery

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Mid-basilar artery infarction  

Rationale:  
• Whirling vertigo, nausea, and nystagmus are classic posterior-circulation (brain-stem/cerebellar) symptoms, not seen with anterior-circulation strokes (internal carotid, MCA, ACA).  
• Combination of an ipsilateral cranial-nerve finding (left facial sensory loss from involvement of the trigeminal nucleus/tract) with contralateral long-tract deficit (right arm and leg weakness from corticospinal tract) indicates a brain-stem “crossed” syndrome.  
• The mid-basilar artery—and its paramedian and short circumferential branches—supplies the mid-pons and adjacent medial–lateral tegmentum where these structures lie; occlusion produces vertigo/nystagmus plus ipsilateral facial sensory loss and contralateral hemiparesis.  
• PICA/vertebral occlusion (lateral medullary syndrome) causes vertigo and ipsilateral facial sensory loss but rarely produces limb weakness because the pyramidal tract is spared; hence the presence of marked hemiparesis points higher, toward a basilar (pontine) rather than PICA lesion.  

Therefore the most likely diagnosis is a mid-basilar artery stroke.

Rationale:

• Insulin resistance – Although a component of metabolic syndrome that may aggravate OA, it is not considered a primary or established independent risk factor in standard clinical lists.  
• Osteoporosis – Low bone density has not been shown to increase OA risk; in fact, OA is more often associated with higher, not lower, bone density.  

Therefore, among the given choices, previous trauma is the definitive recognized risk factor.

Answer: A. Tension headache  

Rationale: Tension-type headaches typically present as a bilateral, band-like or “tight” pressure around the forehead, temples, or neck. • Brain tumors cause progressively worsening headaches, often with neurological deficits or signs of raised intracranial pressure, not relieved promptly by simple analgesics.

Thus the presentation best fits a tension headache.

question: A 37-year-old man is brought to the doctor by his family because of a rapid intellectual decline over the past 2 months. Exam reveals slow writhing movements with dystonic posturing. His father died of a similar illness. What is the likely diagnosis?

###Question: A 37-year-old man is brought to the doctor by his family because of a rapid intellectual decline over the past 2 months. Exam reveals slow writhing movements with dystonic posturing. His father died of a similar illness. What is the likely diagnosis?

###Options:
A.  Parkinson’s disease
B.  Wilson’s disease
C.  Huntington’s disease
D.  Dystonia
E.  Tic

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Huntington’s disease

Rationale:
• Huntington’s disease is an autosomal-dominant neurodegenerative disorder (CAG repeat expansion) that typically presents in the third to fifth decades.  
• Classical features are progressive cognitive decline/dementia together with movement abnormalities—chorea and choreoathetoid (slow, writhing) or dystonic posturing.  
• A positive family history (affected father who died of a similar illness) strongly supports this diagnosis because of the autosomal-dominant inheritance.  
• Parkinson’s disease (A) is characterized by bradykinesia, rigidity and resting tremor rather than writhing dystonia, and usually begins later in life.  
• Wilson’s disease (B) is autosomal recessive, often presents earlier, and is accompanied by hepatic signs and Kayser-Fleischer rings.  
• Primary dystonia (D) or tics (E) do not explain the rapid cognitive decline and inherited pattern seen here.

Therefore, the patient’s presentation is most consistent with Huntington’s disease.

question: An elderly woman notes a tremor associated with slowness of movements and a feeling of gait instability over the past 6 months. The tremor is a slow (3 per second) resting tremor that does not interfere with fine movements. What is the likely diagnosis?

Correct option: A.  Parkinson’s disease

Rationale:
• Resting tremor of low frequency (about 3–6 Hz) that disappears or lessens with voluntary movement is classic for Parkinson’s disease.  
• Bradykinesia (slowness of movement) and postural/gait instability are two additional core parkinsonian features.

• Dystonia involves sustained muscle contractions and abnormal postures, not a resting pill-rolling tremor.  
• Essential tremor is an action/postural tremor that worsens with movement and often interferes with fine tasks.  
• Tics are sudden, rapid, stereotyped movements or vocalizations.

question: A 72-year-old woman is found unconscious at home by her daughter. In the emergency room the patient does not respond to verbal or noxious stimuli. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her condition?

Rationale: Coma results when the cerebral cortex and/or the ascending reticular activating system are diffusely depressed. A unilateral ischemic stroke such as an MCA, ACA, PCA, or lacunar infarct typically produces focal neurologic deficits (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual field loss, etc.) but does not by itself cause complete unresponsiveness unless both hemispheres or the brain-stem are affected. Among the choices, hypoglycemia is the common metabolic disturbance that can rapidly lead to loss of consciousness and deep coma, making it the most likely cause in this presentation.

question: A 60-year-old man with Parkinson’s disease is receiving levodopa/carbidopa therapy and complains of uncontrollable facial movements. Which of the following is correct?
A: Limb and facial dyskinesias are unusual side effects of chronic levodopa therapy
B: Levodopa treatment, while ameliorating symptoms, does not alter the natural history of the disease
C: Bromocriptine works by increasing the release of dopamine from the substantia nigra
D: Trihexyphenidyl and benztropine mesylate have minimal side effects in the elderly

Rationale:

question: A 55-year-old diabetic woman suddenly develops weakness of the left side of her face as well as of her right arm and leg. She also has diplopia on left lateral gaze. The responsible lesion is probably located in which of the following?

###Answer:

Correct option: D.  Left side of the brainstem

Rationale:
• A crossed (alternating) neurological picture suggests a brain-stem lesion: cranial-nerve findings are ipsilateral to the lesion, whereas long-tract (corticospinal) deficits are contralateral.  
• Ipsilateral findings: left facial weakness and diplopia on left lateral gaze indicate involvement of the left facial nucleus/nerve (CN VII) and left abducens nucleus/nerve (CN VI), both located in the pons.  
• Contralateral findings: weakness of the right arm and leg indicates damage to descending corticospinal fibers before they decussate in the caudal medulla.  
Hence a lesion in the left pontine (brain-stem) tegmentum that affects CN VI, CN VII, and the corticospinal tract best explains the clinical picture.

Aside from some difficulty swallowing, she has no ocular, bulbar, or sphincter problems and no sensory complaints. Family history is negative for neurological disease. Examination reveals significant proximal limb and neck muscle weakness with minimal atrophy, normal sensory findings, and intact deep tendon reflexes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?

###Question: A 45-year-old woman presents to her physician with an 8-month history of gradually increasing limb weakness. She first noticed difficulty climbing stairs, then problems rising from chairs, walking more than half a block, and, finally, lifting her arms above shoulder level. Aside from some difficulty swallowing, she has no ocular, bulbar, or sphincter problems and no sensory complaints. Family history is negative for neurological disease. Examination reveals significant proximal limb and neck muscle weakness with minimal atrophy, normal sensory findings, and intact deep tendon reflexes. A.  Polymyositis
B.  Cervical myelopathy
C.  Myasthenia gravis
D.  Mononeuropathy multiplex
E.  Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Polymyositis  

Rationale:  
• The chief clinical picture is a slowly progressive, symmetric proximal limb and neck-flexor weakness that has evolved over months—classic for an inflammatory myopathy.  
• Patients have trouble climbing stairs, rising from a chair, lifting objects above the shoulders, and can develop dysphagia from involvement of striated pharyngeal muscles—all findings present here.  
• Sensory examination is normal and deep-tendon reflexes remain intact until very late, features that distinguish a primary muscle disorder from neuropathies or myelopathies.  
• Cervical myelopathy (B) would produce long-tract signs (hyper-reflexia, spasticity, sensory level) that are absent.  
• Myasthenia gravis (C) typically shows fluctuating fatigable weakness with prominent ocular or bulbar involvement early; it does not cause fixed, steadily worsening weakness over months.  
• Mononeuropathy multiplex (D) produces asymmetric, multifocal deficits with sensory loss, not a symmetric limb-girdle pattern.  
• Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (E) can mimic polymyositis but usually begins in childhood or adolescence, progresses over years, and often shows family history and significant atrophy; adult onset over only eight months is far more typical of polymyositis.  

Hence, the presentation is most consistent with polymyositis.

Neurological exam shows sensory loss to light touch to the knees and wrists in a symmetric pattern. Joint position sensation is less severely affected. Ankle reflexes are absent and she has mild distal weakness. Which of the following is the most likely abnormality on laboratory testing?
B: Macrocytic anemia with a low vitamin B12 level

###Question: A 76-year-old woman presents with numbness and mild weakness in the legs. She has noticed mild numbness in the fingertips bilaterally. The symptoms have been slowly progressive over the past year. She rarely goes to the doctor and takes no medications. Neurological exam shows sensory loss to light touch to the knees and wrists in a symmetric pattern. Joint position sensation is less severely affected. B.  Macrocytic anemia with a low vitamin B12 level
C.  Positive ELISA test for HIV
D.  Low T4, elevated TSH
E.  Oligoclonal banding

###Answer:

Correct option: A. Hyperglycemia  

Rationale:  
The clinical picture is that of a chronic, slowly progressive, symmetric “stocking-and-glove” sensory polyneuropathy with absent ankle reflexes and mild distal weakness—features that are classic for distal symmetric diabetic polyneuropathy. Small-fiber modalities (light touch, pain, temperature) are affected earlier and more severely than large-fiber proprioception, which matches the finding that joint-position sense is “less severely affected.” Diabetes mellitus is by far the most common cause of this pattern of neuropathy in older adults, and many elderly patients are undiagnosed until a complication such as neuropathy appears.  

• Vitamin B12 deficiency (macrocytic anemia) typically causes large-fiber dysfunction with prominent loss of vibration and joint position sense and often produces a myelopathy (subacute combined degeneration), neither of which is seen here.

Therefore, the laboratory abnormality most likely to be found is hyperglycemia.

question: A 56-year-old woman develops difficulty ambulating several weeks after receiving an influenza vaccine. She is found to have distal muscle weakness and areflexia in the lower extremities. During a 2-day observation period the weakness ascends, and she begins to notice weakness of the hands. She notices mild tingling, but the sensory examination is normal. The diagnosis of Guillain-Barré syndrome is strongly suspected. The workup of this patient is most likely to show which of the following?
A: Acellular spinal fluid with high protein
B: Abnormal EMG that shows axonal degeneration
E: Respiratory alkalosis by arterial blood gases

###Question: A 56-year-old woman develops difficulty ambulating several weeks after receiving an influenza vaccine. She is found to have distal muscle weakness and areflexia in the lower extremities. During a 2-day observation period the weakness ascends, and she begins to notice weakness of the hands. She notices mild tingling, but the sensory examination is normal. The diagnosis of Guillain-Barré syndrome is strongly suspected. The workup of this patient is most likely to show which of the following?
###Options:
A.  Acellular spinal fluid with high protein
B.  Abnormal EMG that shows axonal degeneration
C.  Positive Tensilon test
D.  Elevated CPK
E.  Respiratory alkalosis by arterial blood gases

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A.  Acellular spinal fluid with high protein

Rationale:
Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy) classically produces an “albuminocytologic dissociation” on lumbar puncture—markedly elevated CSF protein due to demyelination and inflammation of the nerve roots, with little or no increase in white blood cells. This finding distinguishes GBS from infectious causes of neuropathy. 

• EMG/NCS usually demonstrate demyelination, not primary axonal degeneration (choice B is less typical).  
• A Tensilon (edrophonium) test is used to diagnose myasthenia gravis (choice C).  
• Creatine phosphokinase (CPK) rises with myopathic or rhabdomyolysis processes, not with a primarily demyelinating neuropathy (choice D).  
• Respiratory alkalosis (choice E) reflects hyperventilation, unrelated to the early diagnostic work-up of GBS.

question: Three weeks after an upper respiratory illness, a 25-year-old male develops weakness of his arms and legs over several days. On physical exam he is tachypneic, with shallow respirations and symmetric muscle weakness in both arms and legs. There is no obvious sensory deficit, but motor reflexes cannot be elicited. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

###Question: Three weeks after an upper respiratory illness, a 25-year-old male develops weakness of his arms and legs over several days. On physical exam he is tachypneic, with shallow respirations and symmetric muscle weakness in both arms and legs. There is no obvious sensory deficit, but motor reflexes cannot be elicited. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

###Options:
A.  Myasthenia gravis
B.  Multiple sclerosis
C.  Guillain-Barré syndrome
D.  Dermatomyositis
E.  Diabetes mellitus

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option:  
C. Guillain-Barré syndrome  

Rationale:  
• Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy) often follows an upper-respiratory or gastrointestinal infection by 1–4 weeks.  
• It presents with rapidly progressive, symmetric limb weakness that typically ascends from the legs but can involve arms and respiratory muscles, producing tachypnea and shallow respirations.  
• Deep-tendon reflexes are characteristically absent or markedly depressed, while sensory loss is minimal or absent, matching this patient’s findings.  
• Myasthenia gravis (A) causes fluctuating fatigable weakness, usually beginning with ocular or bulbar muscles, and reflexes remain intact.  
• Multiple sclerosis (B) produces CNS demyelination with visual or sensory disturbances and hyperreflexia, not generalized areflexia.  
• Dermatomyositis (D) causes proximal muscle weakness with skin rash and preserved reflexes.  
• Diabetes mellitus (E) can cause peripheral neuropathy, but it develops chronically and is predominantly sensory.  

Therefore, the presentation is most consistent with Guillain-Barré syndrome.

In ALS:

• Sensory nerve conduction studies remain normal because sensory fibers are spared.  
• Brain CT (or MRI) is usually unrevealing.  
• EEG is normal because cortical electrical activity is not primarily affected.  
• Electromyography (EMG), however, shows characteristic abnormalities of active and chronic denervation (fibrillation potentials, positive sharp waves, large-amplitude polyphasic motor unit potentials), making EMG the laboratory test most likely to be abnormal in this patient.

Therefore option A best summarizes interferon-β’s role.

###Question: Which of the following is not a typical feature of malignant otitis exteerna?
###Options:
A.  Mitotic figures are high
B.  caused ny pseudomonas aerugionsa
C.  Patientsare usually immunocompromised
D.  Presence of granulation tissue
E.  Patients are usually old

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Mitotic figures are high  

Rationale:  
Malignant (necrotising) otitis externa is a severe, life-threatening infection of the external auditory canal, most commonly seen in elderly diabetic or otherwise immunocompromised patients. It is almost always caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa and is characterised clinically by severe otalgia, otorrhoea and granulation tissue at the bony cartilaginous junction of the canal. Despite the word “malignant” in its name, it is an infectious—not neoplastic—process, so histologic features of malignancy such as numerous mitotic figures are not present. Hence option A is not a typical feature.

question: The following is false about COPD
A: COPD seldom shows large responses to inhaled bronchodilators
B: Air trapping and progressively less elastic recoil offering resistance to expiration
C: The lung parenchyma provides progressively less elastic recoil offering resistance to expiration
D: Major site of increased resistance in COPD is in airways less or equal to 2 mm in diameter
E: Respirator bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli walls are involved in emphysema
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: The following is false about COPD
###Options:
A.  COPD seldom shows large responses to inhaled bronchodilators
B.  Air trapping and progressively less elastic recoil offering resistance to expiration
C.  The lung parenchyma provides progressively less elastic recoil offering resistance to expiration
D.  Major site of increased resistance in COPD is in airways less or equal to 2 mm in diameter
E.  Respirator bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli walls are involved in emphysema

###Answer:
outputs:
False statement: B  

Rationale:  
• COPD does show air trapping and a progressive loss of elastic recoil, but loss of elastic recoil does not itself “offer resistance” to expiration – it actually removes the driving force for expiratory flow; the resulting airflow limitation comes from small-airway collapse, not from elastic recoil resisting expiration.  
• The other options are correct:  
  – COPD rarely exhibits large (> 15 % and 200 mL) reversibility with inhaled bronchodilators (A).  
  – Destruction of lung parenchyma progressively diminishes elastic recoil (C).  
  – The chief site of increased airflow resistance is the small airways ≤ 2 mm in diameter (D).  
  – Emphysema involves respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveolar walls (E).

###Answer:

Rationale:  
Aminoglycoside antibiotics (e.g., gentamicin, amikacin, streptomycin) concentrate in the perilymph and endolymph of the inner ear and damage cochlear and vestibular hair cells, producing dose-related, often irreversible hearing loss and balance disturbances—classic “ototoxicity.”

C.  normal
D.  Lateralized to left side
E.  Centralizd

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Lateralize to right side

Rationale:  
The Weber test places a vibrating tuning fork on the midline of the skull.  
• In conductive hearing loss (e.g., middle-ear pathology), bone-conducted sound is perceived as louder in the ear with the conductive defect, because ambient noise is blocked and internal resonance is enhanced.  
• In sensorineural loss, the sound lateralizes to the better (normal) ear.  

A right-sided middle-ear lesion therefore produces conductive hearing loss on the right, so Weber’s test sound will be heard louder (lateralize) in the right ear.

question: Which is the investigation of chice in assessing hearing loss in neonates?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).

###Question: Which is the investigation of chice in assessing hearing loss in neonates?
###Options:
A.  Impedance audiometry
B.  beahvioural audiometry
C.  free fluid audiometry
D.  brain-stem evokded response audiometry
E.  Pure tone audiometry

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. brain-stem evoked response audiometry

Rationale:
Newborns cannot provide reliable behavioural responses, so assessment must rely on an objective, non-invasive test that measures the auditory pathway directly. Brain-stem evoked response audiometry (also called auditory brain-stem response, ABR/BERA) records the electrical potentials generated along the auditory nerve and brain-stem in response to sound stimuli. It can be done while the baby is asleep, requires no active cooperation, and provides information about hearing thresholds down to ~30 dB as well as integrity of the auditory pathway, making it the investigation of choice for neonatal hearing screening. 

The other options either assess only middle-ear status (impedance), rely on behavioural or voluntary responses (behavioural, free-field, pure tone audiometry) and therefore are unsuitable or less accurate in neonates.

question: In the management of salmonella
A: Blood cultures are most sensitive in the 3rd week of infection
B: Widal test is the most sensitive test for the diagnosis of enteric fever
C: Resistance to fluoroquinolones is not documented
D: Eradication of chronic carriage required treatment with antibiotics for 2 weeks
E: Vaccination is an effective method of preventing infection in travelers
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: In the management of salmonella
###Options:
A.  Blood cultures are most sensitive in the 3rd week of infection
B.  Widal test is the most sensitive test for the diagnosis of enteric fever
C.  Resistance to fluoroquinolones is not documented
D.  Eradication of chronic carriage required treatment with antibiotics for 2 weeks
E.  Vaccination is an effective method of preventing infection in travelers

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E  

Rationale  
A – False.  Blood-culture yield is highest during the first week of enteric fever (≈60-90 %) and falls progressively; by the third week positivity is low.  

B – False.  The Widal test has poor sensitivity and specificity and is not regarded as the most reliable diagnostic test; blood culture or bone-marrow culture is superior.  

C – False.  Fluoroquinolone resistance (including to ciprofloxacin and ofloxacin) is well documented worldwide in Salmonella enterica, especially S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi.  

D – False.  Chronic biliary carriage usually needs 4- to 6-week courses of a highly active antibiotic (e.g., ciprofloxacin) and sometimes cholecystectomy; 2 weeks is generally inadequate.  

E – True.  Both the oral Ty21a vaccine and the parenteral Vi-polysaccharide vaccine confer 60-70 % protection and are recommended for travelers to endemic regions as an effective preventive measure.

question: Which of the following is not a symptom of adverse malaria
A: Urine output (24 hours) of <400ml in adults
D: More than two generalized seizures in 24 hours

###Question: Which of the following is not a symptom of adverse malaria
###Options:
A.  Urine output (24 hours) of <400ml in adults
B.  Plasma glucose level of <2.2 mmol\L
C.  Venous lactate level of <5 mmol\L
D.  More than two generalized seizures in 24 hours
E.  Arterial PH <7.25

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Venous lactate level of <5 mmol/L  

Rationale:  
Severe (adverse) falciparum malaria is defined by specific clinical and laboratory criteria set by WHO. These include oliguria (< 0.5 mL kg⁻¹ h⁻¹, ≈< 400 mL in 24 h for an adult), hypoglycaemia (< 2.2 mmol L⁻¹), recurrent generalized seizures (> 2 in 24 h), metabolic acidosis with arterial pH < 7.25, and hyper-lactataemia (venous lactate ≥ 5 mmol L⁻¹). A venous lactate concentration below 5 mmol L⁻¹ is therefore not a criterion of severe/adverse malaria, making option C the correct choice.

###Answer:

Rationale:
Rabies virus characteristically produces distinct, eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions called Negri bodies in neurons, especially in hippocampal pyramidal cells and cerebellar Purkinje cells. Their presence on microscopic examination of brain tissue is virtually pathognomonic for rabies infection. The other listed inclusions are unrelated: psammoma bodies (calcified concentric lamellations seen in certain tumors), Lewy bodies (α-synuclein inclusions in Parkinson’s disease), corpora amylacea (polyglucosan bodies seen in aging brains), and Loofra/Löffler bodies (eosinophilic inclusions in diphtheria).

question: Which of the following is a dominant buffer in plasma

###Question: Which of the following is a dominant buffer in plasma

###Options:
A.  Phosphate
B.  Albumin
C.  Bicarbonate
D.  Protein
E.  Chloride

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Bicarbonate  

Rationale: In the extracellular fluid and therefore in plasma, the principal buffering system is the bicarbonate–carbonic acid pair (HCO₃⁻/H₂CO₃). This buffer is present in the highest concentration, is rapidly regulated by the lungs (via CO₂ elimination) and kidneys (via HCO₃⁻ reabsorption/excretion), and therefore dominates pH control in plasma. Phosphate and protein buffers (including albumin) are more important inside cells or in renal tubular fluid, and chloride is not a major buffer.

###Answer:

question: Which of the following is commonly used as a marker of kidney function in clinical settings
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following is commonly used as a marker of kidney function in clinical settings
###Options:
A.  Serum sodium
B.  Serum urea
C.  Serum creatinine
D.  Serum beta-2-microglobulin
E.  Serum potassium

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Serum creatinine

Rationale: Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the principal measure of renal function. In routine clinical practice, serum creatinine is the most widely used endogenous marker to estimate GFR because it is produced at a relatively constant rate from muscle metabolism, is freely filtered by the glomerulus, and is easy, inexpensive, and rapidly measurable in most laboratories. While serum urea (BUN) and other substances can also reflect renal status, they are influenced by many non-renal factors (dietary protein intake, hydration, catabolic state), making them less reliable for primary assessment of kidney function. Beta-2-microglobulin, although more specific in some settings, is not routinely used. Electrolytes such as sodium and potassium mainly reflect tubular handling and extracellular balance rather than directly indicating GFR. Hence, serum creatinine remains the standard marker in everyday clinical care.

Therefore, ceftriaxone is the recommended first-line choice pending culture results.

question: Which of the following conditions does not cause transudative pleural effusion?

###Answer:

Rationale:  
Transudative pleural effusions result from systemic factors that alter hydrostatic or oncotic pressures without primary pleural inflammation. Classic transudative causes include:

• Heart failure – raised hydrostatic pressure

###Answer:

Rationale:
• Shock in a surgical patient is usually hypovolemic (blood or fluid loss). Rapid restoration of intravascular volume with an isotonic solution is required.

• Dextrose saline (D) is slightly hypotonic and, like 5 % dextrose, does not provide adequate intravascular volume expansion.  

Therefore, Ringer’s Lactate is the ideal choice for correcting shock in surgical patients.

ERCP is reserved for cases in which therapeutic intervention (stone extraction, sphincterotomy, stenting) is anticipated. Ultrasonography often misses distal CBD stones, and IV cholangiography is obsolete.

• Standard initial treatment for drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis in adults is a four-drug regimen: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for the first 2 months (the intensive phase), followed by isoniazid and rifampicin for 4 months (the continuation phase).

• Option E is incorrect: Mycobacterium bovis causes tuberculosis in cattle, and M. tuberculosis can infect cattle as well; hence TB does affect cattle.

###Options:

###Answer:

• Removing the children from the home (D) is unnecessary once the index case begins effective therapy and the children are on prophylaxis.

Therefore, initiating isoniazid therapy is the most appropriate management.

• Persistent airflow obstruction on spirometry (reduced FEV₁/FVC) – option E.  

Therefore, a reduced total lung volume is the finding that is NOT expected in emphysema.

###Answer:

Rationale  

A. True – Owing to lower body‐water content, differences in alcohol dehydrogenase activity and hormonal factors, women develop alcohol-related medical complications (e.g. liver disease, cardiomyopathy, pancreatitis) after a lower lifetime intake than men.  

B. False – There is a clear dose-response relationship: overall mortality, and especially death from liver disease, accidents and some cancers, rises progressively with the amount of alcohol consumed.  

C. True – Numerous population studies show that consumption and the prevalence of alcohol misuse/ dependence fall when the real price of alcoholic beverages rises (and vice-versa).  

D. False – Although light-to-moderate drinking may produce a modest “J-shaped” reduction in coronary heart disease risk, the heavy intake typical of alcohol dependence abolishes this benefit and actually increases cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.  

E. False – The four-item CAGE questionnaire is brief and highly specific, but in unselected community samples its sensitivity is only moderate; therefore it is not regarded as a sufficiently reliable stand-alone screening tool in the general population.

• The child is otherwise well: afebrile, alert, normal mental status, normal deep-tendon reflexes and no long-tract deficits or meningeal signs.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Chi-square test

Rationale:
The trial compares two independent groups (anti-D therapy vs. no treatment) on a categorical outcome—whether or not a child experienced a nose-bleed (or the proportion with nose-bleeds). When the objective is to determine if there is a significant difference in proportions between two independent samples, the appropriate statistical test is the chi-square test of independence (or, with small expected counts, Fisher’s exact test).  
• Independent t-test and paired t-test require a continuous, approximately normally distributed outcome.  
• Analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used when comparing the means of more than two groups.  
• “Non-parametric test” is too nonspecific; common non-parametric counterparts (e.g., Mann-Whitney) also pertain to continuous or ordinal data.  

Therefore, Chi-square is the most suitable choice.

question: Outcome from bacterial meningitis relates to the following except?

D: Development of antibiotic resistance during therapy

D.  Development of antibiotic resistance during therapy

###Answer:
outputs:

Rationale  
Prognosis in acute bacterial meningitis is mainly determined by host factors and by how promptly and effectively the infection is controlled. Documented determinants include:  

• Age of the patient – neonates, infants and the elderly have significantly higher mortality.  
• Time elapsed before the first effective antibiotic dose – every hour of delay worsens outcome.  
• The specific causative organism – e.g., Neisseria meningitidis carries a better prognosis than Streptococcus pneumoniae or Gram-negative bacilli.  
• Emergence of antibiotic resistance during therapy – if the infecting strain becomes resistant, treatment fails and the risk of death or neurological sequelae rises.

In contrast, once standard, appropriately dosed bactericidal antibiotics are given, therapeutic levels are almost always achieved in the inflamed meninges; variations in absolute CSF drug concentration within this therapeutic range are not an independent, clinically recognized predictor of outcome. Therefore, option C is the exception.

question: With respect to lumbar puncture which is true?
D: The less CSF is removed, the less likely coning is to occur
E: Postlumbar puncture headache is related to the size of the needle used

###Question: With respect to lumbar puncture which is true?

###Options:
A.  Coagulopathy is a contraindication
B.  Papilloedema is an absolute contraindication
C.  The procedure may cause meningitis
D.  The less CSF is removed, the less likely coning is to occur
E.  Postlumbar puncture headache is related to the size of the needle used

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, C and E  

Rationale  

A. Coagulopathy is a contraindication – YES. Thrombocytopenia or an elevated INR increases the risk of spinal canal bleeding, so a lumbar puncture should be deferred until the coagulation defect is corrected.  

B. Papilloedema is an absolute contraindication – NO. Papilloedema indicates raised intracranial pressure, but if neuro-imaging has excluded a mass lesion the procedure can be performed; therefore it is not an absolute contraindication.  

C. The procedure may cause meningitis – YES. Although uncommon, organisms can be introduced on the needle or from the skin, producing iatrogenic meningitis.  

D. The less CSF is removed, the less likely coning is to occur – NO. In the presence of a space-occupying lesion even the smallest leak can precipitate transtentorial herniation; the volume removed does not reliably protect against coning.  

E. Post-lumbar-puncture headache is related to the size of the needle used – YES. Larger-bore, cutting-bevel needles leave a bigger dural defect and a higher risk of CSF leakage and post-LP headache; fine, pencil-point (atraumatic) needles markedly reduce this complication.

C.  Thyrotoxic exophthalmos
D.  Symblepharon

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. 5th cranial nerve paralysis  

Rationale:  
Lagophthalmos is the inability to close the eyelids completely. It usually results from either (1) weakness or paralysis of the orbicularis oculi muscle, which is supplied by the 7th cranial (facial) nerve, or (2) mechanical restriction or anterior displacement of the globe that physically prevents lid closure.  
• 7th cranial nerve paralysis → orbicularis oculi weakness → typical cause of lagophthalmos.  
• Thyrotoxic (exophthalmic) protrusion of the globe → lids cannot reach over a forward-displaced eye → lagophthalmos.  
• Symblepharon (cicatricial adhesion between palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva) can tether the lids, mechanically limiting closure → lagophthalmos.  

The 5th cranial (trigeminal) nerve provides corneal and eyelid sensation; its paralysis abolishes corneal reflex blinking and predisposes to exposure keratitis, but voluntary lid closure remains intact because the motor supply is unaffected. Therefore trigeminal palsy does not cause true lagophthalmos.

Rationale:  
After leaving the stylomastoid foramen the facial nerve divides within the parotid gland into a superior (temporofacial) and an inferior (cervicofacial) division.

In this patient there is:

– No motion around the eye (orbicularis oculi)  
These functions belong to the temporal ± zygomatic branches, hence to the superior division.  

Yet the nasal ala flares and the corner of the mouth moves normally, showing that the branches arising from the inferior division remain intact. Therefore the laceration has severed the superior division of the facial nerve within the parotid gland.

Rationale:
• Facial nerve (CN VII) fibers run through the parotid gland. New-onset facial weakness (inability to close eye, weak smile) in the presence of a parotid mass is highly suggestive of malignant infiltration of the facial nerve.  
• Benign parotid tumors (e.g., pleomorphic adenoma, Warthin tumor) virtually never produce facial nerve palsy unless very large or following prior surgery; they are usually painless.  
• Pain plus facial nerve dysfunction are classic red-flag features for a malignant parotid neoplasm such as mucoepidermoid carcinoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, or high-grade acinic cell carcinoma.  
• A facial neuroma would present with isolated nerve dysfunction without a discrete parotid mass, and a mandibular tumor would not typically give parotid-region swelling with nerve palsy.

Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is a malignant tumor of the parotid gland.

Rationale:  
Aortic dissection classically presents with sudden, severe, “tearing” or “shearing” chest and/or back pain and markedly elevated blood pressure. In a hemodynamically stable patient (as here: normal oxygenation, HR 92, BP elevated but stable), the preferred first-line imaging test is CT angiography of the chest. CTA is rapid, widely available in the ED, and has very high sensitivity and specificity for defining the location and extent of an aortic dissection and branch-vessel involvement, guiding urgent management decisions.  

• Plain chest radiograph (A) may show a widened mediastinum but is neither sensitive nor specific and cannot definitively rule out dissection.  
• Transesophageal echocardiography (B) is an excellent bedside test, especially for unstable patients or when CTA is contraindicated, but requires expertise and sedation and is not as universally available.  
• Conventional angiography (C) is no longer first line because it is invasive, time-consuming, and less readily available emergently.  
• Therefore, CTA (D) is the most appropriate initial imaging modality in this stable patient.

###Question: Severe congenital ptosis with no levator function can be treated by:

D.  Fasanella servat operation

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Fascia lata sling operation

Rationale:  
Management of congenital ptosis depends chiefly on the strength of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle.  
• Good-to-fair levator function (>4 mm): procedures that enhance or shorten the levator (levator resection, skin-side or conjunctival-side) are effective.

• Fasanella-Servat is reserved for mild ptosis (≤2 mm) with good levator action.

Therefore, in severe congenital ptosis with no levator function, the appropriate surgery is a fascia lata (frontalis) sling operation.

A mixed upper- and lower-motor-neuron picture implies the simultaneous presence of pyramidal (UMN) signs (e.g., spasticity, hyper-reflexia, extensor plantar) together with features of anterior-horn or root/nerve involvement (LMN) such as muscle wasting, fasciculations, flaccidity or areflexia.

• Guillain-Barré syndrome, however, is an acute peripheral demyelinating neuropathy; it produces purely lower-motor-neuron features (flaccid weakness, areflexia) without any upper-motor-neuron signs.

Therefore Guillain-Barré syndrome is the exception.

• Anticoagulation and observation alone risk irreversible ischemia and limb loss; primary amputation is reserved for limbs already judged non-viable.
