C.  Facial
D.  Glossopharyngeal
E.  Vagus

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Trigeminal

Rationale:
Parasympathetic (visceromotor) outflow from the brainstem is confined to cranial nerves III (oculomotor), VII (facial), IX (glossopharyngeal) and X (vagus).  
• Oculomotor (III) – Edinger-Westphal nucleus → ciliary ganglion → sphincter pupillae & ciliary muscle  
• Facial (VII) – superior salivatory & lacrimatory nuclei → pterygopalatine & submandibular ganglia → lacrimal, nasal, submandibular, sublingual glands  
• Glossopharyngeal (IX) – inferior salivatory nucleus → otic ganglion → parotid gland  
• Vagus (X) – dorsal motor nucleus → thoracic and abdominal viscera up to splenic flexure  

The trigeminal nerve (V) provides somatic sensory and branchial motor fibres; although parasympathetic fibres from III, VII and IX “hitch-hike” along its branches to reach target organs, the trigeminal nerve itself contains no parasympathetic component. Therefore, trigeminal is the exception.

###Answer:

Rationale:
Drug-induced parkinsonism results from blockade or depletion of dopaminergic activity in the nigro-striatal pathway. Agents that antagonize dopamine D2 receptors are the common culprits.

Denial is an immature defense mechanism in which a person consciously or unconsciously refuses to acknowledge an aspect of external reality that is obvious to others because it is too threatening or uncomfortable to accept. In this case, despite having just suffered a severe myocardial infarction, the patient insists he “can’t be kept down” and performs push-ups to prove there is “nothing wrong.” He is rejecting the seriousness of his current medical condition and its limitations—classic denial.

• Reaction formation converts an unacceptable impulse into its opposite (e.g., treating someone you dislike with excessive friendliness).  
• Repression is unconscious blocking of disturbing thoughts or feelings from awareness.

Rationale:  
Every corneal ulcer—whether bacterial, fungal, viral, acanthamoebic, or sterile—produces marked ciliary-body irritation, causing pain, photophobia, blepharospasm, and a risk of posterior synechiae. A cycloplegic-mydriatic (e.g., atropine, homatropine) paralyzes the ciliary muscle and dilates the pupil, thereby:

• Relieving ciliary spasm and pain  
• Reducing photophobia and blepharospasm  
• Preventing formation of posterior synechiae  

These benefits are independent of the infectious agent. In contrast:

• Corticosteroids can exacerbate many infectious ulcers and are contraindicated until the infection is controlled.  
• Antibiotics are essential for bacterial ulcers but not for purely fungal or viral ulcers.  
• Antifungals are required only for fungal ulcers.

Hence, cycloplegics are the one class of drugs routinely indicated in all corneal ulcers regardless of etiology.

question: Which of the following is a cause of post-hepatic portal hypertension?

###Question: Which of the following is a cause of post-hepatic portal hypertension?

A.  Sarcoidosis
B.  Vinyl chloride
C.  Schistosomiasis
D.  Portal vein thrombosis
E.  Budd-Chiari syndrome

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E. Budd-Chiari syndrome

Rationale:
Portal hypertension can be classified by the anatomic site of increased resistance to portal blood flow.  
• Pre-hepatic (before the liver): e.g., portal vein thrombosis  
• Intra-hepatic (within the liver): presinusoidal (schistosomiasis, sarcoidosis), sinusoidal (cirrhosis, vinyl chloride–related injury), postsinusoidal  
• Post-hepatic (after the liver): obstruction of hepatic venous outflow or of the inferior vena cava/right heart

Budd-Chiari syndrome involves thrombosis or obstruction of the hepatic veins, preventing blood from leaving the liver and thereby raising portal venous pressure distal to the obstruction. Therefore it is a classic post-hepatic cause of portal hypertension. None of the other listed conditions obstruct hepatic venous outflow; they act either pre-hepatically or intra-hepatically.

outputs:

Rationale:
The tensile strength of a midline abdominal wound is provided almost entirely by the fascial (aponeurotic) layer; muscle, peritoneum and skin contribute little. Current evidence and guideline recommendations favour a single-layer, continuous closure of the linea alba with a slowly-absorbable monofilament suture (e.g., PDS) using a suture-to-wound-length ratio of at least 4:1. Meta-analyses have shown that continuous fascial closure is at least as safe as, and in several studies superior to, interrupted closure in terms of wound dehiscence and incisional-hernia rates, while being faster to perform. Rapidly absorbed sutures such as Vicryl lose tensile strength too quickly and are associated with higher, not lower, hernia rates; the peritoneum is not routinely closed because its re-epithelialisation is rapid and closure does not reduce adhesions but adds foreign-body material and operating time. The muscle layer itself offers minimal mechanical strength once divided.

Therefore, statement A is true, whereas B, C and D are incorrect.

###Answer:

Rationale:  
• Retroperitoneal fibrosis is an indolent inflammatory-fibrotic process that encases retroperitoneal structures, most notably the ureters. Progressive ureteral entrapment produces unilateral or bilateral hydroureteronephrosis and dull abdominal or flank pain – exactly what is seen on this patient’s ultrasound (mild right hydronephrosis) and examination (vague abdominal/right-flank pain).  
• The same fibrotic/obstructive process can impair lymphatic drainage through the spermatic cord and the inguinal canal, leading to accumulation of fluid in the tunica vaginalis and a non-tender communicating hydrocele; thus the right-sided scrotal swelling fits the picture.  
• Ureterolithiasis usually causes sudden, colicky flank pain and often microscopic or gross hematuria, not a hydrocele.  
• Recurrent pancreatitis produces epigastric pain radiating to the back and elevated pancreatic enzymes; it would neither generate hydronephrosis nor a hydrocele.  
• Mesenteric adenitis affects mesenteric lymph nodes, presenting like appendicitis; it does not obstruct the ureter or produce scrotal fluid collections.  

Therefore, retroperitoneal fibrosis best accounts for the coexistence of vague abdominal/flank pain, unilateral hydronephrosis, and a hydrocele.

• Rapid development of peritonitis once perforation occurs

Esophageal varices or bleeding gastric veins are unlikely in an otherwise healthy 23-year-old trauma patient. Therefore gastric necrosis with perforation is the most worrisome and likely explanation.

question: You are performing a splenectomy on a patient with hypersplenism. Thrombocytopenia is the major problem with this patient. Special attention to which technical aspect of the procedure is advised?
A: Ligation of the splenic artery before the vein
B: Division of the short gastric vessels before approach to the hilum
C: Medial visceral rotation of the entire spleen, pancreas and leftcolon.
D: Minimal touching or manipulation of the spleen
E: Ligation of the splenic vein before the artery
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).

###Question: You are performing a splenectomy on a patient with hypersplenism. Thrombocytopenia is the major problem with this patient. Special attention to which technical aspect of the procedure is advised? 
###Options:
A.  Ligation of the splenic artery before the vein
B.  Division of the short gastric vessels before approach to the hilum
C.  Medial visceral rotation of the entire spleen, pancreas and leftcolon.
D.  Minimal touching or manipulation of the spleen
E.  Ligation of the splenic vein before the artery

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A.  Ligation of the splenic artery before the vein  

Rationale:  
In hypersplenism the enlarged spleen sequesters platelets, so the patient is markedly thrombocytopenic and prone to bleed. Early ligation of the splenic artery stops the arterial inflow while the venous outflow is still patent; this promptly decongests and shrinks the spleen, releases sequestered platelets and red cells into the systemic circulation, and markedly lowers intra-splenic pressure. The result is a smaller, less friable organ and a much safer, drier dissection. If the vein were ligated first the spleen would become even more congested and bleeding risk would increase. Therefore, in splenectomy for hypersplenism, the key technical point is to ligate the splenic artery before the vein.

The combination of right-upper-quadrant pain, fever, and jaundice constitutes Charcot’s triad, which is classic for acute ascending cholangitis (infection of an obstructed biliary tree, most commonly by a common-duct stone).

• Acute cholecystitis gives RUQ pain and fever but jaundice is uncommon.  
• Acute pancreatitis presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back and elevated amylase/lipase, not Charcot’s triad.  

Hence, acute cholangitis is the most likely diagnosis.

###Answer:

Rationale:
Vibrio cholerae produces cholera toxin, which permanently activates adenylate cyclase in enterocytes via ADP-ribosylation of the Gsα subunit. question: Hemolytic disease of The newborn may be due to all of the following except:
rationale:
HDN may develop when a mother and her unborn baby have different blood types. The types are based on small substances (antigens) on the surface of the blood cells.
There is more than one way in which the unborn baby's blood type may not match the mother's.
A, B, AB, and O are the 4 major blood group antigens or types. This is the most common form of a mismatch. In most cases, this is not very severe.
Rh is short for the "rhesus" antigen or blood type. People are either positive or negative for this antigen. If the mother is Rh-negative and the baby in the womb has Rh-positive cells, her antibodies to the Rh antigen can cross the placenta and cause very severe anemia in the baby. It can be prevented in most cases.Anti-c, clinically the most important Rh antibody after anti-D, may cause severe HDN. Anti-C, anti-E, and anti-e do not often cause HDN, and when they do, it is usually mild.
There are other, much less common, types of mismatch between minor blood group antigens. Some of these can also cause severe problems.

###Answer:

Rationale: Factors that increase a woman’s lifetime exposure to oestrogen generally raise the risk of breast cancer, whereas factors that shorten this exposure tend to be protective.

• Multiparity (several full-term pregnancies) → prolonged periods of high progesterone and temporary anovulation → overall protective.

• Breast-feeding suppresses ovulation, reduces cumulative oestrogen exposure and promotes terminal differentiation of breast tissue, so it is protective, not a risk factor.

Thus, among the options listed, breast-feeding is the one that is NOT a risk factor for developing breast cancer.

Perfusion of the systemic tissues depends on the pressure gradient between the arterial side and the venous side of the circulation. Therefore, MAP is the pressure that drives blood into the tissues.

###Question: A 67-year-old female patient complains of fatigue, dizziness, and abdominal distention. On examination, she is pale and an enlarged spleen is palpated. Her full blood count shows an elevated white cell count of 600 x 109/L. Her bone marrow shows the full spectrum of myeloid maturation. Her BCR-ABL 1 is positive. Which one of the following is true about her treatment?
###Options:
A.  She should be initiated on hydroxyurea and allopurinol
B.  She is eligible for a tyrosine kinase inhibitor
C.  She should start chemotherapy with a cytarabine-based protocol
D.  She should undergo white cell apharesis
E.  She should undergo a stem cell transplant

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. She is eligible for a tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

Rationale: The presence of the t(9;22)(q34;q11) translocation producing the BCR-ABL1 fusion protein confirms the diagnosis of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). Current standard first-line therapy for CML in chronic phase is a BCR-ABL1 tyrosine-kinase inhibitor (TKI) such as imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib, or ponatinib. TKIs specifically inhibit the constitutively active BCR-ABL1 kinase, induce durable hematologic and cytogenetic remissions, and have dramatically improved survival, making them the preferred initial treatment in virtually all patients, including the elderly.

Hydroxyurea with allopurinol (option A) may be used briefly for cytoreduction before TKI initiation but is not definitive therapy. Cytarabine-based chemotherapy (option C) is not standard in chronic-phase CML. Leukapheresis (option D) is reserved for symptomatic hyperleukocytosis or leukostasis, which is uncommon in CML chronic phase. Allogeneic stem-cell transplant (option E) is now reserved for TKI-resistant or advanced-phase disease because of its higher morbidity and mortality compared with TKI therapy.

question: When using a zone-based approach to penetrating neck injury, whichzone(s)  are most likely to be explored without further workup or imaging?
E: All zones require imaging before exploration.

###Question: When using a zone-based approach to penetrating neck injury, whichzone(s)  are most likely to be explored without further workup or imaging? 
###Options:
A.  Zone 1
B.  Zone 2
C.  Zone 3
D.  Zone 4
E.  All zones require imaging before exploration.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option:  
B. Zone 2  

Rationale:  
In the traditional “zone‐based” management of penetrating neck trauma, the neck is divided into three anatomic zones. Injuries in Zone II (between the cricoid cartilage and the angle of the mandible) are readily exposed through a standard cervical incision and therefore have historically been taken directly to surgical exploration when there are hard signs of vascular or aerodigestive injury, without the need for pre-operative imaging. In contrast, injuries in Zones I (thoracic inlet to cricoid) and III (angle of mandible to skull base) are more difficult to access surgically; detailed imaging (e.g., angiography, CT-angiography) is usually performed first to guide the operative approach. Accordingly, Zone II is the zone most likely to be explored without further work-up.

Rationale:  
Enteric (typhoid) fever caused by Salmonella typhi produces necrosis of Peyer’s patches in the distal ileum. Tuberculosis usually gives multiple small perforations or strictures; trauma and gallstones would not follow this clinical course nor show the characteristic ileal antimesenteric perforation.

Routine neck ultrasound, bronchoscopy, or esophagostomy are not indicated by the described injuries. Therefore, a CT angiogram of the head and neck is the appropriate next step.

question: The Monroe-Kellie Doctrine describes which of the following?
A: Increased intracranial pressure may result in a physiologic response that involves bradycardia, hypertension with widening pulse pressure, and irregular respirations
B: The different mechanisms by which primary and secondary brain injury result.
C: The skull contains a fixed volume of brain tissue, blood, and  CSF. Anything that increases the volume of one component  must result in a decreased volume of theother two or will cause increased intracranial pressure.
D: The formula from which cerebral perfusion pressure is derived, which explains how meanarterial pressure and intracranial pressure impact cerebral perfusion.
model_prompt:

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: The Monroe-Kellie Doctrine describes which of the following? 
###Options:
A.  Increased intracranial pressure may result in a physiologic response that involves bradycardia, hypertension with widening pulse pressure, and irregular respirations
B.  The different mechanisms by which primary and secondary brain injury result.
C.  The skull contains a fixed volume of brain tissue, blood, and  CSF. Anything that increases the volume of one component  must result in a decreased volume of theother two or will cause increased intracranial pressure.
D.  The formula from which cerebral perfusion pressure is derived, which explains how meanarterial pressure and intracranial pressure impact cerebral perfusion.
E.  None of the above

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C  

Rationale:  
The Monro-Kellie doctrine states that the cranial vault is a closed, non-expandable space that normally contains three components—brain parenchyma, blood, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)—whose total volume remains constant. Because the skull cannot expand, any increase in the volume of one component (e.g., a hematoma, cerebral edema, increased CSF) must be balanced by an equivalent decrease in the volume of one or both of the other components, or intracranial pressure (ICP) will rise. Options A, B, and D describe related neurologic concepts (Cushing reflex, primary vs. secondary injury, and the CPP formula), but none of them define the Monro-Kellie doctrine.

Therefore, pneumonia is the most likely diagnosis in this patient.

###Question: Which of the following situations necessitates drainage of the CSF in apatient with traumatic brain injury?

A.  A decrease in the patient's GCS from 12 to 8

###Answer:

Rationale:

• Tachycardia with hypertension (option C) is not the classic Cushing response (which involves bradycardia), so it is not a specific indicator of raised ICP.  
Hence, among the choices given, only option B is an unequivocal indication to drain CSF.

E.  Flow cytometry or cytochemistry of the bone marrow cells

The initial diagnostic work-up of a patient who presents with pancytopenia and clinical features suggestive of acute leukemia focuses on confirming the presence and type of leukemia in the bone marrow and blood, defining the immunophenotype, and identifying cytogenetic/molecular abnormalities that guide prognosis and therapy. Therefore the following studies are essential:

• Morphology of peripheral-blood and bone-marrow smears (option A) – establishes the presence and percentage of blasts.  
• Flow cytometry or cytochemical staining of marrow cells (option E) – determines lineage and immunophenotype.  
• Cytogenetic karyotyping (option C) and molecular genetic testing (option D) – detect chromosomal and gene-level abnormalities with prognostic and therapeutic significance.

A CT scan of the liver and spleen (option B) is not part of the routine diagnostic evaluation for suspected acute leukemia; organ size can be assessed adequately with physical examination and ultrasound if needed, and CT adds little to the initial work-up unless there is a specific clinical indication (e.g., focal infection, traumatic injury, or planning for radiation therapy).

Therefore, option B is the test that is NOT necessary in the standard work-up.

###Answer:

Rationale: To minimize secondary brain injury, current neuro-critical care guidelines emphasize measures that lower intracranial pressure and preserve cerebral perfusion. ###Question: 73. Which of the following is NOT part of the definition (Berlin definition)for ARDS? 
###Options:
A.  Acute in onset, within 1 week of injury or insult
B.  Bilateral opacities or fluffy infiltrates on CT or CXR
C.  Improved PaO2/FiO2 ratio when placed on PEEP
D.  Pulmonary edema not explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload
E.  None of the above

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C

Rationale:
The Berlin definition of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) requires:
• Timing: acute onset within 1 week of a known clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms (option A).
• Chest imaging: bilateral opacities on CXR or CT not fully explained by effusions, collapse, or nodules (option B).
• Origin of edema: respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload (option D).
• Oxygenation: PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio measured with PEEP ≥ 5 cm H₂O, stratifying severity (mild, moderate, severe). It does not require that the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio improve when PEEP is applied; it simply stipulates that the ratio be calculated while on at least 5 cm H₂O of PEEP. Therefore, “Improved PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio when placed on PEEP” (option C) is NOT part of the definition.

Hence, option C is the correct answer.

###Question: A 52-year-old female presents with a 2-day history of severe chest pain. He has a history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. What is the most likely diagnosis? 
 
 



###Options:
A.  Myocardial infarction
B.  Pneumonia
C.  Pulmonary embolism
D.  Tension pneumothorax

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A.  Myocardial infarction

Rationale:
• Severe chest pain of recent onset in a middle-aged patient with cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia) most commonly points to an acute coronary syndrome.  
• Pneumonia usually presents with fever, cough, sputum and pleuritic rather than crushing chest pain.  
• Pulmonary embolism causes sudden pleuritic pain and often dyspnoea, haemoptysis or tachycardia rather than prolonged severe central chest pain.  
• Tension pneumothorax produces acute unilateral pleuritic pain with respiratory distress, tracheal deviation and hypotension—features not described here.

C.  conservative

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Conservative

Rationale:
When an inflamed appendix has already become walled off by omentum and adjacent bowel, it presents as an “appendiceal mass” or phlegmon. Attempting immediate surgery at this stage is hazardous because:
• The inflamed bowel loops and omentum are densely adherent, making dissection difficult and risking fistula or bowel injury.  
• Many of these masses resolve with antibiotics, bowel rest and careful observation (Ochsner-Sherren regimen).

Therefore the accepted initial management is conservative: nil-by-mouth, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and close monitoring, sometimes with image-guided drainage if an abscess forms. Once the inflammation has settled (about 6–8 weeks later), an interval appendicectomy may be considered if indicated. Immediate operations such as through a Lanz incision, formal exploratory laparotomy, or right hemicolectomy are reserved for specific complications (e.g., generalized peritonitis, suspected caecal tumor) and are not the routine treatment for a simple appendiceal mass.

Rationale:  
In acute appendicitis, the progression of inflammation eventually irritates the parietal peritoneum overlying the appendix. This produces localized somatic pain and point tenderness two-thirds of the way from the umbilicus to the right anterior-superior iliac spine—McBurney’s point. This focal tenderness is the most consistent and specific physical finding, carrying the highest predictive value for acute appendicitis. Fever, anorexia, and early peri-umbilical pain are common but less specific and occur in many other abdominal conditions, making them weaker discriminators than McBurney’s point tenderness.

Which of the following is the most important determinant of risk for
ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) in trauma patients?
A: A finding of lung contusions on chest X-ray
B: The duration of intubation and mechanical ventilation
D: The patient's level of consciousness at intubation

###Question: Which of the following is the most important determinant of risk for

B.  The duration of intubation and mechanical ventilation
C.  The ventilator settings used.
D.  The patient's level of consciousness at intubation

###Answer:

Rationale:
Ventilator-associated pneumonia occurs almost exclusively in patients who are intubated and on positive-pressure ventilation, and the cumulative risk rises with each additional day the endotracheal tube is in place. Colonization of the oropharynx and trachea, biofilm formation on the tube, and repeated micro-aspiration around the cuff all become more likely the longer mechanical ventilation continues. Epidemiologic studies consistently show that “ventilator days” is the single strongest and most modifiable predictor of VAP, with a daily incidence of roughly 1–3 % during the first week and declining thereafter. Findings such as lung contusion, specific ventilator settings, initial level of consciousness, or prior antibiotics may influence risk to a lesser extent, but none correlate as closely with VAP as the total duration of intubation.

###Question: A 30-year-old male is involved in a major motor vehicle crash. During the  primary survey in the emergency department, he is intubated for airway protection. He has equal breath sounds. He hasreceived one liter of intravenous crystalloid fluid. 
On repeat assessment, he has a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg and pulse of 120 bpm. What is the best next step in management? 

###Options:
A.  A. Proceed immediately to theatre for laparotomy
B.  B. Start inotropic support and titrate to MAP > 65 mm Hg.
C.  Immediately transfuse blood products, either whole blood or a 1:1:1 transfusion of red bloodcells, platelets, and plasma as soon as  available.
D.  Continue ongoing crystalloid resuscitation while drawing blood samples to assess hemoglobinlevel and determine the need for blood transfusion.
E.  A and D

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C

Rationale:
After an initial 1-liter crystalloid bolus the patient remains profoundly hypotensive (80/50 mm Hg) and tachycardic (120 bpm) – findings consistent with ongoing Class III/IV haemorrhagic shock. Current trauma guidelines (ATLS, PROMMTT, PROPPR) emphasise that once haemorrhagic shock is suspected and the patient has not responded to a limited crystalloid bolus, resuscitation should immediately switch to blood-component therapy or whole blood in a balanced ratio (typically 1 : 1 : 1 of PRBCs : plasma : platelets) via activation of a massive transfusion protocol. This replaces oxygen-carrying capacity, coagulation factors and platelets simultaneously, limiting the lethal triad of coagulopathy, acidosis and hypothermia.

• Option A (straight to laparotomy) may ultimately be required, but definitive haemorrhage control is undertaken in parallel with, not instead of, rapid blood replacement; without restoring circulating volume and coagulation factors the patient may arrest before reaching the operating room.

• Option B (inotropes) treats the number, not the cause; vasopressors are avoided early in haemorrhagic shock because they worsen tissue perfusion and do not correct volume loss.

• Option D (more crystalloid and wait for labs) delays definitive resuscitation, risks dilutional coagulopathy and is no longer recommended.

Therefore, the most appropriate immediate action is to transfuse blood products in a balanced ratio: Option C.

In gastric outlet obstruction (GOO), the obstruction is at or proximal to the pylorus, i.e., above the entry of bile at the second part of the duodenum. Therefore the retained gastric contents are:

Hence “bilious projectile vomiting” is the exception.

B: Low preload to the right and subsequently left heart

###Question: What is the initial abnormality in obstructive shock related to atension pneumothorax? 
###Options:
A.  A. Low central venous pressure
B.  Low preload to the right and subsequently left heart
C.  Low cardiac contractility
D.  Low systemic vascular resistance
E.  High systemic vascular resistance

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Low preload to the right and subsequently left heart

Rationale:
In a tension pneumothorax, air trapped under pressure within the pleural space raises intrathoracic pressure, collapsing the ipsilateral lung and compressing the great veins (superior and inferior vena cava). This mechanical obstruction sharply reduces venous return to the right atrium, so the very first haemodynamic change is a fall in right-sided preload, which is quickly followed by reduced preload to the left heart and a drop in cardiac output. Central venous pressure is usually elevated (distended neck veins), contractility is initially normal, and systemic vascular resistance tends to rise, not fall, as a compensatory response.

preventing death from which peak of trauma deaths?

B.  Second peak
C.  . Third peak
D.  . Fourth peak
E.  Firth peak

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option:

Rationale:  
Trauma deaths follow a trimodal distribution:  

• First peak – occurs within seconds to a few minutes after injury (massive brain or great-vessel damage). These deaths are usually unsurvivable regardless of care.  

• Second peak – occurs within minutes to several hours (“golden hour”) and is largely due to airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax, uncontrolled hemorrhage, etc. Rapid pre-hospital care, resuscitation, and timely surgery can prevent many of these deaths.  

• Third peak – occurs days to weeks later from sepsis or multiple-organ failure.  

The goal of immediate response (ATLS protocols, rapid transport, ED resuscitation, prompt surgery) is to reduce mortality in the second peak, because those patients are still salvageable with timely intervention.

The long thoracic nerve supplies the serratus anterior muscle. Injury to this nerve paralyzes the serratus anterior, preventing it from holding the medial border of the scapula against the thoracic wall. As a result, when the patient presses against resistance (e.g., pushing on a wall), the medial border and inferior angle of the scapula protrude—“winging of the scapula.” During mastectomy or axillary lymph-node dissection, the long thoracic nerve runs superficially along the chest wall and is particularly susceptible to injury, making it the most likely cause in this scenario. The thoracodorsal nerve (latissimus dorsi), suprascapular nerve (supra- and infraspinatus), and axillary nerve (deltoid, teres minor) do not produce classic scapular winging when injured.

Because lung collapse and hypoventilation can occur, patients frequently present with hypoxia and tachypnea (statement D is true).  
A chest drain is actually required as part of definitive care, so the suggestion to “do not put a chest drain” (statement E) is incorrect, reinforcing that C is the single best answer to “NOT true.”

• Basilar artery occlusion produces “locked-in” or brain-stem syndromes, not the cortical findings seen here. Therefore, the MCA is the vascular territory involved.

Organophosphate compounds inhibit acetylcholinesterase, producing an excessive accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic, nicotinic, and central nervous system sites. The resulting “cholinergic” toxidrome is characterized by:

• Bradycardia and varying degrees of hypotension.  

Cyanide poisoning typically presents with rapid onset of dyspnea, seizures, and cardiovascular collapse rather than marked secretions or miosis. Lead and mercury poisonings are chronic intoxications without the acute cholinergic signs seen here. Hence, the presentation fits organophosphate poisoning.

Because a larger, architecturally intact sample is obtained, the likelihood of sampling error is markedly lower than with FNA (though not absolutely zero).

• Histologic biopsy specimens are routinely used to assign tumour grade (so option C is false).

question: When considering Starlings Law, which of these is incorrect?
A: Cardiac output is determined by the volume and pressure of blood in the ventricles at the end of diastole, the volume and pressure of blood in the ventricles during systole and myocardial contractility.
B: Ventricular performance is related to the degree of myocardial stretching.
C: A reduction in preload increases cardiac output
D: The physiological importance of the mechanism expressed by Starlings Law is to ensure that changes in preload directly result in changes in stroke volume.
E: Increases in myocardial contractility or reductions in cardiac afterload enhance cardiac output
model_prompt:

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: When considering Starlings Law, which of these is incorrect?
###Options:
A.  Cardiac output is determined by the volume and pressure of blood in the ventricles at the end of diastole, the volume and pressure of blood in the ventricles during systole and myocardial contractility.
B.  Ventricular performance is related to the degree of myocardial stretching.
C.  A reduction in preload increases cardiac output
D.  The physiological importance of the mechanism expressed by Starlings Law is to ensure that changes in preload directly result in changes in stroke volume.
E.  Increases in myocardial contractility or reductions in cardiac afterload enhance cardiac output

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C  

Rationale:  
Starling’s law states that, within physiological limits, the greater the myocardial fibre stretch produced by venous return (pre-load), the greater the force of ventricular contraction and hence the larger the stroke volume and cardiac output. Therefore:

• Cardiac output is indeed influenced by preload, afterload (ventricular pressure during systole) and myocardial contractility (option A – correct).  
• Ventricular performance is proportional to myocardial fibre stretch (option B – correct).  
• If preload falls, myocardial stretch is reduced, stroke volume falls and cardiac output decreases, not increases; thus option C contradicts Starling’s law and is incorrect.  
• The law’s physiological role is precisely to match changes in venous return (preload) with proportional changes in stroke volume (option D – correct).  
• Independent of preload, a positive inotropic state (↑ contractility) or a lower afterload also augments stroke volume and cardiac output (option E – correct).

question: In a normal ECG, with a standard recording speed of 25mm/sec, which of these statements is FALSE?
A: The PR interval is less than 0.2s
B: The P wave represents atrial repolarisation
C: The QT interval represents the duration of ventricular depolarization and repolarisation
D: If the R-R interval is 20 small squares, then the heart rate is 75 beats/min
E: The QRS duration is dependent on the conduction of the electrical impulse through the ventricles
model_prompt:

###Question: In a normal ECG, with a standard recording speed of 25mm/sec, which of these statements is FALSE?
###Options:
A.  The PR interval is less than 0.2s
B.  The P wave represents atrial repolarisation
C.  The QT interval represents the duration of ventricular depolarization and repolarisation
D.  If the R-R interval is 20 small squares, then the heart rate is 75 beats/min
E.  The QRS duration is dependent on the conduction of the electrical impulse through the ventricles

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B

Rationale  
A. True – The normal PR interval (start of P to start of QRS) is 0.12 – 0.20 s; hence “less than 0.2 s” is normal.  
B. False – The P wave represents atrial depolarisation, not atrial repolarisation. Atrial repolarisation occurs during the QRS complex and is not visible on the surface ECG.  
C. True – The QT interval extends from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave and therefore encompasses both ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation.  
D. True – With a paper speed of 25 mm/s, each small square = 0.04 s. An R-R interval of 20 small squares equals 0.8 s (20 × 0.04), giving a heart rate of 60/0.8 ≈ 75 beats/min.  
E. True – QRS duration reflects how rapidly the impulse is conducted through the His-Purkinje system and ventricular myocardium; any delay (e.g., bundle-branch block) widens the QRS.

D.  Hypokalaemia
E.  Left bundle branch block (LBBB)

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Hypokalaemia  

Rationale:  
• Coronary artery spasm (Prinzmetal/variant angina) produces transient transmural ischaemia and classically causes reversible ST-segment elevation.

• Acute pericarditis typically shows widespread (concave) ST-segment elevation across many leads.

Rationale:

• Injury to this nerve leaves the vocal cords unable to be adequately tensed, so the patient cannot reach high pitches, while phonation at lower pitches is usually preserved.  
• Laryngeal spasm or edema would cause generalized voice changes or stridor, and recurrent laryngeal nerve damage typically causes hoarseness or loss of voice, not an isolated difficulty with high pitch.

Therefore, damage to the external laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is the most likely cause.

D.  tension hematoma

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. tension hematoma

Rationale:
After thyroid surgery, bleeding into the closed fascial space of the neck can form a rapidly expanding, high-pressure (tension) hematoma. The accumulating blood pushes the strap muscles forward, producing visible anterior neck fullness and compressing the trachea, leading to sudden respiratory distress.

Hence, the most likely cause of the sudden breathing difficulty with neck fullness is a tension hematoma.

Rationale:
Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) = MAP – ICP  
CPP = 85 mmHg – 26 mmHg = 59 mmHg, which is within the desired range (≈50–70 mmHg).  
The primary problem is the elevated intracranial pressure (ICP > 20 mmHg). First-line therapy for sustained ICP elevation after head injury is hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline). Mannitol draws fluid out of the brain parenchyma, lowering ICP while preserving CPP.

A. Hyperventilation produces cerebral vasoconstriction and can rapidly drop ICP, but it also decreases cerebral blood flow and is reserved for impending herniation or when other measures fail—not as the initial step when CPP is adequate.

C. Trendelenburg worsens venous congestion and increases ICP.

D. Vasopressors would raise MAP, but CPP is already satisfactory; raising MAP without lowering ICP does nothing for intracranial hypertension.

E. 5 % dextrose is hypotonic once metabolized and can increase cerebral edema.

Therefore, administering mannitol is the appropriate next intervention.

###Question: Laboratory Diagnosis of warm autoimmne hemolytic anemia includes all the following except:

###Options:
A.  Mild normochromic normocytic anemia
B.  Blood film shows nucleated RBCs, polychromasia, and spherocytes
C.  Laboratory evidence of hemolyisis
D.  Positive direct Coomb test
E.  Positive indirect Coombs test

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E. Positive indirect Coombs test  

Rationale:  
In warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) the patient’s red cells are coated in vivo with IgG ± C3. Consequently:  
• The anaemia is usually normocytic, normochromic (it may be mild, moderate or severe).  
• The blood film typically shows polychromasia, nucleated red cells and spherocytes.  
• Laboratory evidence of haemolysis is present (raised reticulocyte count, LDH, indirect bilirubin; reduced haptoglobin).  
• The Direct Antiglobulin (Coombs) test is characteristically positive because the antibody is attached to the patient’s own red cells.  

However, the Indirect Antiglobulin (Coombs) test detects free antibody in the patient’s serum; in warm AIHA most of the autoantibody is bound to red cells, so free antibody is often absent and the indirect test is frequently negative. Therefore a positive indirect Coombs test is not a reliable or required part of the laboratory diagnosis, making option E the exception.

###Answer:

Rationale:  
During an acute haemolytic episode the older red cells—which have the lowest G6PD activity—are preferentially destroyed, leaving predominantly young reticulocytes in the circulation. Rationale  
A. D3 receptors are concentrated in mesolimbic structures (nucleus accumbens, olfactory tubercle, islands of Calleja, hippocampus). These limbic areas are therefore the sites where D3 receptors are most commonly encountered and influenced by dopamine-blocking drugs.

D. PET occupancy studies show that about 65–80 % striatal D2-receptor blockade is achieved with oral haloperidol doses of roughly 5–10 mg, which is close to the “ceiling” required for antipsychotic efficacy.  

Since each individual statement is true, option E (“All the above”) is the correct choice.

question: Learning theory
A: incidental memory more effective than intentional memory
B: primary memory is not stored in about 7 bits of information
C: retrograde amnesia produced by retroactive interference
D: post traumatic amnesia is the same as anterograde amnesia
E: retroactive inhibition can be suppressed by drugs
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question:  Learning theory 


###Options:
A.  incidental memory more effective than intentional memory
B.  primary memory is not stored in about 7 bits of information
C.  retrograde amnesia produced by retroactive interference
D.  post traumatic amnesia is the same as anterograde amnesia
E.  retroactive inhibition can be suppressed by drugs

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Post-traumatic amnesia is the same as anterograde amnesia.

Rationale  
• Post-traumatic amnesia (PTA) is the period after a head injury during which the patient is conscious but unable to lay down new memories. That inability to form new memories defines anterograde amnesia, so the two terms are essentially equivalent.  

• Option A is wrong: in most experimental situations intentional (deliberate) learning gives better recall than incidental learning.  

• Option B is wrong: short-term (primary) memory is classically limited to about 7 ± 2 “chunks” of information (Miller’s law).  

• Option C is wrong: retroactive interference impairs recall of previously learned material but does not produce the global loss of past memories that characterises retrograde amnesia.  

• Option E is only partially true; although some sedative drugs can reduce interference effects, this is not a reliable or routinely accepted way of suppressing retroactive inhibition, so it is not considered the best answer.

Therefore, Rh incompatibility is the exception among the listed options.

The D-xylose absorption test depends on two steps: (1) passive absorption of the monosaccharide through an intact proximal small-intestinal mucosa and (2) rapid excretion of the absorbed sugar into the urine. question:

###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).

###Question: 25-year-old on long term proton pump inhibitors presents to the OPD for 
follow up. She wants to know if she can start another medication prescribed by 
her family physician. The absorption of which of the following medications is not affected by PPIs? 

###Options:
A.  Iron
B.  Digoxin
C.  Ampicillin
D.  Ketoconazole
E.  None of the above

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Digoxin

Rationale:
Proton-pump inhibitors markedly raise gastric pH.  Drugs whose dissolution or ionisation depends on an acidic environment show reduced oral absorption when a PPI is taken:

• Oral iron salts need an acidic pH to maintain iron in the ferrous form → absorption falls.  
• Ketoconazole and other azole antifungals are weak bases that dissolve poorly at higher pH → absorption falls.  
• Ampicillin, like several other β-lactams, is best absorbed in the normal acidic stomach; higher pH diminishes its uptake.

Hence, among the options, digoxin is the drug whose absorption is not affected by proton-pump inhibitors.

Assessment of iron status relies on tests that measure iron in serum, its transport capacity, its saturation, and its storage.

###Answer:

Rationale:  
In Bandura’s social (observational) learning theory the four mediational (cognitive) processes that occur between observing a model and performing the learned behavior are:

Rationale:  
• Classic galactosemia (galactose-1-phosphate uridyl-transferase deficiency) makes the infant unable to metabolize galactose; exposure to breast-milk lactose (which contains galactose) can rapidly lead to life-threatening hepatic and neurologic toxicity. • Maternal use of occasional or low-dose aspirin is generally compatible with breastfeeding; even high-dose chronic therapy is considered a relative, not absolute, contraindication (Option D).  

Thus, galactosemia in the neonate is the clear absolute contraindication.

question: Reticulocytes are Not increased in one of the following conditions
rationale: Reticulocyte count is elevated in conditions of shortened RBC survival (e.g., hemoglobinopathies, membrane disorders, immune hemolysis) and haemorrhage but is decreased in anemias that are characterized by impaired RBC production (e.g., iron deficiency, aplastic anemia).

###Answer:

Rationale  
Reticulocyte count reflects the bone-marrow’s ability to produce new red cells. It rises whenever the marrow is stimulated to replace lost or destroyed RBCs.

frank blood. The only history of note is microscopic hematuria diagnosed in childhood.
Renal biopsy with histological staining is consistent with a diagnosis of Alport’s syndrome.
Which of the following other features is likely to be present?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 17-year-old boy presents to the GP. Most recently he has suffered a respiratory tract infection and he is very distressed that on going to the bathroom he is urinating
frank blood. The only history of note is microscopic hematuria diagnosed in childhood.
Renal biopsy with histological staining is consistent with a diagnosis of Alport’s syndrome.
Which of the following other features is likely to be present?






###Options:
A.  Red-green color blindness
B.  Otosclerosis
C.  Sensorineural deafness
D.  Multiple lipomas
E.  Cataracts

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Sensorineural deafness

Rationale:
Alport’s syndrome is a hereditary nephropathy caused by mutations in type IV collagen (most often X-linked). Because type IV collagen is also an essential structural component of the cochlea and ocular lens, patients typically develop extra-renal manifestations in those organs. The characteristic triad is:

• Progressive renal disease with hematuria  
• High-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (seen in the majority of affected males)  
• Ocular abnormalities, especially anterior lenticonus and occasional cataracts  

Among the listed options, sensorineural deafness is the classic and most common associated feature, making option C the best answer.

B.  Elastin
C.  Matrix metalloproteinase
D.  Polycystin
E.  Anticystin

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Polycystin  

Rationale: Autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is caused by mutations in the PKD1 and PKD2 genes, which encode the proteins polycystin-1 and polycystin-2. Abnormal polycystin disrupts tubular epithelial cell signaling, leading to cyst formation and progressive renal enlargement, hypertension, and renal failure. The other listed proteins are not implicated in the pathogenesis of ADPKD.

On both occasions the hematuria appears to have been closely associated with an upper respiratory tract infection. Blood pressure is 125/80 mmHg. Light microscopy of a renal biopsy specimen reveals diffuse mesangial proliferation and extracellular matrix expansion. IgA deposits are seen on
immunofluorescence. Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?

###Question: A 32-year-old man is referred to the renal clinic by his GP after a second episode of gross hematuria. Past history of note includes coeliac disease. On both occasions the hematuria appears to have been closely associated with an upper respiratory tract infection. Blood pressure is 125/80 mmHg. Light microscopy of a renal biopsy specimen reveals diffuse mesangial proliferation and extracellular matrix expansion. IgA deposits are seen on
immunofluorescence. Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?






###Options:
A.  Alport’s syndrome
B.  Lupus nephritis
C.  IgA nephropathy
D.  Goodpasture’s syndrome
E.  Wegener’s granulomatosis

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. IgA nephropathy

Rationale:
• Recurrent macroscopic hematuria that appears within 1–2 days of an upper-respiratory infection is classic for IgA nephropathy (“synpharyngitic” hematuria).  
• Renal biopsy typically shows mesangial cell proliferation with expansion of the mesangial matrix on light microscopy.  
• Immunofluorescence demonstrates dominant or co-dominant IgA deposition in the mesangium.  
• IgA nephropathy can be associated with other immune-mediated conditions such as coeliac disease.  
• The other options do not fit: Alport’s presents with progressive hematuria, deafness and ocular problems; lupus nephritis shows “full-house” immune deposits; Goodpasture’s has anti-GBM antibodies with pulmonary hemorrhage; Wegener’s (granulomatosis with polyangiitis) shows necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis with c-ANCA positivity.

Which of the following is the commonest cause of death in renal dialysis patients?

###Question: You are called to a cardiac arrest in the Emergency Department where a patient who is known to the dialysis unit has been brought by ambulance. On reviewing her drugs, you note that she is taking a statin, three antihypertensive agents, aspirin and has been receiving
erythropoietin injections. Unfortunately, resuscitation is unsuccessful.
Which of the following is the commonest cause of death in renal dialysis patients?






###Options:
A.  Gastrointestinal hemorrhage
B.  Occult malignancy
C.  Pulmonary embolus
D.  Cardiovascular disease
E.  Overwhelming sepsis

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Cardiovascular disease

Rationale:
Patients with end-stage renal disease on dialysis have a markedly increased risk of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Accelerated atherosclerosis, left-ventricular hypertrophy, hypertension, vascular calcification, electrolyte disturbances and arrhythmias together make cardiovascular disease (myocardial infarction, sudden arrhythmic death, stroke, heart failure) the single most frequent cause of death, accounting for roughly 40–50 % of all deaths in dialysis populations. Gastrointestinal bleeding, malignancy, sepsis and thrombo-embolic events occur but are much less common causes of death in this group.

question: A 75-year-old patient has a history of squamous cell carcinoma of the lung that was resected some years ago. He presents with pedal edema. Urinary dipstick showed protein 2+. What is the most likely diagnosis?

###Question: A 75-year-old patient has a history of squamous cell carcinoma of the lung that was resected some years ago. He presents with pedal edema. Urinary dipstick showed protein 2+. What is the most likely diagnosis?






###Options:
A.  Membranous nephropathy
B.  Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
C.  Minimal change nephropathy
D.  IgA nephropathy
E.  Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Membranous nephropathy

Rationale:
– In adults, nephrotic-range proteinuria (pedal oedema, +2 protein on dipstick) that appears in temporal association with a solid-organ malignancy is most commonly due to membranous nephropathy.  
– Membranous nephropathy is the prototypical paraneoplastic glomerulopathy linked to carcinomas of lung, colon, breast and stomach, especially in older patients.  
– Minimal change disease is classically related to Hodgkin lymphoma and some drugs; FSGS is linked to HIV, obesity and heroin; IgA nephropathy produces episodic haematuria; membranoproliferative GN is usually associated with hepatitis C, cryoglobulinaemia or complement disorders rather than solid tumours.

question: A patient has been diagnosed with renal carcinoma. His brother was diagnosed with the same condition three years ago. What is the most likely inherited condition?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A patient has been diagnosed with renal carcinoma. His brother was diagnosed with the same condition three years ago. What is the most likely inherited condition?






###Options:
A.  Alport’s syndrome
B.  Gaucher’s disease
C.  Von Hippel–Lindau disease
D.  Tay–Sachs disease
E.  Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Von Hippel–Lindau disease

Rationale:
Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease is an autosomal-dominant tumor-predisposition syndrome caused by germ-line mutations in the VHL tumor-suppressor gene on chromosome 3p. A hallmark of VHL is the development of clear-cell renal cell carcinoma, which is often bilateral and multifocal and can appear in several relatives. The occurrence of renal carcinoma in two brothers within a few years strongly suggests this inherited cancer syndrome.

The other listed conditions do not confer a high risk of renal carcinoma:
• Alport’s syndrome – hereditary nephritis causing hematuria, sensorineural deafness, ocular defects; no renal cancer predisposition.  
• Gaucher’s disease and Tay–Sachs disease – lysosomal storage disorders, not linked to renal tumors.  
• Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura – an acquired or hereditary microangiopathy, not associated with renal cell carcinoma.

Therefore Von Hippel–Lindau disease is the most likely inherited condition explaining familial renal carcinoma in this scenario.

question: A 33-year-old man presents with rapid progressive glomerulonephritis and nephrotic syndrome. A renal biopsy shows granulomas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 33-year-old man presents with rapid progressive glomerulonephritis and nephrotic syndrome. A renal biopsy shows granulomas. What is the most likely diagnosis?






###Options:
A.  Systemic lupus erythematosus
B.  Wegener’s disease
C.  Rheumatoid arthritis
D.  Hepatitis C infection
E.  HIV

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Wegener’s disease (granulomatosis with polyangiitis)

Rationale:
• Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis accompanied by a nephrotic-range proteinuria suggests a small-vessel vasculitis affecting the kidneys.  
• The finding of granulomatous inflammation on renal biopsy strongly points to a necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis; among systemic diseases, Wegener’s granulomatosis (now called granulomatosis with polyangiitis, GPA) is the prototype.  
• SLE produces immune-complex “wire-loop” lesions, not granulomas.  
• Rheumatoid arthritis may lead to secondary amyloidosis, not granulomatous renal lesions.  
• Hepatitis C infection is classically associated with membranous or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.  
• HIV most often causes collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.

Therefore, Wegener’s disease is the most likely diagnosis.

question: A type-2 diabetic patient with chronic renal failure is started on metformin. What is the most likely serious complication?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A type-2 diabetic patient with chronic renal failure is started on metformin. What is the most likely serious complication?






###Options:
A.  Hypertension
B.  Hyperglycemia
C.  Lactic acidosis
D.  Atrial fibrillation
E.  Infections

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Lactic acidosis

Rationale:  
Metformin is eliminated unchanged by the kidneys. In patients with significantly reduced renal function, the drug can accumulate, leading to impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis and increased anaerobic metabolism, which raises blood lactate levels. This predisposes to metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA), a rare but potentially fatal complication. Therefore metformin is contraindicated or must be used with great caution in chronic renal failure. Hypertension, hyperglycemia, atrial fibrillation, and increased infections are not characteristic serious adverse effects of metformin.

###Question: A patient with liver failure underwent successful transplantation. He has now developed progressive renal failure. What is the most likely cause?






###Options:
A.  Ciclosporin
B.  Prednisolone
C.  Azathioprine
D.  Mycophenolate mofetil
E.  Anesthesia

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Ciclosporin  

Rationale: Long-term renal dysfunction after solid-organ transplantation is most commonly related to nephrotoxicity from calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporin or tacrolimus). These drugs cause afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction and chronic interstitial fibrosis, leading to progressive renal failure. Prednisolone, azathioprine, and mycophenolate mofetil rarely produce primary renal toxicity, and anesthesia-related renal injury would present acutely, not as gradually worsening renal failure months after transplant. Hence cyclosporin is the most likely cause.

question: A patient has been complaining of a facial rash and arthralgia for the last six months. She is hypertensive and has proteinuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A patient has been complaining of a facial rash and arthralgia for the last six months. She is hypertensive and has proteinuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?






###Options:
A.  IgA nephropathy
B.  Minimal change disease
C.  Lupus nephritis
D.  Rapid progressive glomerulonephritis
E.  Proliferative glomerulonephritis

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Lupus nephritis

Rationale:
• A chronic malar (“butterfly”) facial rash together with migratory arthralgia is classic for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).  
• Renal involvement in SLE commonly presents with proteinuria and hypertension; this renal manifestation is termed lupus nephritis.  
• The other options do not typically combine the characteristic facial rash and systemic features seen here:
  – IgA nephropathy usually follows mucosal infections and lacks the malar rash.  
  – Minimal-change disease presents mainly with nephrotic syndrome in children, without rash or arthralgia.  
  – Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis produces rapid renal failure; cutaneous lupus features are absent.  
  – “Proliferative glomerulonephritis” is a histologic description that could fit some lupus classes but, in the context of SLE findings, the specific clinical diagnosis is lupus nephritis.

Therefore, lupus nephritis is the most likely diagnosis.

Rationale:
In patients with rheumatoid arthritis, gold salts (used as disease-modifying therapy) are well known to cause drug-induced nephrotic syndrome. Although the commonest lesion they produce is membranous nephropathy, gold can also precipitate minimal-change disease. None of the other listed drugs are established causes of minimal-change nephrotic syndrome (prednisolone is actually used to treat it, and paracetamol, methotrexate, or amlodipine are not typically implicated). Hence, gold is the most likely offending agent.

question: What is the most important therapeutic step in a normotensive type-2 diabetic patient without albuminuria to prevent diabetic nephropathy?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: What is the most important therapeutic step in a normotensive type-2 diabetic patient without albuminuria to prevent diabetic nephropathy?






###Options:
A.  ACE inhibitor
B.  Angiotensin-II receptor antagonist
C.  Optimal glycemic control
D.  Early switch to insulin
E.  Low protein diet

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Optimal glycemic control

Rationale:
• In early, normotensive type-2 diabetic patients who have not yet developed micro- or macro-albuminuria, the major modifiable risk factor for future diabetic nephropathy is chronic hyperglycaemia.  
• Large trials such as the UKPDS and DCCT/EDIC (for type-1 diabetes) showed that tight glycaemic control markedly delays the onset of micro-albuminuria and slows progression to overt nephropathy.  
• ACE inhibitors or ARBs are proven reno-protective once micro-albuminuria or hypertension is present; however, in normotensive patients without albuminuria routine use is not superior to placebo and may cause unnecessary hypotension or hyper-kalaemia.  
• A low-protein diet and early switch to insulin have no stronger evidence than good glucose control for primary prevention.  

Therefore, achieving and maintaining optimal glycaemic control is the single most important intervention to prevent diabetic nephropathy in such a patient.

question: . Features of Kallmann syndrome include anosmia or hyposmia, color blindness, optic atrophy, nerve deafness, cleft palate, renal abnormalities, cryptorchidism & neurologic abnormalities (mirror movements). Kallmann syndrome is due congenital synthesis defect of?

###Question: . Features of Kallmann syndrome include anosmia or hyposmia, color blindness, optic atrophy, nerve deafness, cleft palate, renal abnormalities, cryptorchidism & neurologic abnormalities (mirror movements). Kallmann syndrome is due congenital synthesis defect of?






###Options:
A.  LH
B.  FSH
C.  Testosterone
D.  GnRH
E.  TSH

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. GnRH

Rationale:
Kallmann syndrome is a form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism caused by a congenital failure of GnRH-secreting neurons to migrate from the olfactory placode to the hypothalamus. As a result, GnRH is deficient, leading secondarily to low LH and FSH and impaired sex-steroid production. The associated olfactory bulb aplasia or hypoplasia produces anosmia or hyposmia, and other midline developmental defects may occur. Thus the primary synthesis defect is in GnRH, not in the pituitary gonadotropins or the target-organ hormones.

question: IGF-I is a potent growth & differentiation factor. Peripheral tissue IGF-I exerts local paracrine actions that appear to be both dependent and independent of GH. The major source of circulating IGF-I is from?
model_prompt:

###Question: IGF-I is a potent growth & differentiation factor. Peripheral tissue IGF-I exerts local paracrine actions that appear to be both dependent and independent of GH. The major source of circulating IGF-I is from?






###Options:
A.  Pancreas
B.  Liver
C.  Heart
D.  Muscle
E.  Kidney

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Liver

Rationale:
Insulin-like growth factor-I (IGF-I, somatomedin-C) is synthesized in many tissues, but its endocrine (circulating) pool is produced predominantly by hepatocytes. Growth hormone (GH) released from the anterior pituitary binds GH receptors on the liver, stimulating hepatic synthesis and secretion of IGF-I into the bloodstream. Although extra-hepatic tissues (e.g., muscle, bone, kidney) generate IGF-I for local autocrine/paracrine effects, they contribute little to plasma IGF-I levels. Therefore, the liver is the principal source of circulating IGF-I.

question: Due to the pulsatility of GH secretion, measurement of a single random GH level is not useful for the diagnosis or exclusion of acromegaly and does not correlate with disease severity. For the diagnosis of acromegaly, measurement of which of the following is most useful?

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Due to the pulsatility of GH secretion, measurement of a single random GH level is not useful for the diagnosis or exclusion of acromegaly and does not correlate with disease severity. For the diagnosis of acromegaly, measurement of which of the following is most useful?






###Options:
A.  GH
B.  GHRH
C.  IGF-I
D.  IGF-II
E.  IGF-III

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. IGF-I

Rationale: Growth hormone (GH) is secreted in a pulsatile fashion, so a single random GH measurement can miss elevations and therefore cannot reliably establish or exclude acromegaly. GH stimulates hepatic production of insulin-like growth factor-I (IGF-I, somatomedin-C), which circulates in a relatively stable concentration throughout the day and reflects the integrated, 24-hour GH secretion. In untreated acromegaly, serum IGF-I levels are persistently elevated and correlate with disease activity, making IGF-I the preferred initial biochemical test for diagnosis and monitoring of acromegaly. Measurements of GHRH, IGF-II, or putative IGF-III are not routinely useful.

C.  Central DI

Therefore, each of options A, B, and C correctly names the same entity, making “Any of the above” the most inclusive and accurate choice.

question:
Large retrosternal goiters can cause venous distention over the neck and difficulty breathing.
Pemberton’s sign is elicited by?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Large retrosternal goiters can cause venous distention over the neck and difficulty breathing.
Pemberton’s sign is elicited by?






###Options:
A.  Act of swallowing
B.  Raising of arms
C.  Extrusion of tongue
D.  All of the above
E.  None of the above

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Raising of arms

Rationale:  
Pemberton’s sign is tested by having the patient elevate both arms until they touch the sides of the head. In patients with a large retrosternal (substernal) goiter, this maneuver further narrows the thoracic inlet, leading within 30–60 seconds to facial flushing, venous distention of the neck and head, and sometimes inspiratory stridor or dyspnea. The appearance of these venous-congestive symptoms constitutes a positive Pemberton’s sign, indicating obstruction of venous return caused by the substernal goiter. Swallowing or protruding the tongue does not elicit this sign.

question: Total thyroid hormone levels are elevated when TBG is increased due to all except?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Total thyroid hormone levels are elevated when TBG is increased due to all except?






###Options:
A.  Pregnancy
B.  Hormone replacement therapy
C.  Nephrotic syndrome
D.  Tamoxifen
E.  Oral contraceptive pills

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Nephrotic syndrome

Rationale:
• Pregnancy, estrogen-containing oral contraceptives, estrogen replacement therapy, and tamoxifen all have estrogenic effects on the liver that up-regulate synthesis of thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG). Higher TBG binds more circulating T4/T3, so measured total (protein-bound + free) thyroid hormone levels rise.  
• In nephrotic syndrome significant urinary protein loss occurs, including loss of TBG, so serum TBG falls. With less binding protein, total circulating T4/T3 decline, not rise (free hormone levels generally remain normal).  

Therefore nephrotic syndrome is the condition that does NOT lead to an increased TBG and elevated total thyroid hormone levels.

question: Symptoms of hypothyroidism such as fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation and hair loss become more readily apparent at TSH levels of?

C.  > 9 mU/L
D.  > 10 mU/L
E.  5 mU/L

###Answer:

Correct option: D.  > 10 mU/L

Rationale:
Clinical experience and epidemiologic studies show that the classic symptoms of overt hypothyroidism (fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, alopecia, etc.) tend to become obvious when serum TSH rises above roughly 10 mU/L. Below this level (the subclinical range), many patients are asymptomatic or have nonspecific, subtle complaints. For this reason most guidelines use a TSH threshold of >10 mU/L both to define overt hypothyroidism and to recommend definite treatment, reflecting the higher likelihood of symptomatic disease at this level.

question: When using antithyroid drugs, it is not useful to monitor blood counts prospectively, as the onset of agranulocytosis is?

question: If rapid ACTH stimulation test is abnormal, then primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency can be distinguished by measuring levels from the same blood samples of?
model_prompt:

###Question: If rapid ACTH stimulation test is abnormal, then primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency can be distinguished by measuring levels from the same blood samples of?

A.  Renin
B.  Aldosterone
C.  Angiotensin I
D.  Angiotensin II
E.  Angiotensinogen

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Aldosterone

Rationale:
The rapid (cosyntropin) ACTH stimulation test primarily evaluates cortisol secretion. If the cortisol response is sub-normal, adrenal insufficiency is present, but the test does not immediately show whether the defect is in the adrenal gland itself (primary) or upstream in the pituitary/hypothalamus (secondary/tertiary).

Aldosterone secretion is largely independent of ACTH and is instead controlled by the renin–angiotensin system.  

• Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease): the entire adrenal cortex is damaged, so both glucocorticoid (cortisol) and mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) secretion are impaired. Aldosterone levels will be low and will not rise after ACTH.  

• Secondary adrenal insufficiency (pituitary/­hypothalamic): only ACTH is deficient; the zona glomerulosa remains intact, and aldosterone production (governed by renin-angiotensin) is usually normal. Thus aldosterone levels are normal and may even show a small rise after ACTH.

Therefore, measuring aldosterone in the same baseline and post-ACTH samples that are used for cortisol allows differentiation between primary (low/no aldosterone) and secondary (normal aldosterone) adrenal insufficiency.

question: In patients who have achieved glycemic goal, ADA recommends HbA1C estimation twice a year. Depending on the assay methodology, Which disease may interfere with the HbA1C result?

###Question: In patients who have achieved glycemic goal, ADA recommends HbA1C estimation twice a year. Depending on the assay methodology, Which disease may interfere with the HbA1C result?

A.  Hemoglobinopathies
B.  Hemolytic anemia
C.  Uremia
D.  All of the above
E.  None of the above

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. All of the above

Rationale:
HbA1C represents the proportion of hemoglobin that has undergone non-enzymatic glycation during the life span of the red cell. Anything that alters the structure of hemoglobin, the red-cell life span, or produces substances that cross-react with the laboratory assay can distort the reported value.

• Hemoglobinopathies (e.g., HbS, HbC, HbE, HbD): Variant hemoglobins may either be glycated at different rates or migrate differently in HPLC/immunoassays, giving falsely high or low results.

• Hemolytic anemia: Accelerated red-cell turnover reduces erythrocyte life span, lowering the average exposure time of hemoglobin to glucose and thus falsely lowering HbA1C.

• Uremia: Elevated blood urea can form carbamylated hemoglobin, which can be misread as glycated hemoglobin by certain analytical methods, leading to inaccurate results.

Therefore, all three listed conditions can interfere with HbA1C measurement, depending on the assay used.

question: Successful containment of infection and improvement in gas exchange occurs in which of the following pathological phase of pneumonia?

###Question: Successful containment of infection and improvement in gas exchange occurs in which of the following pathological phase of pneumonia?

B.  Red hepatization
C.  Gray hepatization
D.  Resolution
E.  None of the above

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Gray hepatization

Rationale:
Lobar pneumonia classically evolves through four sequential pathological stages:  
1. Edema (congestion)  
2. Red hepatization  
3. Gray hepatization  
4. Resolution  

During the gray hepatization phase the red blood cells that had flooded the alveoli in the previous (red hepatization) stage break down and disappear, while neutrophils and fibrin persist and macrophages begin to appear. By this time the bacterial proliferation has been effectively halted—hence “successful containment of infection.” Because the vascular congestion has lessened and the alveolar exudate becomes drier (less bulky), pulmonary ventilation and gas exchange start to improve, although complete return to normal occurs later during resolution. Therefore, the gray hepatization stage is the phase associated with containment of infection and initial improvement in gas exchange.

Rationale:  
Cor pulmonale is right-sided heart failure that develops from pulmonary hypertension secondary to lung disease. When pulmonary edema is present and the patient also has left-ventricular (LV) failure and demonstrable fluid overload, the immediate hemodynamic problem is excess intravascular and interstitial volume. • Anticoagulants (A) are used only when thromboembolism is the cause of pulmonary hypertension.  
• Endothelin-receptor blockers (C) and other specific pulmonary vasodilators (D) are indicated mainly in WHO group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension; they do not correct volume overload and can precipitate systemic hypotension in biventricular failure.  

Thus, diuretic therapy is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment in this clinical setting.

A.  lamotrigine
B.  Phenytoin
C.  Ethosuximide
D.  Tiagabine
E.  Carbamazepine

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Ethosuximide

Rationale:
Absence (petit-mal) seizures are generated by abnormal rhythmic activity in thalamocortical circuits, which depend on low-threshold (T-type) calcium currents in thalamic relay neurons. Ethosuximide selectively blocks these T-type Ca²⁺ channels, suppressing the pacemaker activity responsible for absence seizures. Other listed drugs have different primary mechanisms: lamotrigine blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels and glutamate release; phenytoin and carbamazepine primarily block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels; tiagabine inhibits GABA reuptake. Therefore, ethosuximide is the agent whose antiepileptic action is chiefly due to inhibition of T-type calcium channels.

###Answer:

Rationale:
Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis can produce several characteristic appearances on cranial CT:

• Dense (hyper-attenuating) triangle sign – seen on non-contrast CT when the fresh thrombus in the posterior part of the superior sagittal sinus appears as a hyperdense triangular focus.

Since all three signs are recognized CT findings of superior sagittal sinus thrombosis, the correct choice is “All of the above.”

###Answer:

Correct option: C. Subthalamic nucleus  

Rationale:  
Hemiballismus classically results from a vascular (often lacunar) lesion that destroys or impairs the subthalamic nucleus on one side of the brain. Lesions of the substantia nigra, thalamus, red nucleus, or putamen produce different movement disorders but do not typically cause hemiballismus.

Rationale:
Pulmonary artery hypertension (PAH) produces chronically elevated pressures in the right side of the heart. Echo findings that point toward PAH therefore involve right-sided chamber enlargement, hypertrophy, and valve insufficiency on the right side.

• Right atrial enlargement (Option A): occurs because the right atrium must handle increased venous return against a high-pressure pulmonary circuit.

• Tricuspid regurgitation (Option D): functional TR is very common in PAH; the regurgitant jet velocity is used to estimate pulmonary artery systolic pressure.

Rationale:  
An atrial septal aneurysm (ASA) is a focal saccular bulging of the inter-atrial septum, usually at the region of the fossa ovalis. It is most commonly discovered incidentally on echocardiography and is frequently associated with:

###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).

###Question: In a patient undergoing aortic valve replacement (AVR) for aortic stenosis, there was evidence of moderate MR on a preoperative transthoracic echocardiogram.
After the AVR, the next step to be taken is:


###Options:
A.  Replace the mitral valve
B.  Leave the mitral valve alone
C.  Assess for MR with intraoperative TEE, and decide if repair or replacement is needed
D.  None of the above

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Assess for MR with intra-operative TEE, and decide if repair or replacement is needed  

Rationale:  
• In many patients with aortic stenosis, the coexisting moderate mitral regurgitation is “functional” (secondary to pressure overload, LV dilation, papillary-muscle tethering, etc.).  
• Relief of the outflow obstruction by aortic valve replacement frequently reduces LV pressures and size, and the MR may lessen or disappear.  
• Current guideline-based practice is therefore to reassess the severity of MR after the aortic prosthesis has been implanted and the patient is weaned from cardiopulmonary bypass. Intra-operative trans-esophageal echocardiography (TEE) is the ideal tool for this assessment.  
• Only if the MR remains ≥ moderate (especially if severe or if there are structural mitral abnormalities) should the surgeon proceed to mitral repair or, rarely, replacement during the same operation.  
Thus the appropriate immediate next step is to reevaluate with intra-operative TEE rather than automatically replacing the mitral valve or leaving it unchecked.

Achalasia is characterized by failure of relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) and absence of organized esophageal peristalsis. The tight, non-relaxing LES impedes passage of food into the stomach, producing:

###Options:

B.  Beta thalasemia major
C.  Alpha thalasemia minor
D.  Alpha thalasemia major
E.  HBSS disease

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Alpha thalassaemia major

Rationale:
• Alpha-thalassaemia major (deletion of all four α-globin genes) means the fetus cannot make normal HbF or HbA.

• Option E: A short cervix (≤25 mm) detected on ultrasound before 24 weeks is managed with vaginal progesterone in women without a prior preterm birth; cerclage is considered only when there is both a prior spontaneous preterm birth or mid-trimester loss and a short cervix.

question: Heavy but regular period is a likely feature of which of the following condition
model_prompt:
