question: In the following will shift the oxygen dissociation curve to the rignt:
outputs:
Correct option: C. 2,3-DPG

Rationale: A rightward shift of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve means haemoglobin releases oxygen more readily (lower affinity). This occurs when 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) concentration in red cells rises. Alkalosis (↑pH) and presence of foetal haemoglobin both increase haemoglobin’s affinity for O₂, shifting the curve to the left, while cooling/freezing (lower temperature) also shifts it to the left.

question: The following factors inhibit iron absorption:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Antacids

Rationale: Gastric acidity keeps iron in the ferrous (Fe²⁺) form, which is more soluble and more readily absorbed in the duodenum. Antacids raise gastric pH, converting ferrous iron to the less-soluble ferric (Fe³⁺) form and promoting formation of insoluble complexes, thereby reducing iron absorption. 

• Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) increases iron absorption by reducing ferric to ferrous iron and forming soluble complexes.  
• Certain amino acids (e.g., cysteine, histidine) facilitate iron uptake by chelating and keeping it in an absorbable form.  
• Haem iron, found in meat, is inherently better absorbed than non-haem iron. 

Thus, among the given choices, only antacids inhibit iron absorption.

question: Indices required for the calculation of Red Cell Volume (MCV) include:
A: a.	Hb concentration multiplied by haematocrit;
B: b.	Haemoglobin concentration divided by red cell count;
C: c.	Red cell count divided by haematocrit;
D: d.	Haematocrit divided by red cell count
outputs:
Correct option: D. Haematocrit divided by red cell count

Rationale:  
The mean corpuscular (red cell) volume, MCV, expresses the average size of individual erythrocytes. It is calculated from two primary indices: the packed cell volume (haematocrit, Hct) and the red blood cell count (RBC). In conventional units,

MCV (fL) = (Hct [%] × 10) ÷ RBC (×10⁶/μL)

or, in SI units,

MCV (fL) = (Hct [L/L] ÷ RBC [10¹²/L]) × 1000.

Thus the essential components of the calculation are haematocrit divided by red cell count; the other options involve haemoglobin or reversed ratios that do not yield MCV.

question: The Prothrombin Time is a test for the following factors:
outputs:
Correct option(s):  
B. Factor V  
C. Factor VII  

Rationale:  
The Prothrombin Time (PT) evaluates the extrinsic and common pathways of the coagulation cascade. It becomes prolonged when factors in these pathways are deficient, especially:  
• Factor VII (the only clotting factor unique to the extrinsic pathway)  
• Factors V, X, II (prothrombin), and fibrinogen in the common pathway  

Thus PT is a test for Factor V and Factor VII (as well as X, II, and fibrinogen, which were not listed). Tissue factor is the reagent used to initiate the test, not a factor being measured, and Factor VIII belongs to the intrinsic pathway and is assessed with the aPTT, not the PT.

question: The following is a Vitamin K-dependent clotting factors:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Factor VII

Rationale: Vitamin K is required for the γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues in the liver-synthesised clotting factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX and X (as well as the anticoagulant proteins C and S). Among the options listed, only Factor VII is one of these vitamin K-dependent factors. Factors V and XI are not vitamin K-dependent, and Factor III is tissue thromboplastin (not a vitamin K-dependent coagulation factor).

question: Calcium is not required for the activation of the following factor:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Factor XI

Rationale:
Ionized calcium (factor IV) is essential for most vitamin-K-dependent steps in the coagulation cascade (e.g., activation of factors II, VII, IX, and X, and of factor XIII by thrombin).  
The intrinsic-pathway step in which factor XI is converted to factor XIa by factor XIIa (with high-molecular-weight kininogen) is an exception; it proceeds independently of Ca²⁺. Therefore, among the options listed, only the activation of factor XI does not require calcium.

question: Haemoglobin Ms:
B: b.	Are easily reduced by methaemoglobin reductase;
D: d.	Are due to the presence of tyrosine.
outputs:
Correct option: D

Rationale:
Haemoglobin M (Hb M) variants are congenital mutant haemoglobins in which a key histidine residue in the globin chain is replaced by tyrosine. This substitution stabilises the iron in the ferric (Fe³⁺) state, producing met-haemoglobin and cyanosis. Because the ferric iron is firmly held, Hb M is not readily reduced by the normal NADH-dependent methaemoglobin reductase, and the condition does not usually lead to polycythaemia or significant anaemia. Thus, option D is the only correct statement.

question: Folic acid is most useful in the body:
A: a.	Is utilized in its methyl form in the body;
B: b.	Is utilized as Folinic Acid in the body;
C: c.	Is better absorbed as polyglutamate;
D: d.	It Requires an oxidase for conversion to functional state.
outputs:
Correct option: B

Rationale:  
Folic acid (pteroyl-monoglutamic acid) is not itself the metabolically active co-enzyme. Within cells it must first be reduced by the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase to dihydro- and then tetrahydro-folate, and then converted to various one-carbon–substituted derivatives. One of these fully active, naturally occurring co-enzyme forms is 5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate, commonly called folinic acid or “citrovorum factor.” Folinic acid can directly participate in one-carbon transfer reactions without further metabolic activation and is therefore considered the utilizable/functional form of folate in the body.

• Option A is partly true for a single reaction (remethylation of homocysteine) but 5-methyl-THF is only one of several active derivatives, not “the” form in which folate is generally utilized.  
• Option C is incorrect; intestinal absorption occurs primarily after conversion of dietary polyglutamate folates to the monoglutamate form.  
• Option D is incorrect; activation requires a reductase, not an oxidase.

Hence, folic acid is most usefully employed in the body as folinic acid (Option B).

Rationale: By definition, group O red cells do not display either A or B antigens on their surface; therefore they are antigen-negative (option C). Rationale:
The ABO blood-group system is defined by the presence or absence of two carbohydrate antigens on the red-cell surface—A antigen and B antigen—and by the naturally occurring antibodies in the plasma (anti-A and/or anti-B). Individuals with group O possess neither A nor B antigens; “O antigen” does not exist as a distinct antigenic structure. Therefore, “O – Antigen” is not a component of the ABO system, making option B the correct choice.

question: The following does not occur found in the blood group systems:

Therefore, “naturally occurring Anti-D” is the antibody that is not found in normal blood group systems.

Rationale:  
Passive immunoprophylaxis is the prevention of disease by giving pre-formed antibodies; the recipient’s immune system does not have to mount its own response.

• Colostrum-rich breast milk to a newborn (C) – maternal IgA and other antibodies pass to the infant → classic natural passive immunity.  
• Convalescent plasma administration (D) – plasma from recovered patients contains specific antibodies that are transfused to another person → passive immunity.

In contrast:  
• Tetanus toxoid injection (B) and routine vaccinations (E) introduce antigen, stimulating the recipient to make their own antibodies; these are examples of active immunization, not passive.

question: In recombination between two different but closely related viruses, the following may occur:
A: a.	Exchange of fragments of the viral nucleic acid
C: c.	Reassortment of individual segments of viral nucleic acid

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: In recombination between two different but closely related viruses, the following may occur:
###Options:
A.  a.	Exchange of fragments of the viral nucleic acid
B.  b.	Exchange of phenotypic markers
C.  c.	Reassortment of individual segments of viral nucleic acid
D.  d.	Production of interferon
E.  e.	Enhancement of the replication

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option(s): A, B and C

Rationale:
• Recombination involves breakage and re-joining of nucleic-acid strands between two related viruses; thus an exchange of genome fragments is a basic event (A).  
• Because the genotype has been altered, the resulting progeny can display new phenotypic properties (e.g., altered host range, antigenicity, drug sensitivity), so an exchange of phenotypic markers may be seen (B).  
• In viruses with segmented genomes (e.g., influenza, reovirus) coinfection can lead to reassortment—that is, whole genomic segments from the two parent viruses are shuffled into the progeny; this is considered a form of genetic recombination (C).  
• Production of interferon (D) is a host-cell response, not a consequence of viral recombination.  
• Enhancement of replication (E) is seen with phenomena such as complementation or helper viruses, not with recombination per se.

Therefore, A, B and C are correct; D and E are incorrect.

question: The following is/are correct about superficial osteomyelitis;

###Answer:
outputs:

Rationale:  
Superficial (Cierny-Mader type II) osteomyelitis results from contiguous spread of infection from adjacent soft tissue or direct inoculation. Because the infection undermines the entire thickness of the involved cortex, a full-thickness cortical sequestrum is typical. It does not involve a through-and-through (transcortical) segment of bone, nor is it an endosteal (medullary) process.

question: Concerning the diagnosis of septic arthritis;

###Answer:

Rationale:

E. Because only statement D is correct, “All of the above” is wrong.

Therefore, option D is the correct answer.

###Question: In the laboratory diagnosis of anaerobic infections,

###Answer:
outputs:

Rationale:  
• Anaerobes gain much less energy from each molecule of glucose (via fermentation pathways that yield ≈2 ATP) than aerobes that use oxidative phosphorylation (≈38 ATP). The inefficient energy production results in slower multiplication, so statement C is true.  
• Distinguishing pathogenic anaerobes from contaminating members of the normal flora is difficult, not easy (A is false).  
• Because anaerobic susceptibility testing is technically demanding and most strains are predictably susceptible to first-line drugs, routine testing is not performed; it is reserved for severe or refractory cases (B is false).  
• Ordinary transport media such as Stuart’s or Amies’s contain oxygen and do not maintain strict anaerobiosis; special anaerobic transport systems are required (D is false).  
Therefore, option C is the only correct statement.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E. only b is correct

Rationale:
Haemophilus influenzae exists in two biologic forms:

1. Encapsulated (typable) strains – especially type b (Hib).  
   • These are not part of normal nasopharyngeal flora in most people.  
   • Disease usually follows acquisition from an external (exogenous) source, and they give rise to invasive infections such as meningitis, epiglottitis, septicaemia, etc.

2. Non-encapsulated (non-typable) strains – “non-capsulate”.  
   • These commonly colonise the upper respiratory tract as normal flora.  
   • When host defences are impaired they cause infections that arise from this resident flora, i.e., endogenous infections (otitis media, sinusitis, bronchitis, pneumonia).

Hence:
A. Endogenous infections are caused by capsulate strains – incorrect.  
B. Endogenous infections are caused by non-capsulate strains – correct.  
C. Exogenous infections are caused by non-capsulate strains – incorrect.

Therefore only statement b is correct → Option E.

Rationale:  
Right-iliac-fossa (right lower-quadrant) pain classically arises from organs situated in or near that region—e.g., appendix, terminal ileum, caecum, right ureter, right adnexa, or from conditions that can track or radiate to the area (renal colic, tubo-ovarian pathology, Crohn’s disease, gallbladder when an elongated inflamed gallbladder hangs low, etc.).

• Acute pyelonephritis (B) – although primarily causing flank/loin pain, it can radiate toward the right lower quadrant and is considered in the differential.

question: In obstructive jaundice, which of the following statements is correct?
model_prompt:

###Question: In obstructive jaundice, which of the following statements is correct?

B.  Oral cholecystogram is of value
C.  The gallbladder is palpable
D.  There is splenomegaly
E.  Vitamin K absorption is impaired

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: C and E

Rationale  
A. Serum alkaline phosphatase is normal – False. In obstructive (cholestatic) jaundice alkaline phosphatase rises markedly.  
B. Oral cholecystogram is of value – False. It depends on hepatic excretion of contrast into bile; in obstruction the dye does not reach the gall-bladder, so the test is useless.

question: A 47-year man, presents with recent finding of dull grey-brown patches in his mouth and palm of his hands, darkening of previous scars, he gets very dizzy when rising from a seated position. There is history of recent vacation in Nigeria. The most likely diagnosis is:

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 47-year man, presents with recent finding of dull grey-brown patches in his mouth and palm of his hands, darkening of previous scars, he gets very dizzy when rising from a seated position. There is history of recent vacation in Nigeria. The most likely diagnosis is:


###Options:
A.  Addison’s disease
B.  SIADH
C.  Conn’s syndrome
D.  Cushing disease

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Addison’s disease

Rationale:  
• Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease) causes cortisol and aldosterone deficiency. Low cortisol → loss of negative feedback → excess ACTH production; ACTH is synthesized with melanocyte-stimulating hormone, so patients develop diffuse hyperpigmentation, most striking in mucous membranes, palmar creases and old scars (dull grey-brown patches, darkened scars described).  
• Aldosterone deficiency leads to volume depletion and postural (orthostatic) hypotension, hence the dizziness when rising.  
• A recent stay in Nigeria raises the possibility of infections such as tuberculosis or adrenalitis precipitating Addison’s disease.  

Other options do not fit the clinical picture:  
– SIADH causes hyponatraemia without hyperpigmentation or postural hypotension.  
– Conn’s syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) produces hypertension, not hypotension or pigmentation.  
– Cushing disease (excess cortisol) gives centripetal obesity, striae, hypertension; pigmentation is rare and hypotension is not expected.  

Therefore the presentation is most consistent with Addison’s disease.

Therefore, intravenous line sepsis is the complication most often encountered with parenteral feeding.

Rationale:  
The patient’s coarsened facial features, enlargement of jaw, increase in shoe and ring size, deepened voice and excessive sweating are classic manifestations of acromegaly, which results from chronic excess growth hormone (GH). ###Answer:

Rationale  
When large volumes of stored blood are transfused rapidly, several predictable metabolic and haematological problems can appear:

• Hypothermia – blood is stored at 4 °C; rapid infusion lowers the patient’s core temperature.

• Coagulation abnormalities – dilution of platelets and clotting factors, together with hypothermia, produces coagulopathy.  

The acid–base disturbance that usually accompanies massive transfusion is metabolic acidosis (from the acidic preservative solution and the patient’s tissue hypoperfusion), not alkalosis. Hence alkalosis is the exception.

###Question: A 72-year-old man presents with confusion. His care-giver gave history of  lethargic, irritability over the last 2 months. Despite maintaining a good appetite and fluid intake. Blood results are as follows:
 
Sodium 126 mmol/L 
Potassium 4 mmol/L

Urine osmolality 343 mmol/L

• The patient is hyponatraemic (Na⁺ 126 mmol/L) but appears euvolaemic (no mention of oedema, dehydration or orthostatic changes, and he is eating and drinking normally).  
• In SIADH the kidney continues to reabsorb water despite low serum osmolality, so the urine remains inappropriately concentrated. Here the urine osmolality is high (343 mmol/kg), instead of being maximally dilute (<100 mmol/kg) as it should be in true hypovolaemic or primary polydipsic states.

Rationale:
Healing by secondary intention (also called second-intention or secondary union) refers to the repair of large, open, or infected wounds that are not primarily closed. Its defining features include

• Marked inflammation with a greater volume of necrotic debris (B)  
• Profuse formation of granulation tissue that fills the base of the defect (C)  
• Re-epithelialization from the wound edges across the granulation tissue (A)  
• Myofibroblast-mediated wound contraction that reduces the wound size (E)

Crucially, the wound heals “from the bottom up”: granulation tissue forms in the depths first and progressively builds toward the surface, after which epithelium can cover it. Therefore the statement that such wounds “are left to heal from the top to the base” is incorrect and is not a characteristic of secondary intention healing.

question: Which of the following is the fastest promoter of epithelization in wound healing?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following is the fastest promoter of epithelization in wound healing?


###Options:
A.  Leaving the wound open
B.  Tight approximation of wound edges
C.  Occlusive dressings
D.  Steroid application
E.  Iodine application

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Occlusive dressings  

Rationale: Re-epithelialization proceeds most rapidly when migrating keratinocytes can move across a warm, moist surface. Occlusive (or semi-occlusive) dressings seal the wound, prevent desiccation and scab formation, maintain optimal temperature and oxygen tension, and thereby speed keratinocyte migration. Leaving the wound open allows it to dry and form a crust that the epithelium must burrow under, slowing the process. Tight approximation merely reduces gap size but does not influence surface moisture. Topical steroids and iodine are cytotoxic or anti-proliferative and actually delay healing. Hence, occlusive dressings are the fastest promoters of epithelialization.

D.  Lag phase

###Answer:

Correct Option: C. Infection phase

Rationale:
Normal wound healing is classically divided into three (sometimes four) overlapping physiologic phases:

B: it is associated with pseudomembrane formation in infected tissue

###Answer:

Correct options: B, C and D  

Rationale  
A. False – Corynebacterium diphtheriae remains localized to mucosal surfaces; true bacteraemia and septic shock are exceptional.  
B. True – the organism elaborates exotoxin that induces necrosis and a tightly adherent gray-white pseudomembrane on the infected mucosa.  
C. True – tonsillar/pharyngeal (and nasopharyngeal) diphtheria is the form most often complicated by systemic toxin absorption and therefore carries a higher fatality rate than the purely laryngeal (croup) form, whose main danger is mechanical airway obstruction.

E. False – long-term prevention is achieved with the diphtheria toxoid vaccine; equine antitoxin is used for treatment after infection, not for routine prophylactic immunisation.

D.  First week of injury

###Answer:

Correct option: A. First 6 hours of injury

Rationale:
The “golden period” for initial care of an open (contaminated) wound is the first 6 hours after injury. ###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, C, D, and E.

Rationale:
The efficacy of any disinfectant and the level of disinfection achieved depend on several well-recognized variables:

• Time of contact (A): Longer exposure allows the agent to interact more completely with microorganisms.  
• Temperature (C): Higher temperatures generally enhance the chemical reaction rate, increasing disinfectant activity.

• Concentration of disinfectant (E): Up to a point, higher concentrations provide greater antimicrobial activity.

###Question: The following methods ensure sterilization of an object;

B.  2% glutaraldehyde for 12 hours
C.  tyndallization
D.  hydrogen peroxide gas plasma
E.  quartenary ammonium compound

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: B, C and D  

Rationale  
• Pasteurization (A) is a high-level disinfection process; it does not reliably destroy bacterial spores or some viruses, so it is not sterilization.  

• 2 % glutaraldehyde for a prolonged immersion (≈10-12 h) is sporicidal and is accepted as a method of “cold” chemical sterilization (B ✔).  

• Tyndallization (C ✔) involves three successive steam heats at 100 °C on consecutive days; germinated spores are killed during the later cycles, giving true sterilization.  

• Hydrogen-peroxide gas plasma (D ✔) is a low-temperature, vapor-phase process specifically designed for full sterilization of medical devices.  

• Quaternary ammonium compounds (E) are surface disinfectants only; they are not sporicidal and therefore do not achieve sterilization.

question: Major differences between plasmid and transposon;
A: plasmids are extrachromosomal while transposons are chromosomal
B: plasmids are transferable while transposons are not
C: plasmids are circular while transposons are linear
D: plasmids can replicate independently while transposons cannot
E: plasmids cannot jump while transposon can jump
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Major differences between plasmid and transposon;                                                                                                               
###Options:
A.  plasmids are extrachromosomal while transposons are chromosomal
B.  plasmids are transferable while transposons are not
C.  plasmids are circular while transposons are linear
D.  plasmids can replicate independently while transposons cannot
E.  plasmids cannot jump while transposon can jump

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D  

Rationale:  
A plasmid is an autonomous, extrachromosomal replicon – it carries its own origin of replication and therefore can reproduce independently of the bacterial chromosome.  
A transposon, in contrast, is simply a segment of DNA that can “jump” from one replicon to another (chromosome, plasmid, phage DNA, etc.). It has no origin of replication of its own; it is copied only when the DNA molecule into which it has inserted is replicated. Thus the fundamental (and most reliable) distinguishing feature is the ability of the plasmid to replicate independently, whereas a transposon cannot.  

(The other statements are not consistently true: transposons may reside on plasmids as well as chromosomes; some plasmids are non-conjugative; a few plasmids are linear; and certain plasmids can integrate, but they still do not behave like transposons.)

###Answer:

Rationale  
Horizontal (inter-bacterial) transfer of genetic material occurs by three classic mechanisms:

• Transduction – DNA transfer mediated by a bacteriophage.  
• Conjugation – direct cell-to-cell transfer of DNA, usually via a plasmid and a sex pilus.

• Transmutation (option C) and transversion (option E) are terms related to mutation, not to inter-bacterial DNA transfer.

question: Which of the following is NOT True regarding the absorption suture materials?
A: Chromic catgut is degraded within 90days and tensile strength lost within 21days
B: Chromic is absorbed by phagocytosis and enzymatic degradation
D: Polyglyconate is absorbed by enzymatic degradation
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following is NOT True regarding the absorption suture materials?


###Options:
A.  Chromic catgut is degraded within 90days and tensile strength lost within 21days
B.  Chromic is absorbed by phagocytosis and enzymatic degradation
C.  Polyglactin is absorbed by hydrolysis
D.  Polyglyconate is absorbed by enzymatic degradation
E.  Polydiaxanone is absorbed in 108 days

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D  

Rationale  
• Natural absorbable sutures such as plain or chromic catgut are broken down in tissues by inflammatory cells through phagocytosis and proteolytic/enzymatic digestion; they lose most tensile strength in about 2–3 weeks and are completely resorbed by ~90 days – so statements A and B are true.  
• Synthetic absorbable sutures (polyglactin-910/Vicryl, polyglycolic acid/Dexon, poliglecaprone/Monocryl, polyglyconate/Maxon, polydioxanone/PDS, etc.) are degraded almost exclusively by hydrolysis. Hence statement C is true.  
• Polyglyconate is a synthetic copolymer (Maxon) and, like the other synthetic materials, is absorbed by hydrolysis, not by enzymatic degradation. Therefore statement D is NOT true.  
• Polydioxanone (PDS) is a long-acting synthetic absorbable suture; complete absorption takes roughly 6 months (≈180 days). Saying it is absorbed in 108 days is within some reported ranges (90–210 days) and is therefore not unambiguously wrong in the standard texts, whereas the mechanism stated in option D is clearly incorrect.

Hence option D is the single statement that is not true.

C.  Reef knot

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C.  Reef knot

Rationale:  
The square (reef) knot is made by two opposing, mirror-image throws that lie flat and tighten against each other, giving excellent friction and very little tendency to slip. It is therefore regarded as the standard and most secure knot in routine surgical practice.  
• A simple knot is only a single half-hitch and will slip.  
• A surgeon’s knot adds an extra turn in the first throw to prevent loosening under tension, but after subsequent throws it is bulkier and no more secure than a properly laid square knot.  
• A granny knot is two identical throws and is notorious for slipping.

question: Which of the following statements is True about neurogenic shock?
A: It is due to parasympathetic cut off
B: It is due to reduction in blood volume
C: It leads to vasodilatation and decreased vascular tone
D: The patient has cold and moist extremity
model_prompt:

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following statements is True about neurogenic shock?

A.  It is due to parasympathetic cut off
B.  It is due to reduction in blood volume
C.  It leads to vasodilatation and decreased vascular tone
D.  The patient has cold and moist extremity
E.  There is associated tachycardia

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C  

Rationale:  
Neurogenic shock occurs when an injury (most commonly high spinal cord trauma, spinal/epidural anesthesia, or severe head injury) interrupts sympathetic outflow. Loss of sympathetic tone causes widespread vasodilatation, a fall in systemic vascular resistance, and pooling of blood in the peripheral circulation. Because the parasympathetic (vagal) system remains intact, patients typically develop relative bradycardia and warm, dry extremities—features opposite to those seen in hypovolemic shock. It is not produced by loss of parasympathetic activity, is not primarily due to reduced blood volume, does not give cold clammy skin, and does not cause tachycardia. Hence, only statement C is true.

question: A 20-year-old man is brought to the emergency room after rupturing his spleen in a motorcycle accident. His blood pressure on admission is 80/60 mmHg. Rationale:

Shock is characterised by inadequate tissue perfusion leading to cellular hypoxia. Its typical clinical and biochemical manifestations include:

question: In compensated hypovolaemia due to haemorrhage, which of these statements is True?
A: Up to 1000ml of blood may have been lost
B: The vital organs are inadequately perfused
D: There is no significant reduction in systemic blood pressure

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, C and D are true; B and E are false.  

Rationale  
• Compensated (early) haemorrhagic hypovolaemia generally corresponds to an ATLS class I–II blood loss (≤ 15–30 % of circulating volume). In an average 70-kg adult this is up to about 1000 mL, so statement A is true.

• Arterial pressure is maintained (or falls only minimally) through tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction, so there is no significant drop in systemic blood pressure; statement D is true.  

• The cardiovascular response is sympathetic activation, giving tachycardia rather than bradycardia; statement E is false.

question: Concerning fluid and electrolyte balance in a 70 kilogram African man, which of the following statements is True?

C: Fluids containing colloids are used for maintenance

Rationale  
• Insensible water loss (evaporation from skin and respiratory tract) is about 0.5–1 L/day in temperate climates, but in a 70-kg adult living in a hot African environment it is commonly taken as roughly 1.5 L/day.

question: In the treatment of fluid and electrolyte derangement, which of the following statements is NOT True?

question: Which of these statements is Correct regarding healing by secondary intention?

C: There is reduced inflammation and proliferation
D: There is a cosmetically acceptable scar

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B

Rationale:  
In healing by secondary intention the wound edges are not apposed and there is a considerable tissue defect. The repair therefore depends on the formation of abundant granulation tissue to fill the gap, progressive wound contraction mediated by myofibroblasts, and finally epithelialization from the wound margins. In contrast, wounds healing by primary intention have minimal granulation tissue, little contraction and usually form a thin, cosmetically acceptable scar. Skin grafting (option A) is not a defining feature of secondary intention, inflammation is greater rather than reduced (option C), the resultant scar is often wide and cosmetically inferior (option D), and healing is not achieved by contraction and epithelialization alone (option E) because granulation tissue is essential.

Primary osteoarthritis is a degenerative (wear-and-tear) joint disorder. Its characteristic pathologic steps include:

Rationale:
• A hyphaema is blood that has collected in the anterior chamber. The mainstay of treatment is conservative (bed rest, head elevation, eye-shield, topical steroids, cycloplegics, and monitoring of intra-ocular pressure).  
• Microscopic or small hyphaemas are NOT drained surgically; surgery is reserved for selected cases (e.g., total/large hyphaema persisting > 5-7 days, uncontrolled raised IOP, or impending/actual corneal staining).  
• Loss of vision can occur from complications such as re-bleed, secondary glaucoma, optic atrophy, or corneal blood-staining, so it is incorrect to state that it “can never result in loss of vision.”  
• One feared complication is corneal blood-staining when red blood cells and hemoglobin diffuse into corneal stroma, leading to permanent visual impairment if not relieved—hence statement D is true.  
• Conservative (non-surgical) management is indeed part of standard care, making statement E false.

Therefore, statement D is the correct true choice.

question: An 11year old child presented with sudden onset inward deviation of Right Eye, following a febrile illness treated with some injections at a private hospital. He has been complaining of neck pain and staggers when walking. What is the most likely diagnosis?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: An 11year old child presented with sudden onset inward deviation of Right Eye, following a febrile illness treated with some injections at a private hospital. He has been complaining of neck pain and staggers when walking. What is the most likely diagnosis?






###Options:
A.  Childhood Esotropia
B.  3rd Cranial Nerve palsy
C.  Intracranial infection such as Meningitis
D.  Pseudotumor of the orbit
E.  Retinoblastoma

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Intracranial infection such as Meningitis  

Rationale:  
• Sudden inward deviation of one eye in a previously normal child is most commonly caused by an acute unilateral VI-nerve (abducens) palsy, which produces an esotropia because the affected eye cannot abduct.  
• VI-nerve palsy is classically associated with raised intracranial pressure or basal meningitis.  
• The accompanying neck pain and unsteady gait (cerebellar/vestibular involvement) point to an intracranial process rather than an isolated ocular problem.  
• Childhood esotropia (option A) is usually gradual and unaccompanied by systemic or neurologic signs.  
• A III-nerve palsy (option B) would give an outward-deviated eye with ptosis, not an inward deviation.  
• Pseudotumor of the orbit (option D) causes painful proptosis and restriction of multiple extra-ocular movements, not isolated esotropia with neck stiffness.  
• Retinoblastoma (option E) typically presents with leukocoria or strabismus without neck pain or gait disturbance.  

Therefore, the presentation is most consistent with an intracranial infection such as meningitis.

question: Management of sequestration crisis in sickle cell anemia includes the following:
A: Transfusion with 20ml/kg of packed red blood cells
E: Intravenous Normal Saline 30ml/kg over 1 hour to expand intravascular space
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Management of sequestration crisis in sickle cell anemia includes the following:
###Options:
A.  Transfusion with 20ml/kg of packed red blood cells
B.  Intravenous frusemide 2mg/kg
C.  Intramuscular pethidine 1mg/kg 6hrly
D.  Peritoneal dialysis
E.  Intravenous Normal Saline 30ml/kg over 1 hour to expand intravascular space

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A and E  

Rationale:  
In an acute splenic sequestration crisis a large volume of blood suddenly pools in the spleen, producing profound anaemia and hypovolaemic shock. Immediate management therefore has two aims:  
1. Restore circulating volume with an isotonic crystalloid bolus. A rapid infusion of normal saline (about 20–30 mL/kg in the first hour) helps reverse shock and stabilise blood pressure (option E).  
2. Replace the suddenly lost red-cell mass. Once the child is being volume-resuscitated, packed red-cell transfusion (≈15–20 mL/kg PRBC, equivalent to 20 mL/kg whole blood) is given to bring the haemoglobin back toward the patient’s usual baseline (option A).

Loop diuretics (B), intramuscular pethidine for painful vaso-occlusive crises (C), and peritoneal dialysis (D) do not address the pathophysiology of splenic sequestration and are not part of its acute management.

question: Risk factors acute bilirubin encephalopathy include:
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question:  Risk factors acute bilirubin encephalopathy include:
###Options:
A.  Hypoalbuminemia
B.  Elevated free fatty acid
C.  Metabolic alkalosis
D.  Hypothermia
E.  Septicaemia

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, B and E

Rationale  
Acute bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus) develops when the concentration of unbound (free) unconjugated bilirubin in serum rises and/or when the blood-brain barrier becomes more permeable. Situations that either displace bilirubin from albumin or increase BBB permeability therefore increase risk.

A. Hypoalbuminemia – With less albumin available, less bilirubin can be bound; the free fraction rises and more bilirubin can enter the brain.

B. Elevated free fatty acid – Free fatty acids compete with bilirubin for albumin-binding sites and can displace bilirubin, raising the unbound fraction.

E. Septicaemia – Sepsis both increases blood-brain-barrier permeability and can lower albumin affinity, thus facilitating bilirubin entry into the CNS.

C. Metabolic alkalosis – It does not promote bilirubin displacement; acidosis, not alkalosis, is the recognised risk factor.

D. Hypothermia – Temperature extremes are not established precipitants; hyperthermia rather than hypothermia is sometimes cited as a contributing factor.

Hence, A, B and E are the correct choices.

question: Lactation failure may be associated with the following:
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Lactation failure may be associated with the following:
###Options:
A.  Cimetidine therapy
B.  Poor latch-on during feeding
C.  Bottle feeding
D.  Cleft palate
E.  Mastitis in the mother

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: B, C, D and E  

Rationale  
Successful lactation depends on an intact prolactin–oxytocin reflex and regular, effective emptying of the breast. Anything that interferes with suckling or with the mother’s willingness/ability to put the baby to the breast can precipitate “lactation failure”.

B. Poor latch-on during feeding – If the baby is not well attached, milk is not removed effectively, prolactin secretion falls and supply soon diminishes.

C. Bottle feeding – Supplementary bottle feeds reduce the frequency and vigour of suckling; less stimulation of prolactin and oxytocin leads to declining milk production (“nipple/teat confusion”).

D. Cleft palate – An infant with a cleft palate cannot generate adequate negative pressure to suck, so the breast is poorly emptied and milk production falls.

E. Mastitis in the mother – Pain, inflammation and sometimes the advice (wrongly) to stop nursing may cause infrequent or shortened feeds, resulting in inadequate drainage and secondary lactation failure.

A. Cimetidine therapy – Although cimetidine can raise prolactin levels and occasionally cause galactorrhoea, it is not recognised as a cause of suppressed milk production; therefore it is not typically associated with lactation failure.

question: A preterm newborn delivered at 34 weeks plus 4 days is prone to:

• Hypoglycaemia (A): Late-preterm infants have limited glycogen stores and an immature counter-regulatory response, so they frequently develop low blood glucose after birth.

• Hypocalcaemia (E): Diminished maternal calcium transfer in the last trimester, together with immature parathyroid response, predisposes late-preterm babies to early-onset hypocalcaemia.  
• Meconium aspiration syndrome (C) is characteristically seen in term or post-term infants with intra-uterine distress; it is uncommon in preterm neonates.

###Answer:

Rationale  
During an exchange blood transfusion the infant receives large volumes of stored blood that contains citrate and has a high potassium content.

• Hypocalcaemia (Option C) – Citrate in the transfused blood chelates ionised calcium, which can precipitate symptomatic hypocalcaemia unless calcium is supplemented.

A. False – An enlarged spleen grows obliquely downward and medially toward the right iliac fossa, not the left.

A 10-year-old child weighing 75 kg is severely obese, and pediatric obesity is commonly associated with several specific comorbid conditions that clinicians should actively investigate.

###Question: A 6-year old boy presents at the CHER with three days history of fever, passage of dark coloured urine and weakness. B.  Tredenlenburg position
C.  Whole blood transfusion
D.  Intravenous Frusemide 2mg/kg
E.  Digoxin 0.02mg/kg stat

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, C and D  

Rationale  
• The child is in de-compensated heart failure precipitated by severe anaemia (PCV 13 %, tachycardia 156/min, tachypnoea 72/min, tender hepatomegaly). Essential initial measures are those that relieve the cardiac workload and rapidly restore oxygen-carrying capacity.  
• Cardiac (propped-up) position (Option A) lessens venous return and eases work of breathing, therefore is an immediate supportive step.  
• Urgent blood transfusion (Option C) is definitive treatment for anaemic heart failure; in most emergency settings whole blood is given if packed cells are not readily available.  
• Intravenous furosemide 1–2 mg/kg (Option D) is routinely administered just before or at the start of transfusion to prevent circulatory overload in a patient who is already in heart failure.  
• Trendelenburg position (Option B) increases venous return and would aggravate heart failure.  
• Digoxin (Option E) is not an urgent requirement; onset is slow and it is generally deferred until after anaemia is corrected, if still needed.

Hence, the essential management steps are A, C and D.

###Question: A 5 year old girl whose mother is pregnant, was brought in with vomiting and abdominal pain. B.  Gastric lavage is contraindicated
C.  Deferoxamine is indicated
D.  Gastric scarring is a common complication
E.  Blood gas estimation is mandatory

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, C and E  

Rationale  
The presentation strongly suggests accidental iron-tablet poisoning (antenatal supplements).  

A. Plain abdominal X-ray – Iron tablets are radiopaque; an X-ray can confirm ingestion and show how much drug remains in the stomach, guiding further decontamination.  

B. Gastric lavage – Far from being contraindicated, lavage or whole-bowel irrigation may be used early to remove un-dissolved tablets; therefore the statement is incorrect.  

C. Deferoxamine – The specific chelator for iron and indicated in symptomatic patients or when serum iron is markedly raised.  

D. Gastric scarring – Pyloric or antral scarring/obstruction can occur weeks later but is uncommon; it is not considered a “common” complication.  

E. Blood-gas estimation – Severe iron toxicity produces profound metabolic (lactic) acidosis; arterial/venous blood gas measurement is therefore mandatory for assessment and monitoring.

C.  Predominant cause in Nigeria is congenital toxoplasmosis
D.  Cortical atrophy is the basic pathologic manifestation
E.  Mental retardation is a constant feature

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A  

Rationale:  
• In low-resource settings such as most African countries, intrapartum and early-neonatal problems (birth asphyxia, severe neonatal jaundice, sepsis) account for the largest share of cerebral palsy cases; hence perinatal causes outweigh antenatal (prenatal) causes.  
• The spastic forms (especially spastic quadriplegia and diplegia) are the commonest clinical types; choreo-athetoid/dyskinetic CP is much less frequent—so option B is incorrect.  
• Congenital toxoplasmosis is a rare cause of CP in Nigeria; it is not the predominant aetiology (C is wrong).  
• The neuropathology of CP is heterogeneous (periventricular leukomalacia, basal-ganglia necrosis, focal infarcts, etc.); simple “cortical atrophy” is not the uniform or basic lesion (D is wrong).  
• Intellectual disability occurs in roughly half of patients but is far from universal, so mental retardation is not a constant feature (E is wrong).

###Question: The following conditions predispose to foetal macrosomia:

C.  Maternal malnutrition
D.  Beckwith-Wiedermann syndrome
E.  Maternal thyrotoxicosis

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: B and D  

Rationale:  
• Gestational diabetes (B) exposes the fetus to chronic maternal hyperglycaemia; the resulting fetal hyperinsulinaemia is a strong driver of excessive fat and glycogen deposition, producing large-for-gestational-age infants (macrosomia).  

• Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (D) is an overgrowth genetic disorder characterized by somatic gigantism; affected fetuses are typically macrosomic at birth.  

• Maternal anaemia (A) and maternal malnutrition (C) restrict oxygen and nutrient supply, leading to intrauterine growth restriction rather than macrosomia.  

• Maternal thyrotoxicosis (E) is associated with increased maternal metabolism and often results in low-birth-weight or growth-restricted infants, not macrosomic ones.

question: The following bedside urinalysis finding and the disease conditions are well matched:
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: The following bedside urinalysis finding and the disease conditions are well matched: 
###Options:
A.  Ketones - Diabetes mellitus
B.  Nitrites – Cystitis
C.  Urobilinogen – Hepatitis
D.  Blood - Acute glomerulonephritis
E.  Glucose - Renal Tubular Acidosis

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, B, C and D  

Rationale  
A. Ketones – Diabetes mellitus: In uncontrolled diabetes, especially diabetic keto-acidosis, fatty-acid breakdown produces ketone bodies that appear in urine.  
B. Nitrites – Cystitis: Most Gram-negative uropathogens (e.g., E. coli) convert urinary nitrates to nitrites, so a positive nitrite test points to lower urinary-tract infection/cystitis.  
C. Urobilinogen – Hepatitis: Hepatocellular injury impairs clearance of urobilinogen from portal blood, so urinary urobilinogen rises in hepatitis.  
D. Blood – Acute glomerulonephritis: Glomerular inflammation allows red cells to leak into urine, giving a positive “blood” (heme) test.  
E. Glucose – Renal tubular acidosis: Glucosuria is not typical of RTA; it is characteristic of diabetes mellitus or generalized proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome). Hence this pair is not well matched.

question: Causes of loud stridor in childhood include the following:

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Causes of loud stridor in childhood include the following:
###Options:
A.  Acute Laryngotracheobronchitis
B.  Endobronchial tuberculosis
C.  Laryngomalacia
D.  Severe pneumonia
E.  Foreign body in the larynx

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, C, and E.

Rationale  
• Stridor is a harsh, high-pitched sound produced when airflow is obstructed at the laryngeal or tracheal level.  
• Acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup) (Option A) produces edema and inflammation of the subglottic region, classically causing a loud inspiratory stridor.  
• Laryngomalacia (Option C), the commonest congenital cause of stridor, results from collapse of the floppy supraglottic structures during inspiration, leading to persistent inspiratory stridor in infants.  
• A foreign body lodged in the larynx (Option E) produces acute upper-airway obstruction, typically presenting with sudden onset of loud stridor and respiratory distress.  

Why the other options are incorrect  
• Endobronchial tuberculosis (Option B) involves the lower airways (bronchi); it tends to cause wheeze or localized airway obstruction rather than stridor.  
• Severe pneumonia (Option D) impairs the distal air spaces and alveoli, leading to crackles and respiratory distress but not stridor unless accompanied by concurrent upper-airway pathology.

Therefore, the correct choices are A, C, and E.

question: Which of the following are manifestations of sickle cell vaso-occlusion:
model_prompt:

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following are manifestations of sickle cell vaso-occlusion: 
###Options:
A.  Stroke
B.  Priapism
C.  Acute chest syndrome
D.  Hyposthenuria
E.  Papillary necrosis

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, B, C, D and E  (All of the listed manifestations)

Rationale:
Sickle cell vaso-occlusion can obstruct blood flow in virtually any microvascular bed, producing ischemia and infarction in diverse organs.

• Brain → ischemic infarct → Stroke (Option A)  
• Corpora cavernosa of the penis → prolonged painful erection → Priapism (Option B)  
• Pulmonary microvasculature → infarction/inflammation → Acute chest syndrome (Option C)  
• Renal medulla (vasa recta) → impaired concentrating ability → Hyposthenuria/isosthenuria (Option D)  
• Further renal medullary ischemia → sloughing of renal papillae → Papillary necrosis (Option E)

Thus every option listed represents a recognized vaso-occlusive manifestation of sickle cell disease.

question: In hyponatraemia dehydration:
A: Salt is taken in excess of water
B: Mild degree can be treated with dietary modification
C: A common cause of cardiac arrhythmia
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: In hyponatraemia dehydration: 
###Options:
A.  Salt is taken in excess of water
B.  Mild degree can be treated with dietary modification
C.  A common cause of cardiac arrhythmia
D.  Seizures may occur
E.  The skin is typically doughy

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: B and D  

Rationale  
Hyponatraemic (hypotonic) dehydration occurs when sodium loss exceeds water loss (e.g., diarrhoea replaced with plain water).  

A. Salt is taken in excess of water – false; that situation produces hypernatraemia, not hyponatraemia.  

B. Mild degree can be treated with dietary modification – true; in mild cases oral therapy with salt-containing fluids/ORS or extra salt in the diet is sufficient; intravenous hypertonic saline is reserved for severe cases.  

C. A common cause of cardiac arrhythmia – false; significant arrhythmias are far more closely linked to potassium disorders; hyponatraemia mainly causes neurological manifestations.  

D. Seizures may occur – true; low serum sodium produces cerebral oedema and can precipitate irritability, lethargy and convulsions.  

E. The skin is typically doughy – false; a “doughy” or pasty feel of the skin is characteristic of hypernatraemic dehydration, not hyponatraemic dehydration.

question: A 4-day old term neonate delivered at the church presents with poor suck and respiratory difficulty. Examination reveals axillary temperature of 35.1C and hepatosplenomegaly. Which of the following are known risk factors for the likely disease?

B.  Peripartum fever in the mother

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: B and D  

Rationale:  
The neonate’s presentation (poor suck, respiratory distress, hypothermia, hepatosplenomegaly) is most consistent with neonatal sepsis. Established maternal-perinatal risk factors for early/very-early neonatal sepsis include intrapartum maternal fever or chorioamnionitis and prolonged labour or prolonged rupture of membranes, because both situations markedly increase the newborn’s exposure to ascending bacterial pathogens.  
• Vitamin K deficiency (A) predisposes to bleeding, not infection.  
• Antepartum haemorrhage (C) is related to fetal hypoxia and anemia, not directly to neonatal sepsis.  
Therefore, peripartum maternal fever (B) and prolonged labour (D) are the relevant risk factors.

question: A 2-year old presents with occipitofrontal circumference of 55cm, sutural diastasis and prominent scalp veins. The following factors are relevant in the aetiology of the condition:

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: B, C and D  

Rationale:  
The picture described (markedly enlarged head with sutural separation and distended scalp veins) is typical of hydrocephalus. Established aetiological factors for hydrocephalus include:  

• Aqueductal stenosis (C) – the commonest congenital obstructive lesion.  
• Post-haemorrhagic obstruction following intraventricular / subarachnoid haemorrhage (B).  
• Post-infective obstruction after pyogenic (bacterial) meningitis (D).  

Anencephaly (A) is an open neural-tube defect that is incompatible with life and does not produce hydrocephalus, and cerebral malaria (E) raises intracranial pressure but is not a recognized cause of hydrocephalus.

question: A 3-month old child delivered at gestational age of 31 weeks and hospitalized for six weeks presents with recurrent cough of four weeks duration. Examination shows enlarged wrist joints and widely patent anterior fontanelle. The following findings will support the diagnosis:

###Answer:

Correct option: C. Craniotabes

The child’s enlarged wrists and widely open anterior fontanelle are classic early skeletal manifestations of vitamin-D–deficient rickets, which is common in premature infants with prolonged indoor hospitalization and limited sunlight exposure. question: In cerebral malaria:
D: Drug of choice is intravenous artesunate
E: Cortical blindness is a known sequela

B.  Convulsion is a constant feature
C.  Altered sensorium is typical

E.  Cortical blindness is a known sequela

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: C, D, and E

Rationale  
A. Age incidence 6–10 years – Incorrect. In endemic regions cerebral malaria occurs predominantly in younger children, most commonly 2–5 years of age; in non-immune adults it can occur at any age.  
B. Convulsion is a constant feature – Incorrect. Seizures are common, especially in children, but they are not present in every case and therefore are not a “constant” feature.

E. Cortical blindness is a known sequela – Correct. Survivors, particularly children, can develop neurological deficits such as hemiparesis, speech disturbances, epilepsy, and cortical blindness.

question: Duckett Jones minor criteria in acute rheumatic fever include:
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Duckett Jones minor criteria in acute rheumatic fever include: 	
###Options:
A.  Presence of subcutaneous nodules
B.  Elevated Erythrocyte Sedimentation rate
C.  Presence of cardiac murmurs
D.  Arthralgia
E.  Syndeham chorea

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: B and D

Rationale:
The revised Jones (Duckett Jones) criteria classify the manifestations of acute rheumatic fever into major and minor categories.  
• Minor criteria: fever, arthralgia, elevated acute-phase reactants (e.g., ESR or CRP), leukocytosis, and prolonged PR interval on ECG, or a history of previous rheumatic fever.  
• Major criteria: carditis (often manifesting as new cardiac murmurs), polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules.

Therefore:  
B. Elevated ESR – a laboratory marker of the acute-phase response – is a minor criterion.  
D. Arthralgia is also a minor clinical criterion.  

Options A (subcutaneous nodules), C (cardiac murmurs indicating carditis), and E (Sydenham chorea) are major criteria, not minor.

question: A 7-year old girl presents with a 4-week history of painless jaw swelling. The weight-for-height Z-score is -2SD. She has generalized rubbery and discrete lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is correct?
A: Starry –Sky appearance on histology is diagnostic
B: Reed-Steinberg cells on histology is diagnostic
C: Jaw X-Ray shows loss of dental lamina dura
D: Generalized pruritus is a classical finding
E: Acute kidney injury may complicate treatment
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 7-year old girl presents with a 4-week history of painless jaw swelling. The weight-for-height Z-score is -2SD. She has generalized rubbery and discrete lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is correct?
###Options:
A.  Starry –Sky appearance on histology is diagnostic
B.  Reed-Steinberg cells on histology is diagnostic
C.  Jaw X-Ray shows loss of dental lamina dura
D.  Generalized pruritus is a classical finding
E.  Acute kidney injury may complicate treatment

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E.  Acute kidney injury may complicate treatment

Rationale:
The most likely diagnosis in a 7-year-old child with a rapidly enlarging, painless jaw mass and generalized, rubbery lymphadenopathy is endemic (African-type) Burkitt lymphoma. This tumor has an extremely high proliferation rate and a large tumor burden, so chemotherapy commonly precipitates tumor-lysis syndrome. Massive release of uric acid, potassium, and phosphate can lead to acute kidney injury if not anticipated and aggressively prevented/treated with hydration, allopurinol or rasburicase.

• Starry-sky appearance (option A) is characteristic but not specific or diagnostic; other highly proliferative lymphomas can show the same pattern.  
• Reed-Sternberg cells (option B) are diagnostic of Hodgkin lymphoma, not Burkitt lymphoma.  
• Loss of the dental lamina dura on jaw X-ray (option C) is seen in hyperparathyroidism, not in Burkitt lymphoma.  
• Generalized pruritus (option D) is a classical “B-symptom” of Hodgkin lymphoma, not of Burkitt lymphoma.

Hence, option E is the correct statement.

question: Extra-cardiac feature of right ventricular endomyocardial fibrosis include:

Right-ventricular endomyocardial fibrosis behaves as part of a wider fibro-proliferative disorder, so a number of non-cardiac manifestations may accompany the cardiac lesion.

• Gross ascites with little or no pedal oedema (A) – the stiff, fibrotic right ventricle produces severe systemic venous congestion that is expressed mainly as tense ascites, while ankle oedema remains surprisingly slight.

A: History of feed refusal or sore throat is helpful
B: Lesions of papular urticaria on the skin are useful
D: Serum Anti-Streptolysin O titre will be elevated
E: Jaundice will be an unusual finding

###Question: A 3-year old boy presents at the CHER with five-day history of progressive facial and leg swellings. On examination, he has moderate bilateral pitting pedal swelling, tachypnea and blood pressure 120/80mmHg. Urinalysis shows one plus proteinuria. Which of the following statements is valid?

B.  Lesions of papular urticaria on the skin are useful

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E. Jaundice will be an unusual finding.

Rationale:  
The combination of facial / pedal oedema, a (for age) high blood pressure and only mild proteinuria (1+) points to an acute glomerulonephritis rather than a nephrotic syndrome or a hepatic cause of oedema. Because the oedema is renal in origin and the liver is not primarily involved, jaundice is not expected; its presence would suggest an alternative diagnosis (e.g. hepatic disease).  

• A – A preceding sore throat can occur in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, but it is absent in many patients and feed refusal is non-specific, so the statement is not reliably helpful.  
• B – Papular urticaria is unrelated to renal oedema.  
• C – Positive nitrites signify a Gram-negative urinary tract infection, not glomerulonephritis.  
• D – ASO titre may be raised after a throat infection but is frequently normal when the trigger was a skin infection; therefore it is not consistently reliable.  

Hence, the only universally valid statement in this context is that jaundice would be unusual (option E).

B: Stool microscopy will show cysts of Entamoeba histolytica

• Hypertonia, exaggerated reflexes and sustained ankle clonus are classical upper-motor-neuron signs, so in a 9-month-old they point to spastic cerebral palsy (in this case a spastic hemiparesis).

• Pyogenic meningitis, kernicterus, sickle-cell trait or hypertonic dehydration are far less likely to result in an isolated chronic hemiplegic picture; kernicterus in particular produces a dyskinetic (athetoid) rather than spastic pattern.

question: Hyperemesis gravidarum
C: Metabolic alkalosis is a common feature
E: Ondansetron is a useful medication for treatment
model_prompt:

###Question: Hyperemesis gravidarum
###Options:
A.  Hospital admission is mandatory
B.  Associated with electrolyte derangement
C.  Metabolic alkalosis is a common feature
D.  Associated with about 3kg weight loss
E.  Ondansetron is a useful medication for treatment

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: B, C, D and E  

Rationale  

A. Hospital admission is mandatory – FALSE  
Many women can be managed as out-patients or in day-care units; admission is reserved for those who remain dehydrated or ketotic despite ambulatory therapy.  

B. Associated with electrolyte derangement – TRUE  
Persistent vomiting commonly produces hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia and hypochloraemia.  

C. Metabolic alkalosis is a common feature – TRUE  
Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid through repeated vomiting typically results in a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis (although starvation ketosis may give a mild acidosis as well).  

D. Associated with about 3 kg weight loss – TRUE  
Hyperemesis gravidarum is defined as weight loss exceeding 5 % of the prepregnancy weight; for an average woman of ~60 kg this equates to roughly 3 kg.  

E. Ondansetron is a useful medication for treatment – TRUE  
Ondansetron (a 5-HT₃ antagonist) is recommended as an effective second-line/third-line anti-emetic when first-line agents fail, and improves symptoms in many women with hyperemesis gravidarum.

question: In the management of gestational diabetes

###Answer:
outputs:

Rationale  

A. Insulin is not started routinely from the first trimester. It is added only when diet ± exercise fail to keep capillary glucose within target ranges (usually after the mid-pregnancy diagnostic OGTT).

E. TRUE – HbA1c reflects preceding 2–3 months’ glycaemia and is useful for gauging prior control, but because of altered red-cell turnover in pregnancy and the acute onset of gestational diabetes, it is not recommended for diagnosing GDM; a 75 g or 100 g oral glucose tolerance test is required.

Why the other options are incorrect  
A. First-line treatment is medical (propylthiouracil in 1st trimester, carbimazole/methimazole thereafter); thyroidectomy is reserved for drug intolerance or large toxic goitre.  
B. Total T4 rises in pregnancy because of increased TBG; diagnosis relies on free T4 (or total T4 interpreted with a pregnancy-adjusted reference range). Using an unadjusted total T4 is not adequate.

question: You review a thirty-three-year-old woman with a history of congenital heart disease in the antenatal clinic. In making a plan for the management of her pregnancy, which step is least appropriate?
A: Booking a detailed fetal cardiology scan.
B: Avoiding anaemia and prescribing supplementary iron if necessary.
C: Prophylactic antibiotics should operative delivery be required.
D: A birth pool to provide helpful extra analgesia.
E: May benefit from a shortened second stage of labour.
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question:  You review a thirty-three-year-old woman with a history of congenital heart disease in the antenatal clinic. In making a plan for the management of her pregnancy, which step is least appropriate?

###Options:
A.  Booking a detailed fetal cardiology scan.
B.  Avoiding anaemia and prescribing supplementary iron if necessary.
C.  Prophylactic antibiotics should operative delivery be required.
D.  A birth pool to provide helpful extra analgesia.
E.  May benefit from a shortened second stage of labour.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. A birth pool to provide helpful extra analgesia.

Rationale:
• Women with significant congenital heart disease should labour in an environment that allows continuous haemodynamic and fetal monitoring and provides immediate access for assisted delivery, resuscitation or surgical intervention if required.  
• Immersion in a birth pool can produce sudden haemodynamic shifts (increased venous return on entering the water, rapid reduction on leaving it), makes blood-pressure and fetal monitoring difficult and delays emergency evacuation if maternal or fetal compromise occurs. Consequently, most cardiology/obstetric guidelines advise against the use of water immersion or water birth in women with cardiac disease.  

The other steps are appropriate:
A. Detailed fetal cardiac scan (fetal echocardiography) is recommended because of the increased risk of congenital heart disease in the fetus.  
B. Prevention and prompt treatment of anaemia reduces maternal cardiac workload.  
C. When an operative vaginal delivery or caesarean section is required, routine surgical-site antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated (though infective-endocarditis prophylaxis is no longer routinely recommended).  
E. Shortening the second stage (e.g., with forceps or ventouse) limits prolonged Valsalva manoeuvres and reduces cardiovascular stress.

Therefore, using a birth pool is the least appropriate element of the management plan.

question: On routine antenatal blood test, a thirty-year-old woman is found to be Rhesus negative. Which piece of advice regarding the management of her pregnancy is correct?
A: Her fetus will also be Rhesus negative.
B: If there is concern later in pregnancy regarding vaginal bleeding then a Kleihauer test should be performed.
C: She should have a routine dose of anti-D at 23/40.
D: Once she has had two doses of anti-D, further administration will not be required.
E: If this pregnancy is not affected by Rhesus disease, there should be no problem in subsequent pregnancies.

D.  Once she has had two doses of anti-D, further administration will not be required.
E.  If this pregnancy is not affected by Rhesus disease, there should be no problem in subsequent pregnancies.

###Answer:
outputs:

Rationale:  
A Rhesus-negative woman must be protected from sensitisation whenever fetal blood may have entered her circulation. Any episode of vaginal bleeding after 12 weeks’ gestation is treated as a potential sensitising event. Current guidelines recommend that a Kleihauer (fetomaternal-haemorrhage) test is performed to quantify any fetal red cells in the maternal blood and to determine the appropriate dose of anti-D immunoglobulin that should be given.  

• A – The fetus may be Rh-positive if the father is Rh-positive.  
• C – Routine antenatal prophylaxis is given at 28 weeks (± a second dose at 34 weeks), not at 23 weeks.  
• D – Anti-D must be given after every sensitising event and again postpartum if the baby is Rh-positive, regardless of previous doses.  
• E – Sensitisation in this pregnancy can still affect subsequent pregnancies; therefore each pregnancy must be managed individually.

question: A twenty-four-year-old I.V drug user who smokes attends the antenatal clinic. She has continued to use heroin throughout her pregnancy, but has reduced her smoking. Which complication is she most likely to experience?

###Question:  A twenty-four-year-old I.V drug user who smokes attends the antenatal clinic. She has continued to use heroin throughout her pregnancy, but has reduced her smoking. Which complication is she most likely to experience? 


###Options:
A.  Placental abruption.
B.  Cervical incompetence.
C.  Neonatal withdrawal syndrome.
D.  Antepartum haemorrhage.
E.  Severe intrauterine growth restriction.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C.  Neonatal withdrawal syndrome.

Rationale:
Heroin (an opioid) readily crosses the placenta and the fetus becomes physiologically dependent on the drug. After birth, when the placental drug supply ceases, 50–90 % of exposed babies develop neonatal abstinence/withdrawal syndrome, typically within the first 24–72 hours. Although smoking and opioid use also increase the risks of placental abruption, ante-partum haemorrhage and intrauterine growth restriction, these complications occur far less consistently than neonatal withdrawal. Cervical incompetence has no established link with heroin or tobacco use. Therefore the most likely complication in this scenario is neonatal withdrawal syndrome.

A: If no genetic basis is known for a condition, there is little use in genetic counselling for the parents.
B: Less anxiety is caused by performing a test as soon as possible and discussing the condition suspected with results available.
C: A discussion regarding termination should not be raised with the parents unless a test result has shown a serious condition.
D: A 1 per cent risk of miscarriage from an invasive test will be considered acceptable to all parents.
E: A consent form should be signed prior to genetic tests being carried out.

###Question: Choose the best statement in regard to genetic counselling:

B.  Less anxiety is caused by performing a test as soon as possible and discussing the condition suspected with results available.
C.  A discussion regarding termination should not be raised with the parents unless a test result has shown a serious condition.
D.  A 1 per cent risk of miscarriage from an invasive test will be considered acceptable to all parents.
E.  A consent form should be signed prior to genetic tests being carried out.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E

Rationale:
Good genetic counselling must include fully informed, written consent before any genetic (particularly prenatal) test is undertaken. Parents need to understand the purpose, limitations, risks (e.g., miscarriage risk with invasive sampling), and possible outcomes—including options such as continuing or terminating the pregnancy—before agreeing to the investigation.

• Option A is wrong: even when the molecular basis of a condition is unknown, counselling can still address recurrence risks, surveillance, reproductive options, and psychosocial issues.  
• Option B is wrong: counselling and consent should precede testing; simply doing the test first and discussing results later can increase, not decrease, anxiety and is unethical.  
• Option C is wrong: potential outcomes, including the possibility of termination, should be discussed beforehand so parents can make informed choices.  
• Option D is wrong: a 1 % procedure-related miscarriage risk is not acceptable to all parents; acceptability varies greatly and must be individually discussed.  
• Option E is correct: obtaining signed, informed consent prior to testing is a fundamental requirement of good genetic counselling practice.

question: The obstetric doctor on call is asked to review a cardiotocograph performed prior to induction of labour in a 39/40 multigravida. Which of the following features should help to reassure the doctor that this is a normal trace?
A: The baseline heart rate is 100 beats per minute.
B: The baseline variability is <5 beats per minute.
C: An acceleration of 15 beats per minute for 15 seconds is present on the trace.
D: There are no significant accelerations of the fetal heart on the 30-minute recording.
E: The tocograph is picking up regular contractions.
model_prompt:

###Question: The obstetric doctor on call is asked to review a cardiotocograph performed prior to induction of labour in a 39/40 multigravida. Which of the following features should help to reassure the doctor that this is a normal trace? 


###Options:
A.  The baseline heart rate is 100 beats per minute.
B.  The baseline variability is <5 beats per minute.
C.  An acceleration of 15 beats per minute for 15 seconds is present on the trace.
D.  There are no significant accelerations of the fetal heart on the 30-minute recording.
E.  The tocograph is picking up regular contractions.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C

Rationale:  
A normal (reassuring) cardiotocograph (CTG) should have:  
• Baseline fetal heart rate between 110-160 bpm. (Option A shows bradycardia at 100 bpm – non-reassuring.)  
• Baseline variability of 5-25 bpm. (Option B shows reduced variability <5 bpm – suspicious/abnormal.)  
• The presence of accelerations of ≥15 bpm lasting ≥15 s is a reassuring sign of adequate fetal oxygenation and autonomic reactivity. (Option C fulfils this criterion.)  
• Absence of accelerations (Option D) is not abnormal in itself but is not specifically reassuring.  
• Uterine contractions detected on the tocograph (Option E) give no information about fetal well-being.

Therefore, the feature that positively reassures the doctor that the trace is normal is the presence of an acceleration of 15 bpm for at least 15 seconds (Option C).

B: Between 12 and 20 weeks, the crown rump length and the femur length are the most reproducible assessment of gestational age.

D: An increase in nuchal translucency is associated with cardiac defects.

B.  The detection of placenta praevia.
C.  The early detection of twin pregnancies.
D.  The detection of a failed pregnancy.
E.  The detection of uterine abnormalities.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. The detection of placenta praevia.

Rationale:
• The 11-14-week “dating” scan can:
  – Measure crown–rump length to date the pregnancy accurately (A).  
  – Demonstrate embryonic cardiac activity or absence of it, identifying a failed pregnancy (D).  
  – Show the number of embryos and chorionicity, so twin (or higher-order) pregnancies are detected early (C).  
  – Visualise the uterus, allowing recognition of fibroids or congenital uterine anomalies (E).

• Placental localisation this early is unreliable because a low-lying placenta seen in the first trimester often “migrates” upward as the uterus enlarges. A definitive diagnosis of placenta praevia is therefore deferred until the third-trimester scan (around 32 weeks). Hence, detection of placenta praevia is not possible at a routine dating scan.

question: Twin pregnancy
A: Monozygotic twinning occurs at the rate of 4 per 1000 births
B: Incidence is higher with pregnancies induced with clomiphene citrate than in spontaneous conception
C: Zygocity can be determined by ultrasound
D: Perinatal mortality is 6 times higher compared with singleton pregnancies
E: Dichorionic twins are associated with more complications compared to the monochorionic twins

###Question: Twin pregnancy

B.  Incidence is higher with pregnancies induced with clomiphene citrate than in spontaneous conception
C.  Zygocity can be determined by ultrasound
D.  Perinatal mortality is 6 times higher compared with singleton pregnancies
E.  Dichorionic twins are associated with more complications compared to the monochorionic twins

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, B and D  

Rationale  
A. True – The incidence of monozygotic (identical) twinning is remarkably constant worldwide at about 3–4 per 1 000 births (≈0.4 %).  
B. True – Ovulation-induction agents such as clomiphene citrate markedly increase the chance of multiple ovulation and therefore twin (usually dizygotic) pregnancies, so the incidence is higher than in spontaneous conceptions.  
C. False – Ultrasound can reliably establish chorionicity (dichorionic vs monochorionic) and amnionicity, but it cannot determine zygosity with certainty because monozygotic twins may also be dichorionic.  
D. True – Twins carry a substantially higher perinatal mortality; most obstetric texts quote a 4–6-fold increase compared with singletons, so “6 times higher” is within this accepted range.  
E. False – Monochorionic twins have more complications (e.g., twin-twin transfusion syndrome, unequal placental sharing, higher congenital anomaly rate) than dichorionic twins.

B: Arises from hypovolaemic shock following childbirth
C: Gives a funnel shaped appearance on hysterosalpingography
D: Is a cause of secondary amenorrhoea

###Answer:

• Asherman’s syndrome consists of intra-uterine adhesions produced by trauma to the basal endometrium (usually after curettage). It was originally described as “amenorrhoea traumatica”, so option A is true.

question: Tranexenamic acid
B: Better at reducing blood loss than mefenamic acid
C: Effective in reducing Postpartum haemorrhage within 2hours of onset of bleeding
E: Is associated with an increased risk of deep vein thrombosis

###Question: Tranexenamic acid 
###Options:
A.  Works by inhibiting fibrinolysis
B.  Better at reducing blood loss than mefenamic acid
C.  Effective in reducing Postpartum haemorrhage within 2hours of onset of bleeding
D.  Has a role in myomectomy?

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, B, C and D  

Rationale  
A. Tranexamic acid is a synthetic lysine analogue that blocks the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, preventing its conversion to plasmin and thereby inhibiting fibrinolysis.  

B. In heavy menstrual bleeding, tranexamic acid reduces menstrual blood loss by ~40–60 %, whereas NSAIDs such as mefenamic acid produce only a 20–25 % reduction; hence it is clearly more effective.  

C. The WOMAN trial showed that intravenous tranexamic acid given within 3 hours of childbirth significantly lowers death from postpartum haemorrhage, with maximal benefit the earlier it is administered. Giving it within 2 hours lies well inside that effective window.  

D. Multiple clinical studies (both open and randomised) have demonstrated that intravenous tranexamic acid administered before incision during abdominal or laparoscopic myomectomy decreases intra-operative blood loss and transfusion requirements, so it does have a role in myomectomy.  

E. Large randomised trials in trauma (CRASH-2), obstetrics (WOMAN) and various surgical fields have not shown an increased incidence of deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism with short-term use; therefore routine short-term peri-operative/obstetric use is not associated with a raised DVT risk.

###Question: In relation to ovulation: 

###Options:
A.  LH stimulates the thecal cells of the ovary to produce oestrogen.
B.  FSH induces a rise in LH receptors.
C.  Ovulation occurs 4 days after the LH surge.
D.  The release of an oocyte from the follicle requires a sperm to lyse the follicle membrane, and results in ovulation.
E.  Ovulation can be confirmed by measurement of LH on day 14.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B

Rationale  
• LH does not make theca cells secrete oestrogen; it makes them produce androgens that granulosa cells convert to oestrogen (so A is false).  
• Under FSH stimulation, granulosa cells up-regulate LH receptors; this prepares the dominant follicle to respond to the mid-cycle LH surge (B is true).  
• Ovulation follows the LH surge by about 36 h (≈ 1½ days), not 4 days (C is false).  
• Ovulation is the follicle’s own enzymatic rupture and does not require sperm (D is false).  
• A single LH measurement on calendar day 14 cannot “confirm” ovulation because the surge is brief and cycle length varies (E is false).

question: The normal menstrual cycle: Within the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle:
A: The follicular phase is always 14 days long to allow development of the follicle.
B: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) stimulates the granulosa cells to produce oestrogen.
C: Each cycle usually involves the development, growth and ovulation of a single follicle.
D: Follicles over 20 mm need to be drained with ultrasound guidance.
E: Oestrogen and inhibin have a positive feedback on the pituitary to release FSH and luteinizing hormone (LH)
