You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: The normal menstrual cycle: Within the follicular phase of the menstrual cycle:


###Options:
A.  The follicular phase is always 14 days long to allow development of the follicle.
B.  Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) stimulates the granulosa cells to produce oestrogen.
C.  Each cycle usually involves the development, growth and ovulation of a single follicle.
D.  Follicles over 20 mm need to be drained with ultrasound guidance.
E.  Oestrogen and inhibin have a positive feedback on the pituitary to release FSH and luteinizing hormone (LH)

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B

Rationale  
A  – Incorrect.  The luteal phase is fairly fixed at about 14 days; the length of the follicular phase is the variable part of the cycle.  
B  – Correct.  FSH acts on the granulosa cells, inducing aromatase activity that converts theca-derived androgens to oestradiol; rising oestradiol is the hallmark of the follicular phase.  
C  – Not the best answer.  Several follicles start to grow each cycle; only one usually becomes dominant and ovulates, so “development, growth and ovulation of a single follicle” is an oversimplification of what happens within the whole follicular phase.  
D  – Incorrect.  A 20- to 24-mm follicle is the normal pre-ovulatory size and does not require aspiration.  
E  – Incorrect.  Rising oestradiol eventually gives positive feedback on LH (causing the LH surge), but inhibin provides negative feedback on FSH; they do not both exert positive feedback on the pituitary simultaneously.

question: The following are contraindications to external cephalic version:
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: The following are contraindications to external cephalic version: 

###Options:
A.  Polyhydramnios.
B.  Complete breech position.
C.  Pre-eclampsia.
D.  Symphysis pubis dysfunction.
E.  Twin pregnancy.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E. Twin pregnancy.

Rationale  
External cephalic version (ECV) is avoided whenever any condition exists in which a vaginal birth is inadvisable or the manoeuvre is likely to endanger mother or fetus. Absolute (or near-absolute) contraindications include placenta praevia, ante-partum haemorrhage within the preceding week, abnormal fetal monitoring, ruptured membranes with marked oligohydramnios, major uterine anomaly and multiple pregnancy (except when attempting to turn the second twin).

• Polyhydramnios (A) is not a contraindication; the excess liquor may actually make turning easier, although the success rate can still be variable.  
• A complete (frank) breech (B) is the commonest presentation for which ECV is offered; it is certainly not a contraindication.  
• Mild–moderate pre-eclampsia (C) is not listed as a contraindication in major guidelines; only severe maternal compromise needing urgent delivery would preclude ECV, so pre-eclampsia per se is not a routine bar.  
• Symphysis-pubis dysfunction (D) is a musculoskeletal problem and does not preclude the procedure.  
• Twin pregnancy (E) is an absolute contraindication for ECV (except for the second twin after the first has delivered), because manipulation of one fetus may jeopardise the other and the shared uterine space limits room for rotation.

Hence, only option E is correct.

question: During an assisted breech delivery:

B: Pinard’s manoeuvre can be used to deliver the legs in an extended position.
C: Mauriceau–Smellie–Veit is used to deliver extended arms.
D: Forceps should not be applied to the fetal head.

###Question: During an assisted breech delivery:

###Answer:

Correct options: A and B  

Rationale  
A. TRUE – In an assisted breech delivery an episiotomy is usually performed when the fetal anus appears at the fourchette, as this is the point at which the perineum is maximally stretched and the cut will facilitate subsequent delivery of the body, arms and head.

B. TRUE – Pinard’s manoeuvre is specifically designed to flex and abduct a leg that is extended alongside the fetal trunk (frank breech) so that it can be brought down and delivered.

C. FALSE – Extended (nuchal) arms are freed with Lovset’s manoeuvre. The Mauriceau–Smellie–Veit technique is used for delivering the after-coming head.

D. FALSE – Piper (or standard) forceps can be applied to the after-coming head if needed; they are not contraindicated.

E. FALSE – Good analgesia is advisable, but an epidural is not mandatory; delivery can be successfully accomplished with other forms of analgesia or anaesthesia if epidural is not in place.

question: Polyhydramnios is associated with the following:
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Polyhydramnios is associated with the following:


###Options:
A.  Maternal diabetes.
B.  Neuromuscular fetal conditions.
C.  Maternal non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
D.  Post-maturity.
E.  Chorioangioma of the placenta.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, B and E.

Rationale:
• Maternal diabetes (A) → fetal hyperglycaemia → osmotic diuresis → ↑ fetal urine output → polyhydramnios.  
• Neuromuscular fetal conditions (B) such as anencephaly or myotonic dystrophy impair fetal swallowing, so amniotic fluid accumulates.  
• Chorioangioma of the placenta (E) can cause fetal anaemia / high-output cardiac failure and increased transudation, producing polyhydramnios.  

In contrast, maternal NSAID use (C) and post-maturity (D) are classically linked to oligohydramnios because NSAIDs reduce fetal urine production and post-term placental insufficiency lowers fluid volume.

question: Oligohydramnios is associated with the following:

question: The aims of the 18–22 weeks scan include:
B: To determine the chorionicity of a twin pregnancy.
D: Promoting parental bonding with the fetus.

###Question: The aims of the 18–22 weeks scan include: 

###Options:
A.  To locate the placenta.
B.  To determine the chorionicity of a twin pregnancy.
C.  Assessment of amniotic fluid volume.
D.  Promoting parental bonding with the fetus.
E.  To identify fetal structural defects.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, C and E  

Rationale  
The 18- to 22-week (mid-trimester or “anomaly”) scan is performed primarily to evaluate fetal anatomy and pregnancy well-being. Its established objectives are:  
• Localise the placenta (option A).  
• Survey fetal structural anatomy to detect major congenital malformations (option E).  
• Assess liquor volume, as part of the overall biophysical assessment (option C).  

Determination of chorionicity in a multiple pregnancy (option B) is ideally carried out at the first-trimester dating scan (11–14 weeks) when the signs are most reliable; by 18-22 weeks it is less accurate and is therefore not a primary aim of this scan.  

Although parents may enjoy seeing the fetus, using the examination chiefly to promote bonding (option D) is not a clinical purpose and is not listed among the aims of the mid-trimester anomaly scan.

question: Metabolism in pregnancy:
A: Relative insulin resistance is normal in late gestation.
B: High-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol is elevated in pregnancy.
C: Average gestational weight gain is 12.5 kg.
D: Calcium is less readily absorbed from the gut in pregnancy.
E: Total body water increases by about 3 L.

###Question: Metabolism in pregnancy:

B.  High-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol is elevated in pregnancy.
C.  Average gestational weight gain is 12.5 kg.
D.  Calcium is less readily absorbed from the gut in pregnancy.
E.  Total body water increases by about 3 L.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, B and C  

Rationale  
A. True – Placental hormones such as human placental lactogen, cortisol and progesterone produce a state of relative insulin resistance in the second half of pregnancy, ensuring a steady glucose supply to the fetus.  

B. True – All lipid fractions rise in pregnancy; HDL cholesterol rises in early–mid gestation and, although it may fall slightly near term, it remains higher than the non-pregnant level overall.  

C. True – In a woman who starts pregnancy with a normal BMI, the mean gestational weight gain is about 12–13 kg.  

D. False – Intestinal calcium absorption actually increases (almost doubles) in pregnancy to meet the demands of fetal skeletal mineralisation.  

E. False – Total body water expands by roughly 6–8 L (plasma, interstitial and intracellular compartments), considerably more than 3 L.

question: In normal pregnancy:
A: Blood pressure falls in the second trimester.
C: There is a 50 per cent reduction in erythrocyte production.
D: 80 per cent of women have a transient diastolic murmur.
E: There is an increase in polymorphonuclear leukocytes.

###Question: In normal pregnancy:

A.  Blood pressure falls in the second trimester.
B.  Plasma volume decreases throughout gestation.
C.  There is a 50 per cent reduction in erythrocyte production.
D.  80 per cent of women have a transient diastolic murmur.
E.  There is an increase in polymorphonuclear leukocytes.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A and E  

Rationale:  
• A. Blood pressure falls in the second trimester – Systemic vascular resistance drops early in pregnancy, reaching its lowest point in mid-pregnancy; as a result systolic and especially diastolic blood pressures fall during the second trimester.  
• B. Plasma volume decreases throughout gestation – Incorrect; plasma volume expands by about 40–50 % and peaks around 32 weeks.  
• C. There is a 50 % reduction in erythrocyte production – Incorrect; red-cell mass actually rises (≈ 25–30 %).  
• D. 80 % of women have a transient diastolic murmur – Incorrect; a soft systolic ejection murmur is common, but true diastolic murmurs are unusual and warrant evaluation.  
• E. There is an increase in polymorphonuclear leukocytes – Correct; pregnancy is associated with a physiological neutrophilia, especially in the third trimester and labour.

question: A 10-month old infant presents with lack of tooth eruption. Which of the following conditions should be considered as the likely cause?

###Question: A 10-month old infant presents with lack of tooth eruption. Which of the following conditions should be considered as the likely cause?





###Options:
A.  Preterm birth
B.  Hypothyroidism
C.  Hypophosphatasia
D.  Scurvy

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Hypothyroidism

Rationale:
Delayed eruption of primary teeth is most commonly associated with systemic conditions that slow overall growth and skeletal maturation. Congenital or juvenile hypothyroidism (“cretinism”) produces generalized metabolic slowing and delayed ossification, resulting in late eruption of both primary and permanent teeth. 

• Preterm birth can delay tooth eruption slightly (by a few months), but complete absence of eruption at 10 months is more suggestive of an endocrine/metabolic disorder.  
• Hypophosphatasia characteristically causes premature exfoliation of primary teeth rather than failure of eruption.  
• Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) affects periodontal tissues and dentin formation but does not typically delay tooth eruption.

Therefore, hypothyroidism is the most likely cause.

question: Concerning fluids and electrolytes in children
A: 15kg child will require 1500ml of fluid as maintenance in 24 hours
B: Appropriate fluid in vomiting and stooling is Half-Strength Darrows solution
C: .45% Sodium Chloride is the fluid of choice for rapid intravascular space expansion
D: In hypernatremic dehydration, intracranial hemorrhage occurs due to osmolality shift
E: Newborn requires 10% Dextrose/Saline in first 48 hours of life
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Concerning fluids and electrolytes in children 
###Options:
A.  15kg child will require 1500ml of fluid as maintenance in 24 hours
B.  Appropriate fluid in vomiting and stooling is Half-Strength Darrows solution
C.  .45% Sodium Chloride is the fluid of choice for rapid intravascular space expansion
D.  In hypernatremic dehydration, intracranial hemorrhage occurs due to osmolality shift
E.  Newborn requires 10% Dextrose/Saline in first 48 hours of life

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D

Rationale  
A. Maintenance fluid requirements are calculated by the Holliday–Segar method: 100 mL/kg for the first 10 kg (1000 mL) + 50 mL/kg for the next 5 kg (250 mL) = 1250 mL/24 h, not 1500 mL.  
B. For losses due to vomiting and diarrhoea the preferred replacement fluid is an isotonic solution such as Ringer’s lactate or 0.9 % NaCl; half-strength Darrow’s is hypotonic and inappropriate.  
C. Rapid intravascular volume expansion (fluid bolus) requires an isotonic fluid (0.9 % NaCl or Ringer’s lactate). 0.45 % NaCl is hypotonic and should not be used for resuscitation.  
D. In hypernatraemic dehydration plasma osmolality is high; water shifts out of brain cells, causing them to shrink. This stretch on cerebral vessels predisposes to intracranial haemorrhage, especially if serum sodium changes rapidly.  
E. During the first 48 h of life a neonate is usually given 10 % dextrose in water; saline is introduced only after 48 h when renal sodium handling matures.

Therefore statement D is the only true statement.

question: In a 3-year old child with serum potassium level of 2.7mmol/l:

###Answer:

Rationale:
• A – Carpopedal spasm is a manifestation of hypocalcaemia, not hypokalaemia; it is therefore uncommon at a K⁺ of 2.7 mmol/L.

question: A 9-day old infant presents with fever, seizures, setting-sun eye appearance and bulging and tense anterior fontanelle. Which of the following cerebrospinal fluid parameters does not agree with the clinical diagnosis?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 9-day old infant presents with fever, seizures, setting-sun eye appearance and bulging and tense anterior fontanelle. Which of the following cerebrospinal fluid parameters does not agree with the clinical diagnosis?





###Options:
A.  Protein 55mg/dl
B.  Cell count 45/mm3
C.  Glucose 40% of Random Blood Glucose
D.  Lactate 29iu/L

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Protein 55 mg/dl  

Rationale:  
A 9-day-old infant with fever, seizures, a bulging fontanelle and “setting-sun” eyes is most consistent with acute bacterial meningitis with raised intracranial pressure. Typical CSF findings in neonatal/infant bacterial meningitis are:  
• Cell count: markedly elevated, usually >100 cells/mm³ (predominantly neutrophils).  
• Protein: markedly elevated, commonly >100 mg/dl.  
• Glucose: low, generally <40 mg/dl or <40 % of simultaneous blood glucose.  
• Lactate: elevated (>25 IU/L or >3.5 mmol/L).  

Among the given options:  
• Protein 55 mg/dl is only mildly raised and can still be within the upper limit of normal for a neonate; it is not typical of bacterial meningitis.  
• Cell count 45/mm³, Glucose 40 % of blood glucose, and Lactate 29 IU/L all support a bacterial meningitis picture (pleocytosis, low glucose, high lactate).  

Therefore, the parameter that does NOT agree with the clinical diagnosis is Protein 55 mg/dl (Option A).

question: A 12-year old girl whose mother makes soap, gulped some quantity of caustic acid following a disagreement with her parents. Which of the following presentations are expected?

###Question: A 12-year old girl whose mother makes soap, gulped some quantity of caustic acid following a disagreement with her parents. Which of the following presentations are expected? 
###Options:
A.  Sialorrhoea
B.  Difficulty with breathing
C.  Haemoptysis
D.  Haematemesis

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, B, and D  

Rationale:  
Caustic acid ingestion produces immediate chemical burns to the lips, oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus and stomach.  
• Pain and mucosal irritation stimulate profuse salivation → sialorrhoea (A).  
• Oropharyngeal and laryngeal oedema can obstruct the airway, causing stridor and respiratory difficulty → difficulty with breathing (B).

question: Which of the following statements is valid about the characteristics of physical growth?
A: Growth is most rapid in the first four months then declines gradually

question: A 2-year old child presents in CHER with severe pallor (PCV 5%), respiratory distress and tender hepatomegaly. Which of the following management steps is not essential?
E: Administration of digoxin to treat the heart failure.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E. Administration of digoxin to treat the heart failure.

Rationale:
The child has acute, high-output cardiac failure precipitated by profound anaemia (PCV 5 %). Immediate management focuses on:
• correcting the anaemia with a cautious transfusion of packed red cells (10 mL/kg)  
• preventing volume overload while transfusing (IV frusemide 1–2 mg/kg)  
• improving oxygenation (supplemental oxygen)  
• reducing venous return and work of breathing (Fowler’s/upright position)  

Digitalis (digoxin) is useful in low-output failure due to primary myocardial dysfunction, not in the high-output failure of pure anaemia; it begins to act slowly and carries a risk of toxicity. Therefore its administration is not an essential step in this scenario.

###Answer:

Rationale:  
β-thalassemia major (Cooley’s anaemia) is characterised by profound microcytic hypochromic anaemia from early infancy, marked extramedullary haemopoiesis producing massive splenomegaly and hepatomegaly, and a chronically elevated cardiac output that may lead to high-output heart failure. Although mild icterus can be present because of ongoing haemolysis, pronounced or “deep” jaundice is not a typical feature; it is far more characteristic of disorders with predominant intravascular haemolysis such as hereditary spherocytosis or sickle-cell crises. Rationale: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell (bone-marrow) transplantation can replace the patient’s sickle-producing erythroid lineage with donor stem cells that synthesize normal adult hemoglobin, thereby eliminating the underlying genetic defect and curing sickle cell disease.  

• Hydroxyurea (A) raises HbF and decreases vaso-occlusive crises, but it does not eradicate the disease.  
• Exchange transfusion (B) temporarily lowers the proportion of sickled cells; it is a supportive, not curative, measure.  
• Plasmapheresis (C) has no role in correcting the intrinsic RBC defect in sickle cell disease.  
• Hyperbaric oxygen (D) may improve tissue oxygenation transiently but offers no lasting benefit and certainly no cure.

question: In congenital hypothyroidism:

###Answer:

• A – False. Most infants with congenital hypothyroidism are born at term with a normal birth weight and length; they are not characteristically large for gestational age.

• D – True. If diagnosis or treatment is delayed, thyroid-hormone deficiency leads to irreversible intellectual disability (mental retardation) and growth failure.  

• E – True. Transplacental passage of maternal anti-thyroid drugs (e.g., carbimazole, PTU) or maternal TSH-receptor–blocking antibodies can cause transient congenital hypothyroidism in the neonate.

question: Which of the following is not required in the management of severe vaso-occlusive crisis in sickle cell disease?

C.  Hospitalisation
D.  Oxygen therapy
E.  Blood film microscopy.

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E. Blood film microscopy

Rationale:  
Management of a severe vaso-occlusive (pain) crisis in sickle cell disease is primarily supportive and aims to reverse or limit the pathophysiological triggers of sickling and relieve symptoms. Key measures include:

• Adequate analgesia (often opioid-based) to control severe pain.  
• Liberal intravenous and/or oral fluids to treat dehydration and reduce blood viscosity.  
• Hospitalisation to monitor clinical status, provide parenteral medications, and manage complications.  
• Oxygen therapy when hypoxaemia is present to prevent further de-oxygenation and sickling of red cells.

Peripheral blood film microscopy, while useful for diagnosis and routine follow-up of sickle cell disease, does not directly contribute to the acute therapeutic management of a vaso-occlusive crisis. Therefore, it is not required as part of the immediate management plan.

question: Concerning childhood seizures
A: Febrile seizure tends to occurs between 1 year and 6 years
B: Status epilepticus is diagnosed when an episode of seizure lasts more than 30 minutes
C: Status epilepticus is diagnosed when more than two seizures occur within one hour
D: Petit mal seizure is characterized by sudden flexion movement of the trunk
E: Rolandic seizure is a type of complex partial seizure

###Question: Concerning childhood seizures
###Options:

C.  Status epilepticus is diagnosed when more than two seizures occur within one hour
D.  Petit mal seizure is characterized by sudden flexion movement of the trunk
E.  Rolandic seizure is a type of complex partial seizure

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A and B  

Rationale  
A. Febrile seizures occur almost exclusively in young children, most commonly between 6 months and 5–6 years of age; therefore the range “1 year to 6 years” is acceptable → True.  

B. (Traditional definition) Status epilepticus is continuous seizure activity, or a series of seizures without regaining consciousness, lasting ≥30 minutes. Although the modern operational cutoff is ≥5 minutes, most examination sources still cite 30 minutes → True.  

C. “More than two seizures within one hour” is not a diagnostic criterion for status epilepticus → False.  

D. Petit-mal (absence) seizures manifest as abrupt lapses in awareness with staring, not sudden flexion of the trunk (which characterizes infantile spasms) → False.  

E. Rolandic epilepsy produces brief simple partial (focal motor) seizures involving the face; consciousness is usually preserved, so it is not classified as a complex partial seizure → False.

question: Which of the following is not a preventive measure in genetically inherited disorders?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following is not a preventive measure in genetically inherited disorders? 





###Options:
A.  Genetic counselling
B.  Routine neonatal screening
C.  Gene therapy
D.  Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis
E.  Plasmapheresis

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E. Plasmapheresis  

Rationale:  
Preventive strategies for inherited genetic disorders are aimed at avoiding the birth of an affected child or at detecting / correcting the molecular defect as early as possible.  
• Genetic counselling guides prospective parents about their individual risks and reproductive options (primary prevention).  
• Routine neonatal screening identifies treatable genetic diseases in the newborn before symptoms appear (secondary prevention).  
• Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) screens embryos created by IVF so that only unaffected embryos are implanted (primary prevention).  
• Gene therapy seeks to correct or silence the underlying defective gene; although therapeutic, it is classified among genetic preventive / control measures because it tackles the causal mutation itself.  

Plasmapheresis, on the other hand, is an extracorporeal blood-cleaning procedure used mainly to treat autoimmune or toxic conditions (e.g., myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barré, hyperviscosity syndromes). It has no role in preventing genetic disorders, making it the only option that is not a preventive measure in this context.

Rationale:
A 2-year-old who is still unable to sit without support and shows generalized hypertonia must be assessed for cerebral palsy and for the specific motor syndrome involved. • Conductive hearing impairment (E) does not help classify the type of hypertonia.  

Hence, identifying choreoathetosis is the key element in the evaluation.

question: A 2-hour old newborn infant has bluish buccal mucosa with plethoric pulmonary vasculature on chest radiograph. Which of the following should be suspected?
model_prompt:

###Question: A 2-hour old newborn infant has bluish buccal mucosa with plethoric pulmonary vasculature on chest radiograph. Which of the following should be suspected?
###Options:
A.  Endocardiac cushion defect
B.  Tetralogy of Fallot
C.  Truncus arteriosus
D.  Transposition of the great arteries
E.  Patent ductus arteriosus

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Transposition of the great arteries (TGA)

Rationale:
• Early cyanosis (within the first few hours of life) points to a duct-dependent, cyanotic congenital heart disease.  
• On chest radiograph TGA characteristically shows increased or “plethoric” pulmonary vascular markings because the pulmonary circuit receives almost the entire systemic venous return via the transposed right ventricle.  
• Tetralogy of Fallot (option B) produces cyanosis with oligemic (decreased) lung fields.  
• Endocardial cushion defect and patent ductus arteriosus rarely cause immediate neonatal cyanosis, though they may give plethoric lungs.  
• Truncus arteriosus does give pulmonary plethora but cyanosis is usually milder and presentation is not typically within the first few hours.  

Thus a 2-hour-old infant with cyanosis and plethoric lung fields most strongly suggests Transposition of the great arteries.

question: An infant delivered at 40 weeks of gestation weighs 1.75kg, with body length of 50cm and occipitofrontal circumference of 35cm. The aetiologies of this condition include:

question: In Tetralogy of Fallot:

question: Common causes of post-neonatal seizure include the following:
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Common causes of post-neonatal seizure include the following:
###Options:
A.  Hypoglycaemia
B.  Hypertensive encephalopathy
C.  Hypocalcaemia
D.  Pyridoxine deficiency
E.  Hypoxic-Ischaemic Encephalopathy

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, B, C, and D

Rationale  
After the first 28 days of life (post-neonatal period), seizures are most often provoked by metabolic disturbances or acute systemic/neurological illnesses. Frequently encountered causes include:  

• Hypoglycaemia – low blood glucose is a well-recognised precipitator of infant and childhood convulsions.  
• Hypertensive encephalopathy – sudden, severe elevation of blood pressure may cause cerebral oedema and seizures at any age, including infancy.  
• Hypocalcaemia – calcium deficits are one of the commonest metabolic triggers for post-neonatal seizures.  
• Pyridoxine (vitamin B₆) deficiency/dependency – although uncommon, it is a classic metabolic cause of seizures in young infants and is routinely considered in the differential diagnosis; hence it is listed among the “common” metabolic causes in standard paediatric texts.  

Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE) (option E) is primarily a perinatal/neonatal problem; by the post-neonatal period it is no longer an acute cause of seizures, although remote HIE may leave a child epileptic. Therefore option E is not included among the common acute causes in the post-neonatal age group.

outputs:

Rationale: Pale clay-coloured stools with deep greenish jaundice indicate obstructive/acholuric jaundice. Lack of bile salts in the intestine prevents normal absorption of fats and the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). Consequently the child can develop clinical signs of deficiency of each of these vitamins:

• Vitamin D → defective bone mineralisation → rickets (Option A)  
• Vitamin A → ocular manifestations such as xerophthalmia (Option B)  
• Vitamin E → neurological problems, classically spinocerebellar degeneration causing ataxia (Option C)  
• Vitamin K → reduced synthesis of clotting factors → bleeding tendency (Option E)

Mouth ulcers (Option D) are usually related to deficiencies of water-soluble B-complex vitamins, whose absorption does not depend on bile, so this finding is not expected in purely obstructive jaundice.

question: Causes of false-negative tuberculin skin test include the following:

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Causes of false-negative tuberculin skin test include the following:
###Options:
A.  Hypokalaemia
B.  Malnutrition

D.  Measles
E.  BCG vaccination

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options:  
B. Malnutrition  
C. Corticosteroid therapy  
D. Measles  

Rationale: The tuberculin skin test depends on a competent cell-mediated (delayed-type hypersensitivity) immune response. Any condition that depresses this response can produce a falsely non-reactive (false-negative) test. Severe protein-calorie malnutrition, immunosuppression from systemic corticosteroids, and certain viral infections such as measles all diminish T-cell function and can therefore mask a true tuberculin reaction. Hypokalaemia does not affect delayed-type hypersensitivity, and prior BCG vaccination is more likely to give a false-positive, not a false-negative, result.

question: A 7-month old infant should be referred for neurodevelopmental assessment if he:
A: Is unable to reach out for objects
B: Is unable to control the neck
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 7-month old infant should be referred for neurodevelopmental assessment if he:
###Options:
A.  Is unable to reach out for objects
B.  Is unable to control the neck
C.  Demonstrates violent startle reflex
D.  Is unable to crawl
E.  Is unable to coo

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Is unable to control the neck  

Rationale: Good head/neck control is normally achieved by 3–4 months of age. If a 7-month-old infant still cannot hold the head steady, this is a clear red-flag for significant motor delay and warrants prompt neurodevelopmental assessment.  
• Reaching for objects typically appears by 4–5 months; lack of it at 7 months is concerning but slightly less specific than absent head control.  
• Crawling often begins around 8–10 months, so not crawling at 7 months is not yet abnormal.  
• Cooing starts at 2–3 months; absence at 7 months is worrisome for language delay but isolated speech delay without gross-motor delay is usually evaluated later.  
• An exaggerated startle may be seen in some normal infants; while it can suggest neurologic issues, it is not as definitive a red-flag as absent head control.  

Therefore, the most urgent and unequivocal indication for referral is inability to control the neck.

question: The following measures reduce serum potassium levels in the treatment of hyperkalaemia:
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: The following measures reduce serum potassium levels in the treatment of hyperkalaemia:
###Options:
A.  Calcium gluconate
B.  Sodium bicarbonate
C.  Salbutamol
D.  Insulin with Dextrose therapy
E.  Magnesium sulphate

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options:  
B. Sodium bicarbonate  
C. Salbutamol  
D. Insulin with Dextrose therapy  

Rationale:  
• Calcium gluconate (A) stabilises cardiac membranes and prevents arrhythmias, but it does not lower the serum potassium concentration.  
• Sodium bicarbonate (B) produces a systemic alkalosis that promotes intracellular shift of potassium, thereby lowering serum potassium.  
• Salbutamol (C), a β₂-adrenergic agonist, stimulates cellular Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity and moves potassium into cells, reducing serum levels.  
• Insulin given with dextrose (D) activates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and shifts potassium intracellularly, effectively lowering serum potassium.  
• Magnesium sulphate (E) is used mainly for torsades de pointes and eclampsia; it has no significant effect on serum potassium concentration.

question: Which of the following is not a common childhood hematologic disorder in Nigeria?

In Nigeria the common childhood haematologic problems are those driven by nutritional deficiency (iron-deficiency anaemia), endemic infections (malaria-induced haemolytic anaemia), hereditary red-cell enzymopathy (G6PD deficiency) and the sickle-cell gene (including HbSC disease). β-Thalassaemia, though frequent around the Mediterranean, Middle East and parts of Asia, is rarely encountered in West Africa; its carrier frequency in Nigeria is very low compared with the sickle-cell gene. question: Which of the following is not an inherited condition?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following is not an inherited condition? 





###Options:
A.  G6PD deficiency
B.  Beta Thalassemia
C.  Cleft lip and palate
D.  Klinefelter syndrome
E.  Cri-du-chat syndrome

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Klinefelter syndrome  

Rationale:  
• G-6-PD deficiency (X-linked recessive) and β-thalassaemia (autosomal recessive) are classical single-gene disorders that are transmitted from parent to child.  
• Cleft lip and palate show multifactorial (polygenic ± environmental) inheritance; although not Mendelian, the defect can run in families and the recurrence risk rises when an affected relative is present—hence it is still regarded as an inherited predisposition.  
• Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p deletion) can occasionally be passed on from a parent carrying a balanced translocation, so it may be inherited.  
• Klinefelter syndrome (47, XXY) results from a fresh meiotic nondisjunction event; affected males are usually infertile, and the extra X chromosome is not transmitted to offspring. Therefore it is generally a sporadic, non-inherited chromosomal abnormality.

question: Which of the following is not inherited in the X-linked dominant fashion?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following is not inherited in the X-linked dominant fashion? 





###Options:
A.  Fragile X syndrome
B.  Porphyria
C.  Vitamin D resistant rickets
D.  Alport syndrome
E.  Turner's syndrome

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: E.  Turner's syndrome  

Rationale  
• X-linked dominant disorders are produced by a pathogenic allele on the X chromosome that is expressed in heterozygous females and hemizygous males.  
  – Fragile X syndrome, vitamin-D-resistant (hypophosphataemic) rickets and the common form of Alport syndrome are classic examples.  
• Most porphyrias are inherited as autosomal disorders (usually autosomal-dominant); although a very rare X-linked form exists, “porphyria” in standard lists is not classified among the classical X-linked dominant traits.  
• Turner’s syndrome (45,X or mosaics) is not the result of a single-gene mutation transmitted through the germ line; it is produced by nondisjunction or loss of an X chromosome and therefore is not inherited at all, let alone by an X-linked dominant mechanism.

question: A 9-month old child weighs 9kg at the Child Survival Clinic. His road-to-health chart shows that he weighed 11kg at the last clinic visit two weeks ago. Which of the following is not likely to explain the situation?
model_prompt:

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 9-month old child weighs 9kg at the Child Survival Clinic. His road-to-health chart shows that he weighed 11kg at the last clinic visit two weeks ago. Which of the following is not likely to explain the situation?





###Options:
A.  Malaria Infection
B.  Diarrhoeal disease
C.  Vaccination
D.  Maternal deprivation

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C.  Vaccination

Rationale:
A loss of 2 kg (about 18 % of body weight) in only two weeks indicates significant acute or sub-acute nutritional/illness-related stress.

• Malaria infection ― acute febrile illness causing anorexia, increased metabolic demands and sometimes vomiting, all of which can lead to rapid weight loss.  
• Diarrhoeal disease ― fluid loss, malabsorption and reduced intake readily produce marked weight loss over a short period.  
• Maternal deprivation ― inadequate feeding or neglect can quickly translate into insufficient caloric intake and weight reduction in an infant.

Routine vaccination, however, is not associated with sustained anorexia or catabolism severe enough to account for a 2 kg loss in two weeks. At most it may cause a transient low-grade fever or mild malaise lasting a day or two without significant impact on weight. Therefore vaccination is the least likely explanation.

question: A 36-hour old newborn who was delivered in a church presents with fever, inability to suck, inability to cry, severe palor and hepatosplenomegaly. Which of the following is a likely aetiological agent of the illness?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 36-hour old newborn who was delivered in a church presents with fever, inability to suck, inability to cry, severe palor and hepatosplenomegaly. Which of the following is a likely aetiological agent of the illness?





###Options:
A.  Staphylococus epidermidis
B.  Lisseria monocytogenes
C.  Escherichia coli
D.  Group B Streptococcus

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B. Listeria monocytogenes

Rationale:  
• Early-onset neonatal sepsis (first 48 h of life) is usually acquired trans-placentally or during passage through the birth canal.  
• Listeria monocytogenes is a classic cause of very early-onset sepsis that may present with fever, poor feeding/sucking, lethargy, and prominent hepatosplenomegaly (part of the picture called “granulomatosis infantiseptica”). Pallor or anemia can also accompany this disseminated infection.  
• Group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli are also frequent causes of early-onset sepsis, but they characteristically produce fulminant pneumonia or septic shock rather than pronounced hepatosplenomegaly.  
• Staphylococcus epidermidis is generally a late-onset, catheter-associated pathogen in hospitalized neonates, not in a 36-hour-old baby delivered outside a hospital.  

Hence, the presentation most closely fits Listeria monocytogenes.

question: Features of infective endocarditis include the following:

###Question: Features of infective endocarditis include the following:

C.  Tender splenomegaly
D.  Murmur of valvular incompetence
E.  Continuous fever

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options:  A, B, C and D  

Rationale  
• Toxic look – Acute (and many sub-acute) cases of infective endocarditis present with an ill, toxic appearance.  
• Severe anaemia – A normocytic, normochromic “anaemia of chronic disease” is common and may be marked.  
• Tender splenomegaly – Immune-complex deposition and septic emboli can produce a palpable, often tender spleen.  
• Murmur of valvular incompetence – Infection damages valve leaflets, producing or worsening regurgitant (incompetent) murmurs.  
• Continuous fever – Although fever is the commonest feature, it is usually low-grade and remittent or swinging rather than truly continuous; hence option E is not characteristic.

question: A 10-year old boy presents with fever, generalized seizures and loss of consciousness. The cerebrospinal fluid shows protein of 128mg/dl, glucose of 11mg/dl compared to random blood glucose of 72mg/dl and marked pleocytosis. The likely complications arising from this condition include:
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 10-year old boy presents with fever, generalized seizures and loss of consciousness. The cerebrospinal fluid shows protein of 128mg/dl, glucose of 11mg/dl compared to random blood glucose of 72mg/dl and marked pleocytosis. The likely complications arising from this condition include:
###Options:
A.  Cerebral abscess
B.  Hydrocephalus
C.  Cranial nerve X palsy
D.  Febrile convulsion
E.  Subdural effusion

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, B and E  

Rationale  
The CSF picture (very high protein, very low glucose, marked pleocytosis) is typical of acute bacterial meningitis. Well-recognised complications of bacterial meningitis in children include:  
• Cerebral (brain) abscess formation – option A  
• Obstruction of CSF pathways causing communicating or obstructive hydrocephalus – option B  
• Collection of fluid/pus in the subdural space leading to subdural effusion or empyema – option E  

Cranial-nerve palsies may occur, but they most often involve nerves III, VI, VII or VIII, not the vagus (X), so option C is not typical. Seizures due to meningitis are common, but they are not labelled “febrile convulsions”, which are benign seizures occurring with fever in otherwise healthy children; therefore option D is not considered a complication of meningitis.

question: A 5-hour old infant presents with deep jaundice with serum bilirubin of 16mg/dl. Which of the following is appropriate?
A: Mother is likely to belong to Blood group AB
B: Haematocrit is expected to be greater than 55%
C: Mother is likely to belong to Blood group O
D: Reticulocyte count is expected to be less than 5%
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 5-hour old infant presents with deep jaundice with serum bilirubin of 16mg/dl. Which of the following is appropriate?





###Options:
A.  Mother is likely to belong to Blood group AB
B.  Haematocrit is expected to be greater than 55%
C.  Mother is likely to belong to Blood group O
D.  Reticulocyte count is expected to be less than 5%

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C.  Mother is likely to belong to Blood group O  

Rationale:  
• Jaundice that appears in the first few hours of life with a bilirubin level as high as 16 mg/dL is virtually always pathologic and most commonly the result of immune-mediated hemolysis (hemolytic disease of the newborn).  
• The commonest immune cause is ABO incompatibility. This typically occurs when the mother is blood group O (possesses IgG anti-A and anti-B antibodies that cross the placenta) and the infant is group A or B.  
• Hemolysis leads to early, rapid bilirubin rise, anemia (so the hematocrit is usually low, not >55 %), and a compensatory reticulocytosis (>5 %).  
• Therefore, option C is correct, while the other options are inconsistent with the expected findings in immune hemolysis.

question: Which of the following should be searched for in a child who receives systemic corticosteroid for a chronic respiratory disorder?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following should be searched for in a child who receives systemic corticosteroid for a chronic respiratory disorder?





###Options:
A.  Hypoglycaemia
B.  Wizened Old man facie
C.  Hypotensive crisis
D.  Skin striae

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Skin striae  

Rationale:  
Systemic corticosteroids taken for prolonged periods commonly produce Cushingoid changes caused by catabolism of connective tissue and altered fat distribution. Manifestations include truncal obesity, “moon face,” buffalo hump, thinning of skin, easy bruising and the appearance of violaceous striae (stretch-marks) over the abdomen, thighs and axillae. These should be looked for and documented in children on long-term oral steroids.

• Hypoglycaemia (A) is unlikely—glucocorticoids usually raise, not lower, blood glucose.  
• “Wizened old-man facie” (B) is not a recognised steroid effect; it describes certain congenital disorders.  
• Hypotensive crisis (C) relates to adrenal insufficiency; while possible after abrupt withdrawal, it is not something expected while the child is maintained on adequate systemic steroids.

question: Which of the following is not a likely aetiology in a child who makes 3.5ml/kg/hour of urine?

B.  Aldosteronism
C.  Diabetes insipidus
D.  Pyelonephritis

###Answer:

Correct option: D. Pyelonephritis  

Rationale  
Polyuria in children (urine output ≥ 2–3 mL/kg/h) results from conditions that impair renal concentrating ability or create water/osmotic diuresis.  
• Sickle-cell anaemia – causes hyposthenuria and an inability to concentrate urine, leading to true polyuria.  
• Aldosteronism – chronic hypokalaemia produced by excess aldosterone can induce a nephrogenic diabetes-insipidus picture with high-volume urine output.  
• Diabetes insipidus – classic cause of large-volume dilute urine.  
• Pyelonephritis – although it may cause urinary frequency, the voids are usually small; it does not characteristically produce a large total urine volume. Therefore it is the least likely aetiology of the documented 3.5 mL/kg/h urine output.

question: In kerosene poisoning:
A: School age children are most at risk
B: Cough and breathlessness are common manifestations
E: Mental retardation is a risk factor
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: In kerosene poisoning:
###Options:
A.  School age children are most at risk
B.  Cough and breathlessness are common manifestations
C.  Early gastric lavage is recommended
D.  Corticosteroid therapy is helpful
E.  Mental retardation is a risk factor

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options:  B and E  

Rationale  
• Accidental kerosene (hydrocarbon) ingestion occurs predominantly in toddlers and preschool children (<5 yr); therefore school-age children are not the main risk group → option A is incorrect.  
• The chief clinical picture is aspiration-induced chemical pneumonitis, presenting with cough, tachypnoea and breathlessness → option B is correct.  
• Gastric lavage or induction of emesis is contraindicated in simple kerosene ingestion because it greatly increases the risk of further aspiration → option C is incorrect.  
• Corticosteroids have not been shown to improve outcome in hydrocarbon pneumonitis and are not recommended → option D is incorrect.  
• Individuals with pica or intellectual/mental retardation have a higher likelihood of accidental or intentional ingestion of non-food substances, including kerosene; hence mental retardation is considered a risk factor → option E is correct.

question: A 3-year old child has a BMI of 38kg/m2. Which of the following is not likely to be associated with the condition?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 3-year old child has a BMI of 38kg/m2. Which of the following is not likely to be associated with the condition?





###Options:
A.  Cushing syndrome
B.  Prader Willi syndrome
C.  Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
D.  Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS)

Rationale  
• Cushing syndrome – excess glucocorticoids produce characteristic centripetal obesity even in very young children.  
• Prader-Willi syndrome – hypothalamic dysfunction causes hyperphagia and marked early-onset obesity; it is one of the commonest genetic causes of severe obesity in preschool children.  
• Congenital adrenal hyperplasia – children with classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency frequently become overweight or obese, partly because of chronic glucocorticoid treatment and altered energy metabolism.  
• Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome – the hallmark is generalized over-growth (macrosomia, organomegaly, macroglossia) with increased length and lean body mass; excess adiposity and severe obesity are not typical features. Thus BWS is the condition least likely to account for a BMI of 38 kg/m² in a 3-year-old child.

question: Which of the following is not associated with delayed puberty?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following is not associated with delayed puberty?





###Options:
A.  Klinefelter syndrome
B.  Noonan syndrome
C.  Sickle cell anaemia
D.  Hydrocephalus

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Hydrocephalus  

Rationale: 
Delayed puberty is commonly seen in disorders that impair gonadal function or result from chronic systemic disease.  
• Klinefelter syndrome (47, XXY) causes primary testicular failure, so boys often present with delayed or incomplete pubertal development.  
• Noonan syndrome is frequently accompanied by gonadal dysgenesis or cryptorchidism, leading to delayed pubertal onset.  
• Chronic illnesses such as sickle cell anaemia interfere with growth and sexual maturation, producing delayed puberty.  

Conversely, hydrocephalus is classically linked to precocious puberty because raised intracranial pressure or hypothalamic irritation can trigger early activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis; it is not a typical cause of delayed puberty. Hence option D is the one not associated with delayed puberty.

question: Important differential diagnoses in a child presenting with anasarca include:
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Important differential diagnoses in a child presenting with anasarca include:
###Options:
A.  Chronic congestive cardiac failure
B.  Severe hookworm infestation
C.  Nephrotic syndrome
D.  Chronic liver disease
E.  Severe malnutrition

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, C, D and E

Rationale  
Anasarca (generalized oedema) in a child usually results from conditions that lower plasma oncotic pressure or increase hydrostatic pressure/salt-water retention. The principal paediatric causes to be ruled out are:  
• Chronic congestive cardiac failure – raised systemic venous pressure produces generalized oedema.  
• Nephrotic syndrome – heavy proteinuria leads to hypo-albuminaemia and marked oedema.  
• Chronic liver disease – impaired albumin synthesis and portal hypertension give rise to ascites and anasarca.  
• Severe malnutrition (kwashiorkor) – protein deficiency causes profound hypo-albuminaemia and pitting oedema.  

Severe hookworm infestation (option B) mainly produces iron-deficiency anaemia; generalized oedema is not a usual presenting feature, so it is not regarded as a common differential diagnosis of anasarca.

question: Which of the following is the reason a child with rickets may present with inability to walk?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following is the reason a child with rickets may present with inability to walk?





###Options:
A.  Pathological fracture
B.  Cortical atrophy
C.  Osteoarthritis
D.  Severe hypotonia

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Severe hypotonia

Rationale:
Vitamin-D–deficient rickets produces chronic hypocalcaemia and phosphate depletion, leading not only to defective mineralisation of bone but also to proximal muscle weakness and marked hypotonia. The child becomes “floppy,” has difficulty sitting, standing or bearing weight, and therefore may be unable to walk. Pathological fractures can occur but are relatively uncommon and are not the usual initial cause of failure to walk. Cortical atrophy and osteoarthritis are not features of rickets in children.

question: Which of the following is a common clinical presentation of nutritional rickets?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following is a common clinical presentation of nutritional rickets?






###Options:
A.  Recurrent chest infection
B.  Chronic diarrhoea
C.  Osteonecrosis of femoral head
D.  Passage of frothy, dark urine

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Recurrent chest infection  

Rationale: Nutritional rickets is caused by vitamin D deficiency, leading to defective mineralisation of growing bone and cartilage. The softened rib cage and resultant chest wall deformity (e.g., “rachitic rosary,” Harrison’s sulcus) reduce pulmonary mechanics and predispose affected infants and toddlers to repeated lower-respiratory-tract infections, so recurrent chest infections are a common clinical presentation.  

• Chronic diarrhoea (option B) may contribute to malabsorption of vitamin D but is not a typical presenting feature of rickets itself.  
• Osteonecrosis of the femoral head (option C) is characteristic of conditions like Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease, not rickets.  
• Passage of frothy, dark urine (option D) suggests nephrotic or hemolytic disorders, unrelated to rickets.

question: Signs of severe dehydration include:
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Signs of severe dehydration include:
###Options:
A.  Loss of skin turgor
B.  Excessive thirst
C.  Delayed capillary refill
D.  Oliguria
E.  Absent lacrimation

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options: A, C, D, and E  

Rationale  
Severe dehydration (as seen in diarrhoeal illness, vomiting, etc.) produces objective signs of marked intravascular volume loss and tissue hypoperfusion:

• Loss of skin turgor – a skin pinch that returns very slowly (≥ 2 s) is a classic WHO/IMCI criterion for severe dehydration.  
• Delayed capillary refill – prolonged refill (> 2 s) reflects peripheral vasoconstriction and poor perfusion, typical of severe volume depletion.  
• Oliguria – the kidneys conserve water, so urine output falls markedly in severe dehydration.  
• Absent lacrimation – tear production stops as extracellular fluid is critically reduced, so no tears are seen when the child cries.

Excessive thirst (option B) is usually prominent in mild to moderate dehydration; once dehydration becomes severe, sensorium is often depressed and the patient may be unable or unwilling to drink.

question: Which of the following is not a typical laboratory finding in a 32-month old child presents with caput quadratum, wide anterior fontanelle and bilateral genu varum?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following is not a typical laboratory finding in a 32-month old child presents with caput quadratum, wide anterior fontanelle and bilateral genu varum?





###Options:
A.  Reduced serum alkaline phosphatase
B.  Reduced serum calcium
C.  Reduced serum phosphate
D.  Reduced 1,25, Dihydroxylcholecalciferol

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A.  Reduced serum alkaline phosphatase  

Rationale: Nutritional rickets is characterized by defective mineralization at the growth plate. The typical biochemical profile shows:
• Serum alkaline phosphatase – markedly elevated (released from hypertrophic osteoblasts trying to mineralize bone).  
• Serum calcium – low or low-normal (because of vitamin-D–dependent malabsorption).  
• Serum phosphate – low (due to secondary hyperparathyroidism causing phosphaturia).  
• 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol – often low or inappropriately normal when vitamin-D substrate (25-OHD) is deficient.

Therefore a “reduced serum alkaline phosphatase” is NOT a typical finding in rickets, making option A the correct choice.

Rationale:
Juvenile (childhood) hypothyroidism is characterized by slowed metabolic and growth processes. Typical findings include:

• Bradycardia due to reduced basal metabolic rate.  
• Hyperprolactinemia with possible galactorrhea because elevated TRH can stimulate prolactin release.

###Answer:

Rationale:  
Early indicators of cerebral palsy are abnormalities that can be detected during the first months of life, before definite motor delay is evident.

• Scissoring of the lower limbs when the infant is lifted (D) reflects early adductor hypertonia and is a classic early sign of spastic CP.  

• A definite hand preference before about 18 months of age (E) suggests unilateral motor impairment (often spastic hemiplegia) and is regarded as an early warning sign.  

Sialorrhoea (A) results from oromotor dysfunction but typically becomes apparent later, while sensorineural deafness (B) is not a characteristic manifestation of cerebral palsy.

question: Which of the following is not a physiologic effect of thyroxine?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following is not a physiologic effect of thyroxine?





###Options:
A.  Stimulation of lipogenesis
B.  Increase in protein breakdown
C.  Promotion of skeletal growth
D.  Increase in carbohydrate absorption

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A.  Stimulation of lipogenesis  

Rationale: Thyroid hormones (T₄/T₃) raise basal metabolic rate and generally favor catabolic processes: they enhance carbohydrate absorption from the gut, accelerate protein turnover with a net increase in protein breakdown, and are essential for normal skeletal growth and maturation. In lipid metabolism, thyroid hormones promote lipolysis and fatty-acid oxidation and lower circulating cholesterol; they do not stimulate lipogenesis. Hence “stimulation of lipogenesis” is not a physiologic effect of thyroxine.

question: Which of the following should a 36-hour old infant with elevated TSH, depressed T3 and T4 should be examined for?

###Answer:

Correct option: C. Prolonged icterus

Rationale:  
An elevated TSH with low T3 and T4 in a 36-hour-old infant points to congenital (primary) hypothyroidism. Typical early clinical manifestations of neonatal hypothyroidism include lethargy, poor feeding, constipation, hoarse cry, large fontanelles, umbilical hernia, and especially prolonged unconjugated jaundice (prolonged neonatal icterus) due to reduced hepatic glucuronyl-transferase activity. Diaphoresis, a bounding dorsalis pedis pulse, or a high-pitched cry are not characteristic findings of hypothyroidism; in fact diaphoresis and bounding pulses suggest hypermetabolic or cardiovascular states, and a high-pitched cry is more often associated with neurologic disorders. Therefore, the infant should be examined for prolonged icterus.

question: Which of the following investigations is not relevant in a child newly diagnosed with diabetes mellitus?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following investigations is not relevant in a child newly diagnosed with diabetes mellitus?






###Options:
A.  Abdominal ultrasonography
B.  Urine microscopy, culture and sensitivity
C.  Transcranial doppler scan
D.  Fasting lipid profile

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option:  
C. Transcranial doppler scan  

Rationale:  
At the time of first diagnosis of childhood diabetes mellitus (usually type 1), baseline work-up is aimed at (1) confirming the diagnosis, (2) detecting intercurrent infection or ketoacidosis, and (3) identifying metabolic risk factors that will influence future management.  
• Urine microscopy, culture and sensitivity (Option B) is relevant to detect urinary tract infection, which can precipitate or complicate diabetic ketoacidosis.  
• Fasting lipid profile (Option D) is recommended soon after metabolic control is achieved, or at least by early adolescence, to establish cardiovascular risk.  
• Abdominal ultrasonography (Option A) may be ordered in selected cases—for example, when secondary diabetes (pancreatic disease, cystic fibrosis, etc.) is suspected, or to look for associated autoimmune conditions such as celiac disease with hepatobiliary involvement.  

Transcranial Doppler scanning (Option C) is used mainly for cerebrovascular risk assessment in disorders like sickle-cell disease; it has no role in the initial evaluation of a child with newly diagnosed diabetes. Hence, it is the investigation that is not relevant here.

question: Which of the following characterises Diabetic Ketoacidosis?
model_prompt:

###Question: Which of the following characterises Diabetic Ketoacidosis?

A.  Polydipsia
B.  Cheyne-Stokes respiration
C.  Kussmaul respiration
D.  Progressive weight loss

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Kussmaul respiration  

Rationale:  
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) produces a profound metabolic (high-anion-gap) acidosis. To compensate, patients develop deep, rapid, “air-hunger” breathing—classically called Kussmaul respirations. While polydipsia (A) and weight loss (D) are common in uncontrolled diabetes, they are not distinctive for DKA itself. Cheyne-Stokes respiration (B) is a cyclic breathing pattern seen in severe heart failure or neurologic disorders, not in DKA. Thus Kussmaul respiration uniquely characterises DKA.

question: Which of the following is not a known to be associated with Diabetes mellitus?
model_prompt:

###Question: Which of the following is not a known to be associated with Diabetes mellitus?

B.  Diazoxide therapy
C.  Sickle cell disease
D.  Haemochromatosis

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Sickle cell disease

Rationale:
• Cushing syndrome – excess cortisol causes marked insulin resistance and is a well-recognised cause of secondary (steroid-induced) diabetes mellitus.  
• Diazoxide therapy – Diazoxide inhibits pancreatic β-cell insulin release and can induce persistent hyperglycaemia; diabetes may develop during or after prolonged use.  
• Haemochromatosis – iron deposition in pancreatic β-cells leads to “bronze diabetes,” making diabetes a classic manifestation of this disorder.  
• Sickle cell disease – although it has numerous systemic complications, it does not characteristically increase the risk of diabetes mellitus, nor is diabetes a recognised feature of the disease.

Hence, sickle cell disease is the condition in the list that is not known to be associated with diabetes mellitus.

question: Signs of left-sided pleural effusion include:
B: Reduced chest excursion on the left
C: Dull percussion notes on the left
D: Hyper-resonant percussion notes on the right
E: Increased vocal resonance on the left
model_prompt:

###Question: Signs of left-sided pleural effusion include:
###Options:
A.  Tracheal deviation to the left
B.  Reduced chest excursion on the left
C.  Dull percussion notes on the left
D.  Hyper-resonant percussion notes on the right
E.  Increased vocal resonance on the left

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct options:  
B and C  

Rationale:  
A pleural effusion occupies space in the pleural cavity, mechanically restricting movement of the affected hemithorax and blunting transmission of sound. Typical physical findings on the side of the effusion therefore include:  

• Reduced chest expansion (option B) because the fluid-filled hemithorax cannot inflate normally.  
• Dull or “stony dull” percussion note over the fluid (option C) because liquid transmits percussion waves poorly compared with aerated lung.  

Other options are incorrect:  
A. Large effusions push the mediastinum away, so a left-sided effusion would deviate the trachea to the right, not the left.  
D. Hyper-resonance is produced by excess air (e.g., pneumothorax), not fluid.  
E. Vocal (and tactile) resonance is decreased, not increased, over an effusion because the fluid dampens sound conduction.

question: A 36-hour old newborn who was delivered in a church presents with fever, inability to suck, inability to cry, severe pallor and hepatosplenomegaly. Which of the following is a likely aetiological agent of the illness?

###Question: A 36-hour old newborn who was delivered in a church presents with fever, inability to suck, inability to cry, severe pallor and hepatosplenomegaly. Which of the following is a likely aetiological agent of the illness?

B.  Listeria monocytogenes
C.  Escherichia coli
D.  Group B Streptococcus

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. Group B Streptococcus

Rationale:
• Early-onset neonatal sepsis (within the first 72 h of life) is almost always acquired during labour or delivery, especially when hygienic conditions are poor (e.g., home or church delivery).  
• Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae) is the single most common cause of early-onset sepsis worldwide. Typical features include temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy/poor cry, pallor, hepatosplenomegaly and rapid clinical deterioration—all seen in this infant.  
• Escherichia coli and Listeria monocytogenes are also recognised pathogens, but they are less common than GBS in term infants.  
• Staphylococcus epidermidis predominantly causes late-onset, hospital-acquired infections related to indwelling devices, not early-onset sepsis in a term neonate.

Therefore, Group B Streptococcus is the most likely etiological agent in this scenario.

question: Which of the following characterises physiologic jaundice in a term infant?
B: Peak of bilirubin occurs at 10 days of age
model_prompt:

###Question: Which of the following characterises physiologic jaundice in a term infant?




###Options:
A.  Onset at 20 hours of age
B.  Peak of bilirubin occurs at 10 days of age
C.  Peak serum bilirubin not exceeding 12mg/dl
D.  Phototherapy is a required intervention

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: C. Peak serum bilirubin not exceeding 12 mg/dl

Rationale:
Physiologic (normal) jaundice in a healthy term newborn:
• Appears after the first 24 hours of life (typically days 2–3).  
• Peaks between days 3 and 5 with a total serum bilirubin that generally does not exceed about 12 mg/dl (205 µmol/L).  
• Declines and usually resolves by day 7–10 without treatment.  
• Because bilirubin levels stay in a safe range, phototherapy or other interventions are usually unnecessary.

Option A (onset at 20 hours) and option B (peak at 10 days) describe patterns suggestive of pathologic jaundice. Option D is incorrect because routine phototherapy is not required in physiologic jaundice.

question: A 7-month old infant who was delivered at term has a head circumference of 39cm. What is the best explanation to give the parents?
B: The child may have cortical atrophy

###Question: A 7-month old infant who was delivered at term has a head circumference of 39cm. What is the best explanation to give the parents?

D.  The child may have anencephaly

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B.  The child may have cortical atrophy  

Rationale:  
• A term neonate’s average head circumference (HC) is ≈35 cm.  
• HC grows ~2 cm/month for the first 3 months and ~1 cm/month for the next 3 months, reaching ≈45 cm by 7 months.  
• An HC of 39 cm at 7 months is well below the 3rd percentile, indicating microcephaly.  
• Microcephaly is commonly due to reduced brain growth or cortical atrophy; thus option B best explains the small HC.  
• Hydrocephalus (option C) causes an enlarged head, not a small one, and anencephaly (option D) is incompatible with survival beyond the neonatal period.  
Therefore, cortical atrophy-associated microcephaly is the most likely explanation.

question: A 10-year old child presents with fever, vomiting and frequent stooling. His pulse rate is 144/minute and thready in nature while the blood pressure is 45/30mmHg. Which of the following is most desired in the management of the child?
D: IV Full Strength Darrows 30ml/kg over 30 minutes
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: A 10-year old child presents with fever, vomiting and frequent stooling. His pulse rate is 144/minute and thready in nature while the blood pressure is 45/30mmHg. Which of the following is most desired in the management of the child?



###Options:
A.  IV 10%Dextrose-in-Water 4ml/kg fast
B.  IV Hartmann's Solution 30ml/kg over 30 minutes
C.  IV Digoxin 0.02mg/kg fast
D.  IV Full Strength Darrows 30ml/kg over 30 minutes

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: B

Rationale:
The child is in hypovolaemic (hypotensive) shock from acute fluid losses due to vomiting and profuse diarrhoea. The first-line, lifesaving intervention in paediatric hypovolaemic shock is a rapid bolus of an isotonic crystalloid (0.9 % saline or Ringer’s lactate/Hartmann’s solution) at 20–30 mL /kg, given as fast as possible (typically within 15–30 minutes), and repeated as needed while monitoring the pulse and blood pressure.

• Option A (10 % dextrose in water) is hypotonic and will not adequately expand the intravascular space; it risks causing hyponatraemia.  
• Option C (digoxin) has no role in hypovolaemic shock.  
• Option D (full-strength Darrow’s) is hypertonic, potassium-containing, and inappropriate for rapid volume resuscitation.

Therefore, IV Hartmann’s solution 30 mL /kg over about 30 minutes (option B) is the most appropriate initial management.

question: A 4-year old presents with frequent generalised spasms and muscle rigidity of 12 hours duration. Which of the following is not useful in the evaluation of the child?
A: History of recent inability to open the mouth
D: History of recent inability to close the eyes

C.  Presence of diaphoresis
D.  History of recent inability to close the eyes

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: D. History of recent inability to close the eyes  

Rationale:  
In a child who presents with generalised spasms and rigidity, tetanus is a prime diagnostic consideration. Features helpful in evaluating possible tetanus include:  
• Trismus (inability to open the mouth) – a classic early sign.  
• Possible portals of entry such as chronic suppurative otitis media (chronic ear discharge) in otogenic tetanus.  
• Autonomic over-activity, which may manifest as diaphoresis, tachycardia, labile blood pressure, etc.  

Inability to close the eyes (lagophthalmos) is typically associated with a lower motor neurone facial-nerve palsy and is not a recognised feature of tetanus; therefore it is not useful in the evaluation of this presentation.

question: Causes of haematuria in a 2-year old child include:
model_prompt:

###Question: Causes of haematuria in a 2-year old child include:

B.  Schistosoma japonicum infestation
C.  Cyclophosphamide therapy
D.  Minimal change disease
E.  Rifampicin therapy

###Answer:

Correct options: A and C  

Rationale  
• Urethritis – Inflammation or infection of the urethra can produce blood at the beginning of micturition even in very young children, so it is a recognised cause of haematuria in a 2-year-old.  

• Cyclophosphamide therapy – The drug’s metabolite (acrolein) can provoke haemorrhagic cystitis, giving rise to frank haematuria at any age, including toddlers who receive the drug for oncologic or rheumatologic indications.  

• Schistosoma japonicum (option B) mainly involves the mesenteric/portal venous system and produces intestinal and hepatic disease; urinary haematuria is characteristic of Schistosoma haematobium, not S. japonicum.  

• Minimal-change disease (option D) classically produces heavy proteinuria with little or no haematuria; its presence would be atypical, especially as a presenting feature.  

• Rifampicin (option E) can turn urine orange-red, but that discoloration is due to the drug itself, not blood, and true haematuria is not a recognised side-effect.

question: Which of the following is valid about a 50 hour old infant presents with bilaterally profuse, purulent eye discharges?
A: Gentamicin eye drop within 12 hours of birth is recommended prophylaxis
B: Chlamydia tracomatis is the likely aetiology
D: History of fever will be unusual
model_prompt:

###Question: Which of the following is valid about a 50 hour old infant presents with bilaterally profuse, purulent eye discharges?

B.  Chlamydia tracomatis is the likely aetiology

###Answer:

Correct option: C

Rationale  
A 50-hour-old baby with a copious, bilateral, purulent discharge most characteristically has gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum.

• Prophylaxis for ophthalmia neonatorum is classically 1 % silver nitrate, 0.5 % erythromycin or 1 % tetracycline ointment. Gentamicin drops are not recommended for routine prophylaxis (so A is wrong).  
• Chlamydial conjunctivitis usually appears later (5-14 days after birth) and the discharge is initially watery, so Chlamydia trachomatis is not the likely aetiology here (B is wrong).  
• Untreated gonococcal infection can rapidly extend to involve the cornea, cause ulceration, perforation and even progress to panophthalmitis with loss of the eye; hence panophthalmitis is a recognised (expected if untreated) complication (C is correct).  
• Gonococcal disease may disseminate and neonates can have systemic signs including fever; therefore absence of fever is not a reliable feature, making statement D incorrect.

Thus, the only valid statement is C.

question: A 9-year old child presents at CHER with history of dog bite which occurred two days prior. Which of the following is not important in the evaluation of the child?

For deciding the management of a dog-bite victim we must obtain information that will alter specific prophylactic measures:

question: A 4-year old presents with bilateral, itchy, papular lesions in the inter-digital webs. Which of these complications is expected?

question: A 7-year old presents with fever and multiple boils on the skin. Which of the following full blood count findings is helpful?

C.  Neutrophils - 72%

###Answer:

Correct option: B.  Total WBC – 3,500/mm³

Rationale:  
Recurrent or multiple skin boils (usually staphylococcal infections) in a child raise the suspicion of an underlying defect in neutrophil number or function, because neutrophils are the primary defence against pyogenic bacteria. A total white-cell count of 3,500/mm³ is distinctly low for a 7-year-old (normal ≈ 5,000–12,000/mm³) and strongly suggests neutropenia or bone-marrow suppression, both of which predispose to recurrent bacterial skin infections. The other listed values (PCV 37 %, neutrophils 72 % of a low total, platelets 176 × 10⁹/L) are within, or close to, the expected range and add little diagnostic value in this clinical context.

question: Which of the following is not an anti-infective property of human milk?
model_prompt:
###Instruction: The following are multiple choice questions (MCQs).
You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: Which of the following is not an anti-infective property of human milk? 





###Options:
A.  Casein
B.  Lactobacillus bifidus
C.  Lactoferrin
D.  Interferons

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A. Casein  

Rationale: Human milk contains several constituents that actively protect the infant from infection. These include:

• Lactobacillus bifidus–promoting factors that encourage colonization by this protective organism in the gut, inhibiting growth of pathogenic bacteria.  
• Lactoferrin–binds iron, depriving many bacteria of the iron needed for their growth and exerting direct antimicrobial effects.  
• Interferons–cytokines present in breast milk that have antiviral activity.

Casein, on the other hand, is the principal nutritional protein in milk; its primary roles are to supply amino acids and aid in mineral absorption, not to provide direct anti-infective or antimicrobial activity. Hence, casein is not considered one of the anti-infective factors of human milk.

question: The chest radiograph of a 3-year old child shows cardiomegaly. What does that radiographic finding imply?
B: Increased convexity of right heart border suggests RVH
C: Displaced apex inferio-laterally is a pointer to LVH
D: Flattening of left upper cardiac border is a sign of LAH
model_prompt:

You should directly answer the question by choosing the correct option and then provide a rationale for your answer. 

###Question: The chest radiograph of a 3-year old child shows cardiomegaly. What does that radiographic finding imply?





###Options:
A.  A cardio-thoracic ratio of 0.54:1.
B.  Increased convexity of right heart border suggests RVH
C.  Displaced apex inferio-laterally is a pointer to LVH
D.  Flattening of left upper cardiac border is a sign of LAH

###Answer:
outputs:
Correct option: A  

Rationale:  
On a plain post-ero-anterior chest radiograph cardiomegaly is defined by an increased cardio-thoracic (C/T) ratio.  
• In infants (< 2 yr) a C/T ratio up to 60 % is still normal.  
• In children older than 2 yr and in adults the upper limit of normal is about 50 %.  

Therefore, in a 3-year-old child a C/T ratio of 0.54 : 1 (54 %) exceeds the normal limit and by itself is enough to label the heart as enlarged (cardiomegaly).  
Findings such as increased right-heart border convexity, apex displacement, or left upper border flattening refer to hypertrophy/enlargement of specific chambers (RV, LV, LA respectively) and cannot be inferred merely from the statement “cardiomegaly.”

question: Which of the following will not cause central cyanosis?

###Question: Which of the following will not cause central cyanosis?
